In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL). Using $\pi_{0.5}$ and a LEAP hand, we evaluate five fine-tuning recipes across two simulation tasks using only a handful of demonstrations. Our empirical analysis yields three key insights: (1) SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, meaning the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective to steer; (2) freezing the vision-language model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert produces the most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements; and (3) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the least steerable approach. Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how to adapt Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to dexterous multi-finger hands using SFT and diffusion-steering RL, finding that freezing the VLM and training only the action expert works best while SFT rollout success poorly predicts post-RL performance.
AI.motivation: Most VLA datasets use parallel-jaw grippers, making adaptation to dexterous multi-finger hands difficult, especially when teleoperation demonstrations are scarce.
AI.method: Using pi_0.5 and a LEAP hand across two simulation tasks with few demonstrations, the authors evaluate five fine-tuning recipes combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL).
AI.result: SFT success correlates poorly with post-DSRL success, freezing the VLM while fully training the action expert yields the most steerable policy for both in-distribution and out-of-distribution placements, and LoRA is the least steerable recipe.
AI.conclusion: Adapting VLAs to dexterous manipulation is best achieved by freezing the VLM, fully tuning the action expert, and avoiding SFT rollout success for checkpoint selection.

title: Evaluating Governed LLM-Driven ML Experimentation: Lifecycle, Provenance, and Failure Metrics
comment: 22 pages. Presented at the KDD 2026 Workshop on Evaluation and Trustworthiness of Agentic AI (ETAAI; non-archival). Code and trial ledgers: this https URL (DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24174991)
summary: Autonomous agents that run ML experiments are usually judged by the best score they reach. That score says nothing about how it was reached: whether the agent stayed within the files it was allowed to edit, whether failed trials were kept or silently dropped, and whether each keep or discard decision can be traced to its evidence. We propose evaluating such systems on their experimental process as well as their outcome, and we build a governed harness that makes this possible. A control plane, not the LLM that proposes changes, owns each trial's lifecycle, checks its edit scope, decides keep or discard, and appends one record per trial to an append-only ledger. Governance metrics such as the invalid-action rate, the repeated-bad rate and provenance completeness are computed from that ledger. Across six ML tasks, from synthetic logistic regression to language-model training, and 1,445 trials, the same contract applied unchanged. The ledger exposed failures that a task score hides: a no-memory arm in which all 120 trials failed, a benchmark adapter whose bounded proposals ran out, and a reset failure that reproducibility hashes revealed, after which the affected campaigns were rerun. In a matched counterfactual, a loop that logs only successful trials left no record of 43 of 50 trials, while the governed ledger recorded all 50. Memory ablations show that memory's effect on repeated bad proposals depends on the task. We release the ledgers of all 1,445 trials, so that every number reported for them can be recomputed.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes evaluating autonomous ML experimentation agents on process governance alongside task scores, introducing a control-plane ledger that exposes hidden failures across 1,445 trials.
AI.motivation: Autonomous ML experiment agents are typically judged only by best achieved score, hiding whether they respected edit scopes, silently dropped failed trials, or made traceable keep/discard decisions.
AI.method: The authors build a governed harness where a control plane—not the LLM—manages trial lifecycles, enforces edit scopes, decides keep/discard, and logs every trial to an append-only ledger to compute governance metrics (invalid-action rate, repeated-bad rate, provenance completeness).
AI.result: Across six ML tasks and 1,445 trials, the ledger exposed failures hidden by task scores (including a 120-trial all-failure arm and a reset failure), whereas a success-only logger missed 43 of 50 trials in a matched counterfactual.
AI.conclusion: Process-level governance ledgers are essential for auditing, reproducing, and diagnosing autonomous LLM-driven ML experimentation.

title: Measuring the Conservatism of Latent Safety Filters for World Models
summary: A latent safety filter decides from the latent of a world model whether a planned action is safe. Conformal calibration sets the threshold of the filter so that it accepts an unsafe action only with a small probability. However, the filter can still be conservative and refuse many safe actions, depending on the latent. To measure the conservatism that a latent forces on the filter, we group similar latents and actions into cells. A filter that gives one decision per cell can refuse the unsafe transitions of a cell only by refusing the safe ones in it as well. We call the share of safe transitions that lie in such cells the overlap. We prove that the overlap is the minimum share of safe transitions that such a filter has to refuse in order to accept no unsafe transition in the data. Both the overlap and the conformal calibration can be applied to any latent. We use this to compare three existing designs, in which the safety labels train a classifier on top of the world model, the world model itself, or a separate encoder beside it. In a visual navigation task, the separate encoder has the lowest overlap, and at the same conformal level its filter refuses the fewest safe actions and lets the planner reach the most goals of the three.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the "overlap" metric to measure the minimum conservatism forced by a world model's latent representation on conformal safety filters, showing a separate safety encoder minimizes unnecessary refusals.
AI.motivation: Conformal calibration ensures latent safety filters rarely accept unsafe actions, but a poor latent representation can force the filter to be overly conservative and refuse many safe actions.
AI.method: The authors group similar latents and actions into cells, define "overlap" as the share of safe transitions in cells containing unsafe transitions, prove it bounds minimum safe-action refusals, and compare three safety-filter designs on visual navigation.
AI.result: In visual navigation, training a separate encoder beside the world model achieves the lowest overlap, refuses the fewest safe actions at the same conformal level, and enables the planner to reach the most goals compared to world-model or classifier-on-top designs.
AI.conclusion: The overlap metric provides a general, representation-level diagnostic for comparing and designing less conservative latent safety filters.

title: MoMoVL: Modality-Aware Adaptive Compression for On-Device Sparsely-Activated Vision-Language Models
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures, Accepted at WSDM 2027 Findings
summary: The rise of the agentic web has been accompanied by growing demand for on-device Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that perform diverse cross-modal web tasks with enhanced privacy and reduced latency. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are widely adopted in modern VLMs for compute-efficient scalability, yet their multi-expert architecture poses deployment challenges due to substantial memory demands. Mixed-precision quantization is an effective compression technique that reduces bit-widths while adapting to the heterogeneous hardware budgets of edge devices, particularly well-suited for MoE due to its inherent structural sparsity, which causes imbalanced importance among experts. While prior work has applied quantization for efficient MoE inference at the edge, we point out that in MoE-based VLMs, the modality-specific characteristics of visual and text tokens further impact expert quantization. To address this issue, we present MoMoVL, a modality-aware adaptive compression framework for MoE-based VLMs that brings vision-language inference within reach of on-device resource budgets. Motivated by our empirical findings on modality-induced disparities across experts, MoMoVL jointly exploits the per-expert activation profile and per-modality quantization sensitivity to guide bit-width assignment. Experimental results show that MoMoVL improves the accuracy-compression trade-off relative to state-of-the-art mixed-precision baselines and reduces memory footprint by up to 15.44% with a modest drop in accuracy over its uniform-precision baseline. Our code and data are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper presents MoMoVL, a modality-aware mixed-precision quantization framework for MoE-based vision-language models that reduces memory footprint by up to 15.44% while improving the accuracy-compression trade-off.
AI.motivation: Deploying Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) VLMs on edge devices is constrained by high memory demands, and existing MoE quantization methods overlook how visual and text tokens induce different expert quantization sensitivities.
AI.method: MoMoVL jointly uses per-expert activation profiles and per-modality quantization sensitivity to guide mixed-precision bit-width assignment across experts.
AI.result: MoMoVL outperforms state-of-the-art mixed-precision baselines in accuracy-compression trade-off and reduces memory footprint by up to 15.44% with only a modest accuracy drop relative to a uniform-precision baseline.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for modality-specific expert sensitivity enables more effective mixed-precision compression for on-device MoE VLMs.

title: Do 3D Point Representations Encode Architectural Functions? Probing Supervised and Pretrained Models on Urban Facades
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Physical World AI: Geometry, Characteristics, and Multimodal Sensing
summary: Semantic labels say what a building element is, not what it does: two identical-looking windows on one facade may be operable or fixed, a column may carry load or only decorate. We ask whether 3D point representations encode such architectural function. On 22 mobile-LiDAR buildings with 15 functional attributes per element, we hold out entire buildings and compare hand-crafted descriptors, networks trained from scratch and frozen self-supervised point transformers. Descriptors and frozen features are read by the same linear layer. No network trained from scratch, from PointNet to a 108M-parameter PTv3, clearly exceeds the descriptors (0.610 mAP on functionally ambiguous elements), whereas frozen Utonia reaches 0.732. Random-weight controls of the same architectures (0.649 and 0.652) attribute the gain to pretraining (Utonia: +0.080, 95% building interval [+0.035, +0.124]). Pretrained features improve at every tested number of labelled buildings while descriptors and random features plateau, and, in the configurations we tested, fine-tuning erodes the benefit: at today's data scale, function is better read from pretrained representations than learned from scratch.

AI.tldr: This paper probes whether 3D point representations encode architectural functions on urban facades, finding that frozen self-supervised point transformers outperform networks trained from scratch and hand-crafted descriptors.
AI.motivation: Semantic labels identify what a building element is (e.g., window or column) rather than its architectural function (e.g., operable vs. fixed, load-bearing vs. decorative), and it is unknown whether 3D point models capture such function.
AI.method: On 22 mobile-LiDAR buildings with 15 functional attributes and held-out building splits, the authors compare linear probes on hand-crafted descriptors, networks trained from scratch (PointNet to 108M-parameter PTv3), random-weight controls, and frozen self-supervised point transformers (Utonia).
AI.result: Networks trained from scratch do not clearly beat descriptors (0.610 mAP on functionally ambiguous elements), whereas frozen Utonia reaches 0.732 mAP (+0.080 over random-weight controls), improves with more labeled buildings, and outperforms fine-tuned variants.
AI.conclusion: At current data scales, architectural function is better read out from frozen self-supervised 3D representations than learned from scratch or fine-tuned.

title: STORM: A Lightweight Structure-Free Model for Binding Affinity Prediction
summary: Accurately predicting a small molecule's binding affinity to a protein, a critical task in drug discovery, remains challenging. Physics-based approaches like free-energy perturbation (FEP) have very high computational costs and require expert setup. Recent machine learning--based cofolding models have reported accuracy approaching that of FEP---and at least one of them, Boltz-2, has already been widely adopted for affinity prediction---but they remain expensive for large computational screens and even more expensive for retraining on newly collected experimental data. To address these challenges, we introduce STORM: Similarity Transfer from Observed Reference Molecules. STORM is a fast, simple machine learning model that ensembles many small model fusions of diverse protein and molecule representations for binding affinity prediction. Trained on the same data, STORM matches or exceeds the accuracy of Boltz-2 on multiple evaluation datasets, while delivering a speed improvement of over five orders of magnitude for both inference and training. Our results also suggest opportunities to substantially improve affinity prediction accuracy by integrating historical experimental affinity data with structural and biophysical information.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces STORM, a lightweight, structure-free machine learning ensemble for protein-ligand binding affinity prediction that matches or exceeds Boltz-2 accuracy while running over five orders of magnitude faster.
AI.motivation: Physics-based free-energy perturbation (FEP) and ML cofolding models like Boltz-2 are too computationally expensive for large-scale virtual screening and rapid retraining on new experimental data.
AI.method: STORM ensembles many small model fusions of diverse protein and small-molecule representations trained on historical experimental affinity data without requiring 3D structure prediction.
AI.result: Trained on the same data, STORM matches or exceeds Boltz-2 accuracy across multiple evaluation datasets while achieving over five orders of magnitude speedup in both training and inference.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight structure-free ensembles offer a practical, high-throughput alternative to cofolding models for binding affinity prediction.

title: Continual Tool-Space Extension Learning for Multimodal Agents
summary: Multimodal agents largely rely on generic tools such as cropping, search, and code execution, leaving specialist vision models outside their tool space. However, bringing such a model into an already trained agent is not straightforward. The challenge is to learn each new tool efficiently while retaining the ability to use existing ones. This work proposes COTEX, continual tool-space extension learning, that adds new tools at efficient adapter-level cost. COTEX locates two sets of parameter directions; one triggers a tool call and thereby opens a multi-turn reasoning trajectory, while the other determines which tool is chosen. The adapter of a new tool is restricted to the calling directions that leave earlier tool choices unaffected by orthogonal constraint. We further introduce a protocol that converts specialist models' existing task-specific annotations into verified tool-use trajectories. Experiments on two representative agents and three specialist tools show gains on ten vision-language benchmarks, with at most a 0.3-point drop on existing tools.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes COTEX, a continual tool-space extension framework that adds specialist vision tools to multimodal agents via orthogonally constrained adapters without degrading existing tool use.
AI.motivation: Multimodal agents rely mostly on generic tools, and adding specialist vision models to an already trained agent risks disrupting its ability to select and use existing tools.
AI.method: COTEX identifies parameter directions for triggering tool calls versus selecting specific tools, constrains new tool adapters to calling directions orthogonal to existing tool choices, and converts specialist annotations into verified tool-use trajectories.
AI.result: Evaluated on two agents and three specialist tools across ten vision-language benchmarks, COTEX improves task performance while limiting performance drops on existing tools to at most 0.3 points.
AI.conclusion: Orthogonal adapter constraints enable efficient, continual integration of specialist vision tools into multimodal agents without catastrophic forgetting.

title: RePlan-VLA: Progress-Aware Replanning for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: Apoorva Vashisth and Manav Kulshrestha contributed equally to this work. Prof. Zachary Kingston and Prof. Aniket Bera jointly advised this work
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet their performance often degrades on long-horizon tasks that require multiple interdependent manipulations. Instead of burdening the VLA policies with long-horizon reasoning, memory, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery, we argue for leveraging their short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework. To this end, we introduce \textnormal{\textbf{RePlan-VLA}}, a VLA-agnostic framework that translates a VLA's short-horizon capabilities into reliable long-horizon execution. RePlan-VLA explicitly monitors the robot's motion for progress evaluation, and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes. We preserve the underlying VLA policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning. Experiments on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN benchmarks show an improvement of 21.9% and 10.4% in success rate over the next strongest baseline. We also validate our approach for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RePlan-VLA, a training-free, VLA-agnostic framework that monitors robot motion progress and adaptively replans long-horizon manipulation tasks, boosting success rates on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN.
AI.motivation: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models degrade on long-horizon tasks with interdependent steps when burdened with long-horizon reasoning, memory, and error recovery inside the policy itself.
AI.method: RePlan-VLA wraps an unmodified, frozen short-horizon VLA policy in an execution-aware framework that explicitly monitors robot motion for progress evaluation and adaptively revises future plans based on observed outcomes.
AI.result: Without additional fine-tuning, RePlan-VLA improves success rates by 21.9% on RoboCasa365 and 10.4% on CALVIN over the next strongest baseline, and is validated on a real Franka Research 3 robot.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling progress-aware replanning from frozen short-horizon VLA policies provides a reliable, plug-and-play path to long-horizon robotic manipulation.

title: A Fast, Programmable GPU-to-CPU Invocation Layer for GPU-Initiated Communication
summary: Modern GPU workloads increasingly rely on device-initiated communication to let GPU kernels communicate directly without synchronizing with the host at kernel boundaries. Existing libraries commonly favor placing transport control on GPU threads, an approach known as GPUDirect Async (GDA), and treat reverse offload to host proxy threads as a slower fallback. We argue that reverse offload can outperform GDA and should be a first-class communication path. We further propose exposing reverse offload as a programming interface that lets users define workload-specific communication operations. We present KIWI, a programmable reverse-offload framework that achieves sub-microsecond one-way device-to-host latency and hundreds of millions of operations per second. We address practical challenges of scaling reverse offload, including contention on shared queues, polling overhead, and load imbalance across proxies. KIWI-P2P, a SHMEM-like library built on KIWI, outperforms state-of-the-art GDA implementations in both latency and bandwidth. More importantly, KIWI-EP redesigns low-latency mixture-of-experts dispatch and combine kernels around workload-defined operations, lowering expert-parallel communication latency by up to 2.3x over the best existing backend on AMD GPUs and time per output token in vLLM by up to 29%. The source code of KIWI is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper presents KIWI, a programmable GPU-to-CPU reverse-offload framework for GPU-initiated communication that outperforms GPUDirect Async and cuts vLLM time per output token by up to 29%.
AI.motivation: Existing GPU-initiated communication libraries favor GPU-side transport control (GPUDirect Async) and treat reverse offload to host proxy threads as a slow fallback.
AI.method: KIWI provides a programmable reverse-offload interface addressing queue contention, polling overhead, and proxy load imbalance, supporting a SHMEM-like library (KIWI-P2P) and redesigned mixture-of-experts kernels (KIWI-EP).
AI.result: KIWI achieves sub-microsecond one-way device-to-host latency and hundreds of millions of ops/sec; KIWI-P2P beats GDA in latency and bandwidth, and KIWI-EP cuts expert-parallel communication latency by up to 2.3x on AMD GPUs and vLLM time per output token by up to 29%.
AI.conclusion: Programmable reverse offload can serve as a first-class, high-performance communication path for modern GPU workloads.

title: Neural Memory Orchestration
summary: Modern HPC workloads increasingly stall on the memory hierarchy rather than on compute, and page faults from mmap'd files, swap, and tiered memory are a growing fraction of wall time. Heuristic prefetchers in the kernel handle stride-like and temporally clustered patterns well but degrade sharply on the irregular, data-dependent access streams typical of these workloads. Learned prefetchers have been shown to capture such patterns in simulation but have not been taken to a deployed pipeline running against live workloads on real hardware. We present Overseer, an end-to-end learned page-prefetching system. An eBPF collector observes page faults on the target host, a transformer predictor (OverNet) runs on network-attached inference hardware and emits future page addresses, and a kernel-resident enforcer materializes those pages into the target's address space before they are demanded. OverNet encodes fault sequences through per-instance ordinal ranks over deltas, which lets a single trained model serve any target process without retraining. On two page-fault-heavy workloads, Overseer reduces runtime by roughly 35% on Hilbert-curve traversal and by roughly an order of magnitude on dense matrix multiplication, with corresponding reductions in major-fault counts.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Overseer, an end-to-end learned page-prefetching system using eBPF, a network-attached transformer (OverNet), and a kernel enforcer, cutting runtime by ~35% to ~10x on page-fault-heavy workloads.
AI.motivation: Modern HPC workloads stall on irregular, data-dependent page faults from mmap'd files, swap, and tiered memory, where kernel heuristic prefetchers fail and prior learned prefetchers have only been tested in simulation.
AI.method: Overseer uses an eBPF collector to observe page faults, runs a transformer predictor (OverNet) encoding fault sequences via per-instance ordinal delta ranks on network-attached inference hardware, and materializes predicted pages via a kernel-resident enforcer without per-process retraining.
AI.result: On live hardware running page-fault-heavy workloads, Overseer reduces runtime by roughly 35% on Hilbert-curve traversal and by roughly an order of magnitude on dense matrix multiplication, with corresponding drops in major-fault counts.
AI.conclusion: Rank-encoded learned page prefetching can be deployed end-to-end on real hardware to substantially accelerate irregular memory-bound workloads.

title: LAGR: Language-Aware Grasp Re-Ranking for Task Oriented Grasping
comment: Manav Kulshrestha and Shreyans Jain contributed equally to this work
summary: Grasping is a fundamental capability for robotic manipulation, with the appropriate grasp depending on the downstream task. For example, a hammer should be held by its handle for hammering but by its head when it is handed over. Selecting such a grasp requires consideration of two criteria: physical feasibility on the object and suitability for the task. Developing such an approach requires dense grasp labels with both feasibility and task scores on real observations, but existing task-oriented grasping datasets are small, synthetic, or costly to annotate. To address this gap, we construct a dataset of 2.68 million scored 5-DoF grasp annotations over 100,911 image-task pairs from $17$ object categories. Additionally, we introduce LAGR, a task-oriented grasp detection method that explicitly addresses both these challenges. Given vision-language inputs, LAGR first generates task-independent grasp proposals along with a physical feasibility score, and then scores the generated grasps with a language-conditioned re-ranker that reasons over all proposals jointly. Experiments show that LAGR outperforms the next best method by 9.3 percentage points. We further validate LAGR on real objects by executing task-oriented grasps with a Franka Research 3 robot.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce a 2.68M-grasp dataset and LAGR, a language-aware grasp re-ranking method for task-oriented robotic grasping that outperforms prior methods by 9.3 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Task-oriented grasping requires both physical feasibility and task suitability, but existing datasets with dense labels for both criteria on real observations are small, synthetic, or costly to annotate.
AI.method: They build a dataset of 2.68 million scored 5-DoF grasp annotations over 100,911 image-task pairs across 17 object categories, and propose LAGR, which generates task-independent grasp proposals with physical feasibility scores before scoring them jointly with a language-conditioned re-ranker.
AI.result: LAGR outperforms the next best method by 9.3 percentage points and is validated on real objects using a Franka Research 3 robot.
AI.conclusion: Combining a large-scale feasibility-and-task-annotated dataset with joint language-conditioned re-ranking enables more effective task-oriented robotic grasping.

title: In Situ Training of Optical Neural Networks by Coding Agents
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures. Our project website is at this https URL
summary: Optical neural networks promise fast, energy-efficient computing, but every device departs from its design and must be trained with the hardware. In situ training relies on an expert-built calibrated digital model of each device or on gradient-free trial and error. Coding agents, large language models that write and run programs, have shown an emergent ability to understand and edit the weights of digital neural networks. Here we introduce optics as code, a method in which a coding agent trains an optical neural network from measurements alone, through a harness that returns camera images of its probes and requires a hypothesis per request. We discovered that the agent forms a physical understanding of the optics and reparametrizes the network with interpretable optical elements tuned on the hardware. It outperforms gradient-free methods in classification and image encoding, approaching backpropagation through a calibrated model at a fraction of the cost. Needing neither per-device calibration nor gradients through the hardware, and improving with more capable models, optics as code offers a practical route to large, scalable optical neural networks and a general tool for calibrating and optimizing optical experiments.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce optics as code, where a coding agent trains an optical neural network in situ using only camera measurements and hypothesis-driven probes, outperforming gradient-free methods.
AI.motivation: Optical neural networks depart from their designs on real hardware, and existing in situ training relies either on expert-built calibrated digital models or on gradient-free trial and error.
AI.method: A coding agent interacts with the optical hardware through a harness that returns camera images of probes and requires a hypothesis per request, forming a physical understanding and reparametrizing the network with interpretable optical elements.
AI.result: Optics as code outperforms gradient-free methods on classification and image encoding, approaching backpropagation through a calibrated model at a fraction of the cost, and improves with more capable models.
AI.conclusion: Coding-agent-driven in situ training offers a practical, calibration-free, and gradient-free route to scaling optical neural networks and optimizing optical experiments.

title: Accelerating Distributed Digital Ising Machines
summary: Ising machines, dedicated accelerators built around the dynamics of Ising-like spin models, have emerged as a leading platform for combinatorial optimization and probabilistic sampling. The problems that motivate them require millions of spins, far beyond the on-chip capacity of any single device, so a practical Ising machine must distribute its computation across many devices. Prior work reports throughput at a single operating point, leaving the binding resource unidentified and platform crossovers measurable only by experiment; no calibrated cross-platform cost model of distributed Ising machines has been reported, nor have systematic techniques to accelerate their Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) workloads. This work presents a calibrated cost model that decomposes digital Ising sweep time into compute, memory, synchronization, and inter-device communication terms, validated with 4.8% mean error across three GPU generations, FPGA and ASIC up to 1 million spins. Guided by the model, we address each term in turn and propose: (i) a data placement strategy, worth up to 4.2$\times$ speedup; (ii) multi-rate and bounded-staleness schedules that relax the barrier that Gibbs sampling imposes, cutting time-to-solution (TTS) by up to 3.16$\times$ on three benchmarks; and (iii) a phase-offset streaming dataflow that hides boundary exchange behind interior computation whenever a link satisfies a latency-transparency criterion, yielding up to 1.25$\times$/1.74$\times$/2.01$\times$ on an H200 pair, a ZCU106 pair, and a four-board XEM8320 $2{\times}2$ mesh. The streaming dataflow is also implemented on a fabricated four-chip 28 nm ASIC sustaining 28.1 Gflips/s at 4.81 pJ/flip.

AI.tldr: The authors present a calibrated cross-platform cost model for distributed digital Ising machines and three acceleration techniques that yield speedups across GPUs, FPGAs, and a fabricated 28 nm ASIC.
AI.motivation: Practical Ising machines require millions of spins distributed across multiple devices, yet prior work lacks a calibrated cross-platform cost model and systematic techniques to accelerate their MCMC workloads.
AI.method: They decompose digital Ising sweep time into compute, memory, synchronization, and inter-device communication terms, and propose a data placement strategy, multi-rate and bounded-staleness schedules, and a phase-offset streaming dataflow.
AI.result: The cost model achieves 4.8% mean error up to 1 million spins across three GPU generations, FPGA, and ASIC; data placement gives up to 4.2x speedup, relaxed schedules cut time-to-solution by up to 3.16x, and streaming yields up to 1.25x/1.74x/2.01x speedups on H200, ZCU106, and XEM8320 systems, with a four-chip 28 nm ASIC sustaining 28.1 Gflips/s at 4.81 pJ/flip.
AI.conclusion: Model-guided placement, relaxed synchronization, and latency-hiding streaming dataflows substantially accelerate distributed digital Ising machines.

title: CoSlice: Coordinated Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for 5G Network Slicing Allocation
summary: Radio Access Network (RAN) slicing is a shared resource allocation problem: each slice seeks to satisfy its Service Level Agreement (SLA) with minimal radio-resource consumption, while all slices compete for a limited resource budget. This creates both an intra-slice trade-off between SLA assurance and resource efficiency and an inter-slice conflict over shared resources, calling for specialized yet coordinated control. In this work, we present CoSlice, a coordinated multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for inter-slice physical resource block allocation in Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN). CoSlice uses preference-conditioned slice agents for fast resource allocation and an LLM-based coordinator to adapt their objectives using global network observations at a slower timescale. We formulate the problem as a multi-objective partially observable stochastic game (mo-POSG), establish the existence of a Preference Correlated Equilibrium, and derive a sublinear regret bound for the learning procedure. We implement the algorithm by using a two-stage training procedure that consists of multi-objective pretraining and joint optimization. We build a network slicing evaluation environment using ORANSlice and its radio-frequency simulator (RFsim), supporting realistic protocol-stack execution and application traffic across multiple slices. Experimental results show that CoSlice reduces both average and tail SLA violations compared with other centralized and multi-agent baselines under diverse slice workloads.

AI.tldr: The authors propose CoSlice, a coordinated multi-agent reinforcement learning framework with an LLM-based coordinator for 5G O-RAN network slicing allocation that reduces SLA violations.
AI.motivation: RAN slicing creates both an intra-slice trade-off between SLA assurance and resource efficiency and an inter-slice conflict over shared physical resource blocks.
AI.method: CoSlice models the problem as a multi-objective partially observable stochastic game, pairing preference-conditioned slice agents for fast allocation with a slower-timescale LLM coordinator, trained in two stages and evaluated on ORANSlice with RFsim.
AI.result: CoSlice establishes the existence of a Preference Correlated Equilibrium with a sublinear regret bound and reduces both average and tail SLA violations compared with centralized and multi-agent baselines.
AI.conclusion: Combining fast preference-conditioned MARL agents with slow-timescale LLM coordination provides theoretically grounded and effective resource allocation for O-RAN slicing.

title: How Complete Must an Environment Be to Train a Capable GUI Agent?
summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are widely trained in executable GUI environments. To lower cost, build environments in batches, and reduce manual effort, each work trades away part of the environment through its construction choices. We describe these choices along three dimensions: reward coverage, the goal-reaching trajectories the verifier rewards; data coverage, the application data the agent is exposed to beyond what the task reads or writes; and feature coverage, the application features beyond what the task uses. Existing works set each dimension on engineering grounds, but they do not measure its effect on training. How complete must an environment be to train a capable agent, and along which dimensions? In MobileGym, we adjust each dimension separately, train Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, and evaluate every policy in the original full environment. A verifier that rewards only one reference path lowers success by 10.53 points, and removing unneeded records also lowers success. Pruning unneeded features instead raises success from 51.61% to 56.13%, entirely on tasks whose environments it left unchanged. The gain reverses when each episode is weighted equally and vanishes when only episodes on the pruned tasks are balanced. Without pruning, length weighting there reinforces long detour successes that erode skills on other tasks. Following these findings, we build MobileGym-Lite, which keeps reward and data coverage complete and prunes unneeded features. It outperforms Full in the full environment (55.48% versus 51.61% success) with lower construction cost.

AI.tldr: The authors study how environment completeness affects GUI agent training in MobileGym and introduce MobileGym-Lite, which prunes unneeded features while keeping reward and data coverage complete to improve success at lower cost.
AI.motivation: Existing GUI agent environments trade off reward, data, and feature coverage on engineering grounds without measuring how each dimension affects training.
AI.method: In MobileGym, they vary reward, data, and feature coverage separately, train Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, and evaluate all policies in the full environment, leading to MobileGym-Lite which retains complete reward and data coverage while pruning unneeded features.
AI.result: Rewarding only one reference path lowers success by 10.53 points and removing unneeded records also hurts, whereas pruning unneeded features raises success from 51.61% to 56.13% (and MobileGym-Lite reaches 55.48% vs. 51.61% for Full) by avoiding length-weighted reinforcement of long detours.
AI.conclusion: Keeping reward and data coverage complete while pruning unneeded features yields more capable GUI agents at lower environment construction cost.

title: Rethinking Contrastive Targets in Radiology Language-Image Pretraining
summary: CLIP-style contrastive image-text pretraining is widely used in radiology data, where each image is paired with one report and every other report in the batch is treated as a negative. Under this recipe, two failures appear, neither of which is systematically addressed by existing contrastive learning theory: zero-shot evaluation peaks then degrades while training loss keeps decreasing, and training fails to learn from large batches. We hypothesize the cause is structural rather than radiology-specific: many unpaired reports share clinical findings with a given image, so CLIP's paired-identity target is systematically biased, not merely noisy. To test this, we construct CLEVR-Radiology, a synthetic testbed that preserves only this overlapping-fact structure and reproduces both failures. With evidence that the structure is sufficient to reproduce the failures, we develop a target-misspecification theory that explains both failures from a single deterministic gradient bias amplified by batch size, and use it to motivate a minimal compatibility-based correction, CorLIP: text is treated as positive whenever its clinical assertions agree with the image, with no architecture changes. Beyond benchmark improvements, CorLIP largely removes the post-peak degradation, makes large-batch training succeed where it previously collapsed, substantially amplifies the gains from more data, and is the only configuration that remains stable up to B=2048. The correction transfers from chest X-ray to 3D CT modalities.

AI.tldr: The authors show that CLIP-style radiology pretraining suffers from target misspecification due to shared clinical findings across unpaired reports, and propose CorLIP to fix post-peak degradation and large-batch collapse.
AI.motivation: In radiology CLIP pretraining, zero-shot performance peaks then degrades while training loss drops, and large batches fail to learn, yet existing contrastive theory does not explain these failures.
AI.method: They build a synthetic testbed (CLEVR-Radiology) reproducing both failures, derive a target-misspecification theory, and propose CorLIP, which treats any report whose clinical assertions agree with an image as positive without architectural changes.
AI.result: CorLIP largely eliminates post-peak degradation, enables large-batch training up to B=2048, amplifies data-scaling gains, and transfers from chest X-ray to 3D CT modalities.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for overlapping clinical findings in contrastive targets resolves systematic gradient bias and stabilizes large-batch radiology vision-language pretraining.

title: Semi-Supervised GAN-Based Segmentation of CTPA Scans for Pulmonary Emboli Boundary Extraction
comment: 2026 IEEE 39th International Symposium on Computer-Based Medical Systems (CBMS), Limassol, Cyprus
summary: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a pulmonary vascular disease associated with high morbidity and mortality, where delayed diagnosis can be fatal. While computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the clinical gold standard for PE detection, interpreting these scans manually is time-consuming and error-prone. In this work, we propose a semi-supervised segmentation method, employing generative adversarial networks (GANs) to leverage large pools of unlabeled CTPA scans. The proposed method addresses more effectively the challenges of CTPA image segmentation than previous methods by employing the dice loss and the cross-entropy loss to tackle the highly imbalanced nature of CTPA scans, the feature matching loss to encourage the generator to produce anatomically plausible segmentation maps that are indistinguishable from ground truth, as well as the self-training loss to reinforce learning from highly-confident pseudo-labeled samples. The experimental evaluation on a publicly available dataset shows that the proposed method maintains accurate segmentation, despite a limited number of labeled CTPA scans. with a Dice coefficient of 88.75% and a 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of 1.74, outperforming fully supervised baselines.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a semi-supervised GAN-based segmentation method for CTPA scans that accurately extracts pulmonary emboli boundaries from limited labeled data.
AI.motivation: Manual interpretation of CTPA scans for pulmonary embolism is slow and error-prone, while labeled medical scans are scarce and highly imbalanced.
AI.method: They train a GAN using unlabeled CTPA scans with Dice and cross-entropy losses for class imbalance, feature matching loss for anatomically plausible segmentations, and self-training loss on high-confidence pseudo-labels.
AI.result: On a publicly available dataset with limited labeled CTPA scans, the method achieves a Dice coefficient of 88.75% and an HD95 of 1.74, outperforming fully supervised baselines.
AI.conclusion: Semi-supervised GAN training with feature matching and confident pseudo-labeling enables accurate pulmonary embolism segmentation under label scarcity.

title: Recurrent Domain Incremental Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models
summary: Pretrained Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) provide strong representations for downstream classification tasks. Yet adapting a TSFM under changing operating conditions remains challenging. A model must improve on each newly observed condition without sacrificing conditions it has already learned, often from only a small labeled calibration set and without knowing the operating condition at inference time. We find that this difficulty has an important geometric structure. Under an operating-condition shift, the embedding space of a TSFM does not move uniformly: some local regions change substantially, while others remain nearly unchanged. Consequently, a global adaptation can unnecessarily move embeddings that were already correctly classified. To address this, we propose the novel PACT (Piecewise Adaptation via Chart Transport). PACT partitions the frozen source embedding space into local charts and learns lightweight residual transports for the regions affected by each new condition. An explicit identity path is always retained, and a learned gate softly selects among the identity and accumulated transports for each input. The pretrained TSFM encoder, classifier head, and previously learned transports remain fixed. With only 5% labeled calibration data per arriving condition and no condition identity at test time, PACT maintains an average macro-F1 above 0.95 across a four-condition bearing-fault stream. Under homogeneous tasks and label spaces, similar retention-adaptation behavior is observed across public benchmarks. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The authors propose PACT, a method for recurrent domain incremental adaptation of time-series foundation models that preserves prior operating conditions using local chart transports.
AI.motivation: Adapting time-series foundation models to new operating conditions without forgetting old ones, using small calibration sets and no condition identity at inference, is difficult because global adaptation shifts already-correct embeddings.
AI.method: PACT partitions the frozen source embedding space into local charts, learns lightweight residual transports for affected regions, retains an explicit identity path, and uses a learned gate to softly select among transports while keeping the encoder and classifier fixed.
AI.result: With 5% labeled calibration data per condition and no test-time condition ID, PACT maintains an average macro-F1 above 0.95 across a four-condition bearing-fault stream and shows similar retention-adaptation behavior on public benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the local geometric structure of embedding shifts enables continual adaptation of time-series foundation models without catastrophic forgetting.

title: Training Language Models for Introspective Oversight
summary: Language models increasingly exhibit behaviors that are difficult to detect in transcripts, such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Asking the assistant follow-up questions about its actions is unreliable, since models are generally not trained to report their own misbehavior. As a result, approaches to oversight typically involve querying external models. These face limitations: external transcript monitoring operates only on visible model outputs, and activation decoders lack full context and are prone to confabulation. We introduce introspective oversight, which trains a new role in the model to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant, rewarding answers that are verified against the assistant's actual behavior. We implement this by adding a separate, third-person observer role that answers these queries, which we can train solely for accuracy and separately from the assistant. On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on Qwen3.6-27B obtains a mean AUROC of 0.907, outperforming honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796). We further find that training an observer makes the assistant itself easier to monitor, with every baseline method improving on average when applied to the fine-tuned assistant. These results suggest that training models to answer verifiable questions about themselves is a tractable approach to overseeing unintended behavior.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce introspective oversight, training a separate third-person observer role inside a language model to answer verifiable questions about the assistant's actual behavior.
AI.motivation: Language models can exhibit hidden misbehaviors like reward hacking and deception, and neither follow-up questioning of the assistant nor external transcript monitors and activation decoders reliably detect them.
AI.method: They add a third-person observer role within the model and train it separately for accuracy on queries verified against the assistant's actual behavior.
AI.result: On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on Qwen3.6-27B achieves a mean AUROC of 0.907, outperforming honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796), while also making the fine-tuned assistant easier for baselines to monitor.
AI.conclusion: Training models to answer verifiable third-person questions about their own behavior is a tractable and effective approach to oversight.

title: Where the Tokens Go: Heat, Entropy and Error in Agentic Coding
comment: 43 pages, 10 figures, 11 tables; includes supplementary information with 3 further figures
summary: Coding agents are billed by the token, yet software engineering says nothing about what a token actually buys. Here we introduce a theory of software thermodynamics. The theory draws analogues from classical and stochastic thermodynamics, extends them, and applies them to modern agentic coding. We count the tokens an agent generates as its cost and divide that cost into work and heat. The test suite acts as a software Maxwell's daemon that judges every coding change. We test the theory with an analogue of the experiments in which a single molecule is pulled open and let fold again: an agent makes a change to a repository (coding) and then undoes it (uncoding), many times over, and we count the tokens of every model call. The cycle returns the requested edits to where they began, with each direction started from a stored reference tree, and the spread of its cost over repeated cycles defines a software temperature, which rose with the sampling temperature of the model. About 80 per cent of the tokens of a successful run are generated in model calls that leave the requested change where it was, and we call these tokens heat. The free energy of a change, which we estimate by analogy with the equality of Jarzynski, is 14 to 22 per cent of the mean cost of a successful coding run. Coding costs 1.1 to 1.5 times as much as uncoding. The daemon is imperfect: the verdict of a test suite varies with its environment, and a suite that accepts a broken change has a cost in tokens. The practical implication of the proposed theory could be new tools for analysing and optimising coding agents through the lens of thermodynamics.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a theory of software thermodynamics for agentic coding, showing that roughly 80% of tokens in successful runs act as wasted "heat" rather than useful work.
AI.motivation: Coding agents are billed per token, yet software engineering lacks a theoretical framework connecting token expenditure to actual progress on code changes.
AI.method: They model token cost as work plus heat with the test suite as Maxwell's daemon, and run repeated coding-uncoding cycles from a stored reference tree to measure software temperature and Jarzynski-analogue free energy.
AI.result: About 80% of tokens in successful runs are heat (calls leaving the requested change unchanged), free energy is 14% to 22% of mean cost, coding costs 1.1 to 1.5 times as much as uncoding, and software temperature rises with model sampling temperature.
AI.conclusion: Software thermodynamics provides a quantitative lens for analyzing token efficiency and optimizing agentic coding systems.

title: HardwareDx: A Foundational Graph Model System for Datacenter Machine Repairs
summary: The rapid scale-up of AI infrastructure has made datacenter reliability a cornerstone of the cloud business economy. Since hardware failures in hyper-scale AI clusters can stall multi-million dollar training workloads, the downtime of individual machines can cause outsized economic losses. Minimizing machine downtime, therefore, is more important than ever. To address this, we present Hardware Diagnoser (HardwareDx), an AI-driven hardware diagnosis system that applies a graph foundation model approach to automated datacenter maintenance. It allows a single model to diagnose many platforms and accelerate onboarding of new hardware products. Deployed at production scale at Google, HardwareDx yields substantial efficiency gains across diverse compute architectures. Real-world evaluations demonstrate that it reduces production downtime by 18.3% on GPU platforms and 16.1% on TPUs. Furthermore, it significantly accelerates hardware deployment, cutting quality assurance (QA) time by 28.3% for GPUs and 25.1% for TPUs. These results establish HardwareDx as a field-tested solution for maximizing the reliability and cost efficiency of next generation AI fleets.

AI.tldr: The authors present HardwareDx, a production-deployed graph foundation model system at Google that automates datacenter hardware diagnosis and reduces downtime and QA time.
AI.motivation: Hardware failures in hyperscale AI clusters can stall expensive training workloads, so minimizing machine downtime and accelerating new hardware onboarding are critical.
AI.method: HardwareDx applies a graph foundation model approach to diagnose hardware failures across multiple compute platforms using a single model.
AI.result: In production at Google, HardwareDx reduces downtime by 18.3% on GPUs and 16.1% on TPUs, and cuts hardware QA time by 28.3% for GPUs and 25.1% for TPUs.
AI.conclusion: A single graph foundation model can effectively automate cross-platform hardware diagnosis and improve fleet reliability at hyperscale.

title: LusoClin: A Synthetic Clinical Note Dataset for Medical Information Retrieval in European Portuguese
summary: Access to large-scale clinical text collections is crucial for advancing medical information retrieval research, including clinical note search, patient cohort identification, and domain-adapted retrieval models. However, real clinical notes are rarely available due to privacy regulations, which particularly limits progress for low-resource languages such as European Portuguese. We present LusoClin, a publicly released dataset of synthetic clinical notes in European Portuguese, created to support privacy-preserving research on clinical text retrieval. LusoClin was generated by pre-processing real clinical data, fine-tuning the open-source Llama 3.2 (3B) instruction-tuned model using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation, and applying prompt-based clinical note generation. To facilitate semantic indexing and clinical search, the notes are automatically annotated with clinical entities using a BERT-based model. We evaluate LusoClin in terms of utility, fidelity, diversity, and privacy using automatic metrics and human evaluation. Results indicate that the dataset captures clinically relevant language patterns and can support downstream IR applications such as clinical document retrieval and domain-specific model adaptation, although annotators can often distinguish synthetic from real notes and some medical inconsistencies persist.

AI.tldr: The authors release LusoClin, a synthetic European Portuguese clinical note dataset generated with a QLoRA fine-tuned Llama 3.2 (3B) model and annotated with clinical entities for medical IR.
AI.motivation: Privacy regulations restrict access to real clinical notes, hindering medical information retrieval research especially in low-resource languages like European Portuguese.
AI.method: They preprocess real clinical data, fine-tune Llama 3.2 (3B) with Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation, generate synthetic notes via prompting, and automatically annotate clinical entities using a BERT-based model.
AI.result: Automatic and human evaluations show LusoClin captures clinically relevant language patterns and supports clinical document retrieval and domain adaptation, though annotators can often spot synthetic notes and some medical inconsistencies remain.
AI.conclusion: LusoClin provides a privacy-preserving resource to advance clinical information retrieval and domain adaptation in European Portuguese.

title: VeriMath: Human-in-the-Loop Generation and Verification of Curriculum-Aligned Mathematics Assessment Items
summary: Automatic generation of mathematics assessment items is a growing area in educational artificial intelligence, yet classroom deployment remains challenging. Generated questions must satisfy multiple constraints: mathematical correctness, curriculum alignment, appropriate cognitive difficulty, and educator reviewability. While prior work has advanced text generation, reliable assessment authoring requires granular control over localized examination formats and expert educational judgment. To address this challenge, we present VeriMath, a generalized, human-in-the-loop framework for generating rigorous, curriculum-constrained mathematics assessment drafts. Using annotated reference items, the framework anchors generation to the requested examination section and cognitive reasoning level, then applies sequential automated verification and guided repair before submitting drafts for expert review. We evaluate VeriMath through a national curriculum case study using 4,555 mathematics items from the Vietnamese Grade 12 curriculum and 50 distinct generation requirements covering multiple-choice, true/false, and short-answer formats. Across two model backbones, the framework produces verifier-accepted drafts for 94% (47/50) of requirements per run. Blind expert evaluations confirm high mathematical accuracy and curriculum alignment, with strict teacher-readiness assessments accepting up to 56.8% of generated items. Analysis of rejected drafts reveals persistent domain-agnostic challenges involving formatting, statement validity, and solution-step completeness. These findings demonstrate that VeriMath can bridge generative AI and dependable educational applications by producing highly reviewable assessment drafts within tightly constrained national curriculum frameworks.

AI.tldr: The authors present VeriMath, a human-in-the-loop framework for generating curriculum-aligned mathematics assessment drafts that achieves a 94% automated verifier acceptance rate.
AI.motivation: Classroom deployment of automatically generated math questions is hindered by strict requirements on mathematical correctness, curriculum alignment, cognitive difficulty, and educator reviewability.
AI.method: VeriMath anchors generation to annotated reference items specifying exam section and cognitive level, then applies sequential automated verification and guided repair before expert review.
AI.result: Evaluated on 4,555 Vietnamese Grade 12 math items and 50 generation requirements across two backbones, VeriMath produces verifier-accepted drafts for 94% (47/50) of requirements per run, with blind expert reviews accepting up to 56.8% as teacher-ready.
AI.conclusion: Combining curriculum-anchored generation with automated verification and human review produces dependable, reviewable math assessment drafts.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations
summary: Purpose. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and image navigation behavior of vision-language model (VLM) agents under varying exploration strategies. Materials and Methods. In this retrospective study, six VLMs read 100 emergency CT and MRI examinations published in a public archive (March 2025-August 2026) under four conditions (free navigation, navigation from a key slice, and all slices or key slices in a single request), twice each (4800 runs). Nine radiologists read 30 of those cases. A large language model judge validated against two radiologists graded the answers. Conditions were compared with generalized estimating equations clustered by case. Results. Pooled accuracy was lowest under free navigation (32.6%; 391/1200), followed by navigation from a key slice (37.9%; 455/1200; P = .003), and highest with all slices (42.2%; 506/1200) or key slices (42.5%; 510/1200) in one request (both P < .001). On the 30 cases read by radiologists, freely navigating models were correct in 30.0% of runs (108/360) versus 77.0% for radiologists (208/270; P < .001). Models formed a first hypothesis after a median of 10.8% of the slices and kept it in 63.1% of runs (755/1196); final answers were correct in 12.4% of runs after a wrong first hypothesis (110/885) versus 90.4% after a right one (281/311; P < .001). Median stated confidence in the final answers was 90%, whereas 38.9% of them were correct (1861/4778). Conclusion. Across all exploration strategies, VLM agents remained far less accurate than radiologists. They adopted an early hypothesis and usually kept it, seldom correcting a wrong one.

AI.tldr: The authors evaluate six VLM agents reading 100 emergency CT and MRI exams and find they are far less accurate than radiologists and rarely correct wrong initial hypotheses.
AI.motivation: It is unclear how different image navigation strategies affect the diagnostic accuracy and reasoning behavior of vision-language model agents on emergency cross-sectional imaging.
AI.method: Six VLMs read 100 emergency CT and MRI cases under four navigation conditions twice each (4,800 runs), compared against nine radiologists on 30 cases using generalized estimating equations and an LLM judge validated by two radiologists.
AI.result: Pooled accuracy was 32.6% for free navigation, 37.9% from a key slice, and 42.2%-42.5% with all or key slices in one request; on the 30-case subset, freely navigating VLMs scored 30.0% vs. 77.0% for radiologists, kept their first hypothesis in 63.1% of runs, and scored 12.4% after a wrong first hypothesis despite 90% median stated confidence.
AI.conclusion: Current VLM agents substantially underperform radiologists on emergency CT and MRI and suffer from premature diagnostic anchoring and overconfidence.

title: BeFit: Shifting Complexity from Weights to Bernstein Activations for Resource-Constrained Sensing
summary: Time-series sensing increasingly relies on neural networks, yet deployment on resource-constrained microcontrollers remains challenging. Aggressive model compression can reduce accuracy, while restricting weights to multiplication-free representations introduces further losses. We present BeFit, an end-to-end framework that shifts model capacity from weights to learnable Bernstein polynomial activations. BeFit (i) finds compact Bernstein-activated convolutional neural networks (BeCNNs) through hardware-aware neural architecture search and trains them via knowledge distillation; (ii) projects their weights to multiplication-free codes, freezes the codes, and recovers the resulting accuracy loss through the learnable activations; and (iii) generates model-specific kernels that exploit the projected weights for multiplication-free convolutions. On human activity recognition, BeCNNs are 2.75 percentage points (pp) more accurate on average than ReLU CNNs of identical architecture. On a TI CC3220SF (Cortex-M4), weight projection speeds BeCNNs up by 2.2x on average while losing 0.8 pp, compared with 2.4 pp for ReLU CNNs. Against the MLPerf Tiny DS-CNN reference model running on TensorFlow Lite Micro with CMSIS-NN, the unprojected BeCNN achieves 1.0 pp higher accuracy, 2.2x lower latency, and 6.4x lower flash, while the projected model remains within 1.0 pp of the reference accuracy and runs 5.9x faster. In emulation on a RISC-V core without a hardware multiplier, the instruction-count reduction relative to the DS-CNN increases from 5.2x on the Cortex-M4 to 147x. BeFit also extends to transformers and MLPs, and across all tasks the final models stay within 1.56 pp of their float32 teachers on average.

AI.tldr: The authors present BeFit, a framework that shifts complexity from weights to learnable Bernstein polynomial activations for multiplication-free microcontroller inference.
AI.motivation: Deploying neural networks on resource-constrained microcontrollers is challenging because aggressive compression and multiplication-free weight constraints degrade accuracy.
AI.method: BeFit uses hardware-aware NAS and distillation to find compact Bernstein-activated CNNs (BeCNNs), projects weights to frozen multiplication-free codes, recovers accuracy via the learnable activations, and generates model-specific kernels.
AI.result: On human activity recognition, BeCNNs beat ReLU CNNs by 2.75 pp; on a Cortex-M4, weight projection speeds BeCNNs up by 2.2x with 0.8 pp loss, and against the MLPerf Tiny DS-CNN, projected BeCNN runs 5.9x faster within 1.0 pp accuracy (and cuts RISC-V instruction count by 147x).
AI.conclusion: Shifting representational capacity into learnable Bernstein activations enables fast, accurate, multiplication-free neural inference on tiny microcontrollers.

title: FACET - Facet Aware Contrastive Embeddings for Traits- Big Five Estimation from Life Narratives
summary: Personality is only weakly and inconsistently signaled by written language, and existing text-based methods typically combine language-model and psycholinguistic representations at the input or decision level. It remains open whether a more deliberate combination of the two views, and a decomposition of the prediction target, can recover more of the signal. We present a three-phase framework for estimating Big Five personality domain scores from life-narrative interview text. It encodes text and psycholinguistic features separately and combines them by concatenation or by a learned weighting, decomposes each domain into contrastively trained facet embeddings instead of predicting the domain directly, and pools the facet embeddings by attention into a domain-level prediction. We compare end-to-end with staged training and ablate the input modalities, their combination, and the facet-pooling strategy. On 1,332 participants from the St. Louis Personality and Aging Network (SPAN) study, facet embeddings reach AUC up to 0.740, and domain-level R2 reaches 0.328, highest for Openness. End-to-end training gives lower error than staged training in every domain, and attention pooling gives the lowest error in every domain. Combining the two views lowers error relative to text alone for Conscientiousness and Agreeableness, whereas a learned weighting of the views shows no consistent advantage over concatenation. The framework provides facet- level predictions that a domain-only model cannot, and it improves modestly on a regression from the raw features in four of the five domains.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce FACET, a three-phase framework that estimates Big Five personality traits from life narratives by decomposing domains into contrastively trained facet embeddings.
AI.motivation: Personality is weakly signaled in text, and existing methods combine language-model and psycholinguistic features without testing deliberate fusion or facet-level target decomposition.
AI.method: FACET encodes text and psycholinguistic features separately, combines them via concatenation or learned weighting, learns contrastively trained facet embeddings, and pools them with attention into domain predictions.
AI.result: On 1,332 SPAN study participants, facet embeddings reach up to 0.740 AUC and domain R2 reaches 0.328 (highest for Openness), with end-to-end training and attention pooling outperforming staged training and other pooling methods.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing personality domains into contrastively learned facet embeddings improves trait estimation from life narratives and provides interpretable facet-level predictions.

title: LProp: Propagating Latent Uncertainty through Evidence-Conditioned Belief Revision in LLM Agents
summary: When LLM agents pass intermediate judgments downstream without uncertainty, later decisions may treat tentative assumptions as facts. Effective uncertainty propagation must preserve information for correction and update inherited beliefs as new evidence arrives. Yet scalar scores omit information needed for revision, while detailed descriptions and reflection incur additional costs. We introduce Latent Uncertainty, a latent-space estimator that preserves uncertainty-relevant information without lengthy descriptions. Building on this, we propose LProp (Latent Uncertainty Propagation), which revises inherited answer distributions using latent representations and new evidence without additional trajectory sampling. We evaluate both methods across multiple-choice, yes/no, open-ended question answering, and mathematical reasoning tasks. Our approach outperforms baselines on most metrics, while LProp achieves the lowest mean inference-token usage in all eight propagation settings. Matched feature ablations further demonstrate that inherited latent content improves error recovery beyond answer probabilities or model capacity alone.

AI.tldr: The authors propose Latent Uncertainty and LProp to propagate and revise uncertainty across LLM agent steps using latent representations without extra trajectory sampling.
AI.motivation: Passing scalar confidence scores or intermediate judgments without rich uncertainty causes downstream LLM agents to treat tentative assumptions as facts, while verbalized reflection adds token cost.
AI.method: They introduce Latent Uncertainty, a latent-space estimator, and LProp, which updates inherited answer distributions using latent representations and new evidence without additional trajectory sampling.
AI.result: Across multiple-choice, yes/no, open-ended QA, and math reasoning tasks, their methods outperform baselines on most metrics while LProp achieves the lowest mean inference-token usage across all eight propagation settings.
AI.conclusion: Propagating latent-space uncertainty enables evidence-conditioned belief revision and better error recovery at lower token cost.

title: Receiver-Conditioned Clarification for Multi-Agent Food Assistance
summary: Food insecurity creates a pressing need for guidance that helps households find usable food resources and assess food choices in light of their circumstances. Such guidance must connect eligibility requirements, practical access constraints, and dietary needs rather than return isolated listings or generic nutritional advice. Multi-agent food assistants can coordinate these tasks, with uncertainty indicating when clarification or verification is needed before a recommendation. However, uncertainty can be lost across agent handoffs, allowing tentative interpretations to propagate as facts and obscuring opportunities for correction. Moreover, confidence that a service requirement has been interpreted correctly is not confidence that a recommendation satisfies the user's needs; local confidence cannot simply be reused as downstream reliability. We introduce an inference-time, receiver-conditioned clarification framework that preserves shared premise identities and replays consistent interpretations across dependent agents. Each receiver exposes admissible decisions and remaining evidence obligations, so question relevance reflects both decision changes and missing support. Information questions and user-confirmable fallback adjustments are evaluated together with their anticipated follow-up interactions under shared budgets. This structure connects clarification to jointly supported plans for resource navigation, nutritional reasoning, and supply-side planning.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce an inference-time, receiver-conditioned clarification framework for multi-agent food assistance that preserves shared premise identities and aligns questions with downstream decision needs.
AI.motivation: In multi-agent food assistance, uncertainty is lost across handoffs and local interpretation confidence does not guarantee that a final recommendation satisfies a household's eligibility, access, and dietary constraints.
AI.method: Each receiving agent exposes admissible decisions and remaining evidence obligations, allowing the framework to replay consistent interpretations, preserve premise identities, and evaluate clarification questions and fallback adjustments under shared budgets.
AI.result: The framework structures clarification around decision changes and missing evidence support across resource navigation, nutritional reasoning, and supply-side planning.
AI.conclusion: Receiver-conditioned clarification connects uncertainty tracking directly to jointly supported multi-agent plans for food assistance.

title: ARISE: Practical Self-Evolving Memory for Accurate and Cost-Efficient Enterprise Agents
summary: Enterprise LLM agents operate in dynamic environments where foundation models evolve rapidly, workflows update frequently, and deployments need to satisfy accuracy and cost requirements. We propose ARISE (Agent Refinement through Iterative Self-Evaluation), a practical memory architecture in which the agent's memory evolves from its own failures without updating model weights, tools, or workflow logic. ARISE uses the model itself or a teacher model to attribute the failures and propose corrections. Then, ARISE keeps the corrections as retrievable micro memory, consolidates them into macro rules, and accepts a rule update only if held-out accuracy rises. Across 14 enterprise-workflow domains from SOP-Bench and $\tau^2$-bench using 5 models, ARISE-Teacher, which uses Claude Opus 4.6 for attribution and consolidation, gains 10.9 pp over the baseline on SOP-Bench and 5.8 pp on $\tau^2$-bench. ARISE-Teacher also outperforms GEPA by 4.5 pp on $\tau^2$-bench and 1.4 pp on SOP-Bench. With the deployment model as its own attributor, ARISE-Self still gains 10.0 pp on SOP-Bench. ARISE-Teacher uses 4.0% fewer model calls and 5.2% fewer output tokens at comparable per-task cost (-1.0%).

AI.tldr: The authors propose ARISE, a self-evolving memory architecture for enterprise LLM agents that turns failure attributions into validated macro rules, improving accuracy on SOP-Bench and tau2-bench.
AI.motivation: Enterprise agents operate in dynamic workflows where weights and tools cannot be frequently updated, requiring a practical way to learn from failures without hurting accuracy or cost.
AI.method: ARISE uses the agent or a teacher model to attribute failures, stores corrections as retrievable micro memory, consolidates them into macro rules, and accepts rule updates only when held-out accuracy improves.
AI.result: Across 14 domains on SOP-Bench and tau2-bench with 5 models, ARISE-Teacher (Claude Opus 4.6) gains 10.9 pp on SOP-Bench and 5.8 pp on tau2-bench over baselines, beats GEPA, and reduces model calls by 4.0% and output tokens by 5.2%, while ARISE-Self still gains 10.0 pp on SOP-Bench.
AI.conclusion: Held-out-validated memory consolidation from failure attribution enables accurate, cost-efficient self-evolution for enterprise agents.

title: RefinementGuard: Counterexample-Directed Semantic Qualification for Hidden Agent-Tool Execution
summary: Tool runtimes can lower an agent-selected operation into a hidden parallel graph, reducing latency and context while risking semantic mistranslation. We introduce RefinementGuard: translation validation for hidden, effectful agent-tool lowerings, coupled to artifact-bound, fail-closed runtime admission. Qualification compares a candidate graph with an independent reference on isolated state using explicit parent-operation obligations. We evaluate two repository-level contracts, bug localization and patch validation, on controlled repositories. Among 100 activated, non-equivalent development/qualification faults adjudicated by one human, parent-semantic validation rejects 49/100 (operator-cluster bootstrap 95% CI [33.7%, 64.8%]). The objective is selective admission, not maximum mutation rejection: exact equality rejects 100/100 faults but also all 60 valid variants, whereas obligation-based validation accepts 60/60; its 51 residual misses identify concrete specification gaps. On a frozen disjoint input split, the held-out B2-B3 result is localization-only because 21 patch mutants fail structurally; B3 rejects 38/56 localization defects. In a controlled asynchronous-delay regime, the localization serial/guarded median-latency ratio is 4.50x, and hidden execution exposes 74.3% less parent-visible context than visible execution. Patch validation shows no demonstrated speedup; zero-delay runs expose overhead. End-to-end qualification thus detects lower-layer misses while preserving localization's parallelism.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce RefinementGuard, a translation-validation and fail-closed runtime admission system for hidden parallel agent-tool lowerings.
AI.motivation: Lowering agent-selected tool operations into hidden parallel graphs reduces latency and context size, but risks semantic mistranslation.
AI.method: RefinementGuard validates candidate graphs against an independent reference on isolated state using explicit parent-operation obligations, evaluated on bug localization and patch validation contracts.
AI.result: On 100 human-adjudicated faults, parent-semantic validation rejects 49/100 while accepting 60/60 valid variants; on a held-out split it rejects 38/56 localization defects, achieves a 4.50x serial/guarded latency ratio for localization, and reduces parent-visible context by 74.3%, though patch validation shows no speedup.
AI.conclusion: Obligation-based translation validation catches lower-layer semantic errors while preserving the parallelism and context savings of hidden tool execution for localization.

title: Searching the Pareto Front: Multi-Objective Retrieval for Heterogeneous Scientific Modalities
summary: In cosmology, surveys span different sky regions and wavelength ranges, resulting in uneven modality coverage across observational datasets. Such heterogeneity can be addressed through either multimodal foundation models (FMs), which learn shared embedding spaces, or independently learned modality embeddings combined via late fusion. We investigate whether the latter provides an adaptive alternative to FM-based scientific retrieval. We evaluate this approach on a galaxy retrieval task spanning diverse modalities--history of star formation, spectra of light emitted, and multi-wavelength observations from two telescopes--comparing an FM baseline with separately trained embeddings fused through multi-objective optimization based on Pareto optimality. We find that the FM baseline achieves strong embedding-space proximity, but our method preserves modality-specific distance structure that allows scientists to inspect which physical signals drive similarity. Our method also achieves improved fidelity in raw-data space: across six measured properties, its nearest neighbor is 8% closer to the query on average than that retrieved by kNN in the FM embedding space (spread 0.128 vs. 0.139). These results suggest that multi-objective retrieval can surface astrophysically coherent candidates that single-objective search alone may overlook.

AI.tldr: The authors show that multi-objective Pareto retrieval over separately trained modality embeddings outperforms a multimodal foundation model baseline in raw-data fidelity for galaxy retrieval.
AI.motivation: Astronomical surveys have uneven modality coverage, and it is unclear whether late fusion of independent modality embeddings can outperform shared-space multimodal foundation models.
AI.method: They evaluate galaxy retrieval across star formation history, spectra, and multi-wavelength telescope observations by fusing separately trained modality embeddings via Pareto-optimal multi-objective optimization.
AI.result: Compared to kNN in a multimodal foundation model embedding space, their method preserves modality-specific distance structure and retrieves nearest neighbors that are 8% closer to the query in raw-data space across six measured properties (spread 0.128 vs. 0.139).
