AI.conclusion: Multi-objective retrieval over separate modality embeddings offers an interpretable, higher-fidelity alternative to single-objective foundation-model search for heterogeneous scientific data.

title: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents
summary: Clinicians reviewing a diagnostic work-up will ask what was considered at each step and why the assessment changed. Agents powered by free text can reach physician-level diagnostic accuracy, but their written reasoning does not always reflect the factors that went into the decision. Here, we present Decision2Care, a decision agent that works up the acutely ill patient without producing any text. A decision model assigns a probability to each permitted EHR action, and fixed rules carry out the most probable one. We evaluated Decision2Care on the records of 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases. Decision2Care reached a diagnostic accuracy of 86.5%, compared with 86.1% for the MIRA-v2 agent, and required a median of 2.2 s per work-up, compared with 92-100 s. Each work-up tracked which options Decision2Care was considering at each step. In 10 of the 12 diseases, the differential diagnosis changed most at the test on which the guideline bases the diagnosis. Where Decision2Care was most confident after a single work-up, all but four of its diagnoses were correct (98.5%). We traced each of these four errors back to a single imaging report. Three of them were corrected when that report was removed. The same kind of decision was used to select the treatments, and Decision2Care's drug orders were judged guideline-adherent more often than MIRA-v2's. In emergency patients, its prediction of death was comparable to that of three intensivists on the same cases. In five of the eight intensive care cohorts, it exceeded the best of the three 24-h severity scores within 2-6 h of records. Our results show that decision agents can carry out clinical work-ups while recording the options, probabilities, and execution rules behind each action for audit.

AI.tldr: The authors present Decision2Care, a text-free clinical decision agent that achieves 86.5% diagnostic accuracy across 546 emergency admissions in a median of 2.2 seconds while logging auditable probabilities.
AI.motivation: Free-text LLM clinical agents can reach high accuracy, but their written rationales do not reliably reflect the actual factors driving their decisions.
AI.method: Decision2Care uses a decision model to assign probabilities to permitted EHR actions and fixed rules to execute the most probable action, recording considered options and probabilities at every step without generating text.
AI.result: Across 546 emergency admissions and 12 diseases, Decision2Care matches MIRA-v2 accuracy (86.5% vs. 86.1%) while cutting median work-up time from 92-100 s to 2.2 s, achieves 98.5% accuracy on its most confident cases, produces more guideline-adherent drug orders, and matches intensivists on mortality prediction.
AI.conclusion: Text-free decision agents can deliver fast, accurate, and fully auditable clinical work-ups and treatment selection.

title: KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch
comment: Ongoing work. 67 pages with 34 figures and 37 tables. Project website: this https URL GitHub: this https URL
summary: The growing volume of topically similar papers makes it difficult to identify new work that can offer useful research insights or methodological guidance. We present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight discovery tool that combines multiple sources of evidence into personalized reading priorities. Users specify topics, priorities, exclusions and dates; the system brings together topical relevance, recency, author research histories, collaboration paths and direction-specific institutional context. By exposing each score component and its supporting sources, KnowMe helps readers select promising papers for their current questions and discover relevant work beyond familiar authors. Automatic acquisition, version merging and graph-cache reuse keep this workflow convenient without large language model (LLM) inference during ordinary use. Experiments on 174,640 acquired records show more than threefold faster repeated context preparation, while cached abstracts improve normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 (NDCG@10) from 0.412 to 0.598 on expert-judged retrieval tasks. Complementary analyses examine how the same accumulated records support semantic retrieval, research-history modeling and literature-grounded planning. A browser interface and a structured command-line interface (CLI) make these capabilities available to both researchers and research agents, positioning KnowMe as a practical upstream tool for literature-informed recursive self-improvement (RSI) workflows.

AI.tldr: The authors present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight, LLM-free literature discovery tool that combines topical, recency, author, and institutional signals into transparent reading priorities.
AI.motivation: Rapidly growing volumes of similar papers make it hard for researchers and research agents to identify genuinely promising work.
AI.method: KnowMe aggregates topical relevance, recency, author histories, collaboration paths, and institutional context with automatic acquisition, version merging, and graph-cache reuse, exposing each score component via browser and CLI interfaces.
AI.result: On 174,640 acquired records, cached abstracts improve NDCG@10 from 0.412 to 0.598 on expert-judged retrieval tasks and speed up repeated context preparation by more than threefold without LLM inference.
AI.conclusion: Transparent, multi-signal scoring with cached literature graphs provides a fast, practical upstream discovery tool for researchers and recursive self-improvement agents.

title: Modeling LLM Reasoning Dynamics with Structural Representations
summary: Language-model reasoning alternates between sustained activities and local operations. We study how this temporal structure predicts continuation and the computation needed to analyze it. T/E/S combines text, local events, and spans of activity. Across reasoning and information-seeking tasks, events and spans improve next-outcome prediction in 70 of 76 evaluation groups for a Transformer and 74 of 76 for Qwen with LoRA. Span duration and preceding events are associated with transitions, and retaining event history across span boundaries improves prediction. We formulate budget-allocation counting and action-conditional continuation queries, prove counting hardness under explicit encodings, and derive conditions for affordable decision certification. In finite-process experiments, bounds that cancel shared continuation mass recover the same optimal actions as full dynamic programming while reducing mean inference CPU time by 77.7%. On 71 held-out HotpotQA and MuSiQue questions, a compact structural observer improves prediction of whether a fixed inference procedure finishes within a CPU allowance: Brier loss falls from 0.0836 to 0.0756. An annotation audit identifies substantial errors in that observer, separating this computational result from semantic validation of its features.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce T/E/S, a structural representation combining text, local events, and activity spans, to model LLM reasoning dynamics and reduce dynamic-programming decision certification CPU time by 77.7%.
AI.motivation: LLM reasoning alternates between sustained activities and local operations, and understanding this temporal structure is needed to predict continuation and budget allocation efficiently.
AI.method: They represent reasoning traces with T/E/S, formulate budget-allocation counting and action-conditional continuation queries, prove counting hardness, and derive cancellation bounds for decision certification.
AI.result: Events and spans improve next-outcome prediction in 70/76 groups for a Transformer and 74/76 for Qwen with LoRA; cancellation bounds recover optimal actions with 77.7% less CPU time, and a compact observer lowers Brier loss from 0.0836 to 0.0756 on 71 HotpotQA/MuSiQue questions (though an audit notes observer annotation errors).
AI.conclusion: Structural event-and-span representations capture LLM reasoning transitions and enable much faster budget-allocation certification.

title: Metrics-in-the-Loop: Complexity Feedback Reshapes Agent-Written Code
comment: Agent Evaluation Science Symposium, Fall 2026, New York City
summary: Coding agents now write whole codebases in long autonomous runs, guided mainly by whether their tests pass. Yet passing tests alone does not reveal accumulating complexity or gaps in test coverage, which then persist as agents extend their own code. We introduce metrics-in-the-loop, an inference-time intervention that gives agents in-flight feedback: cheap, automatically computed code metrics injected into the agent's context during the trajectory. After each code-changing agent turn, we insert short feedback messages naming changed functions whose cyclomatic complexity exceeds a limit (complexity feedback) or changed lines that are skipped by tests (coverage feedback), giving the agent the opportunity to refactor code or strengthen tests before continuing. We run extensive experiments and ablations comparing several interventions across three long-horizon coding benchmarks and four strong models. We find that complexity feedback significantly reduces erosion, a measure of complexity concentration of code, without affecting held-out correctness of the code. Broadly, our experiments investigate a practical form of agent "re-railing", where timely, actionable measurements redirect agents before weaknesses become the foundation they keep building on. As agents scale to codebases with millions of lines, such interventions become critical to sustaining effective development and long-term code maintainability.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce metrics-in-the-loop, injecting automated cyclomatic complexity and test-coverage feedback during coding-agent runs to reduce code complexity erosion without hurting correctness.
AI.motivation: Coding agents guided only by passing tests accumulate hidden code complexity and coverage gaps that persist as they extend their own codebases.
AI.method: After each code-changing turn, they inject short messages flagging changed functions exceeding a cyclomatic complexity limit or changed lines skipped by tests, prompting immediate refactoring or test strengthening.
AI.result: Across three long-horizon coding benchmarks and four strong models, complexity feedback significantly reduces code complexity erosion without degrading held-out correctness.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight, in-flight code metric feedback effectively re-rails coding agents to maintain long-term codebase maintainability.

title: Evidence-Based Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards enables search-augmented language models to interleave reasoning and retrieval without step-level annotations, yet outcome supervision assigns identical credit to every search in a trajectory regardless of whether it retrieved useful information. This limitation is especially severe when all sampled rollouts for a question fail, collapsing group-centered outcome advantages to zero even when trajectories gather markedly different evidence. We present Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), which augments terminal outcome rewards with a training-only auxiliary signal measuring how retrieved documents improve the likelihood of a reference answer. Rather than scoring the full dialogue prefix, ECA queries a frozen snapshot of the current policy under an evidence-only prompt containing solely the question and the deduplicated documents observed so far, isolating the utility of retrieved passages from surface variations in generated thoughts or search queries. Within this framework, we compare two return formulations, ECA-Step (which accumulates step-clipped potential increments) and ECA-Horizon (which preserves the telescoping horizon gain in potential), paired with cross-fold group normalization, novelty gating, and search-local token assignment. Across seven Search QA benchmarks, ECA-Horizon improves strict macro exact match over an outcome-only GRPO baseline by 1.03 and 4.80 percentage points on Qwen2.5-3B- and 7B-Instruct, respectively, outperforming both RLOO and GiGPO. Zero-shot evaluation on MultiHop-RAG further demonstrates strong transfer to multi-hop inference queries.

AI.tldr: The authors propose Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), an auxiliary RL reward measuring how retrieved documents improve reference-answer likelihood, boosting Search QA performance on Qwen2.5 models.
AI.motivation: Outcome-only RL assigns identical credit to all searches in a trajectory and yields zero advantage when all rollouts fail, ignoring differences in retrieved evidence quality.
AI.method: ECA queries a frozen policy snapshot with an evidence-only prompt containing only the question and deduplicated retrieved documents, comparing step-clipped (ECA-Step) and telescoping (ECA-Horizon) formulations with cross-fold normalization, novelty gating, and search-local assignment.
AI.result: Across seven Search QA benchmarks, ECA-Horizon improves strict macro exact match over outcome-only GRPO by 1.03 pp on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and 4.80 pp on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, outperforming RLOO and GiGPO and transferring zero-shot to MultiHop-RAG.
AI.conclusion: Isolating the marginal likelihood gain of retrieved documents provides effective step-level credit assignment for search-augmented language models.

title: RoboBuilder: Agentic Robot Co-Design with Real-world Video Feedback in the Loop
summary: Can AI agents design robots that work in the real world? We introduce RoboBuilder, a benchmark in which coding agents co-design a robot's hardware and program from standard parts, motors and a custom 3D-printed part, and every design that passes in simulation is built and tested on a physical course. Simulation alone is not enough: under public part data, none of 15 initial passing designs crossed the real course, so an agent learns the simulator from measurements it requests and videos of real runs. Across four frontier coding agents, ten obstacles at three difficulty levels, 16,427 simulations of 12,774 distinct robots and 135 physical robots built in an estimated 240 hours, agents solve nearly all easy obstacles and invent mechanisms our search baselines do not reach, but falter at harder levels, when one robot must cross every obstacle, and in the real world, where 66% of simulated passes hold across all levels. Closing the loop helps: shown a video of its real failure, an agent redesigns the robot, sometimes correcting its simulator, and removes 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures. RoboBuilder measures progress toward agents that engineer real machines. Project Page: this https URL

AI.tldr: The authors introduce RoboBuilder, a hardware-and-software robot co-design benchmark with physical course testing, showing that real-world video feedback removes 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether coding agents can engineer robots that work in the real world, where simulation gaps cause simulated passes to fail physically.
AI.method: Coding agents co-design robot hardware (from standard parts, motors, and a custom 3D-printed part) and control code, test in simulation, build passing designs physically, and iterate using measurements and real-world failure videos.
AI.result: Across four frontier agents, 16,427 simulations, and 135 physical robots, agents solve easy obstacles and invent novel mechanisms, but 66% of simulated passes hold in reality; providing real-world failure videos enables redesigns that eliminate 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures.
AI.conclusion: Closing the loop with real-world video feedback is critical for enabling AI agents to engineer functional physical robots.

title: Asking but Missing: Decision Coverage in Natural-Language Data Querying
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to translate natural language questions about structured data into executable programs. A fundamental challenge is recognizing when a question admits multiple computational interpretations and identifying the decisions needed to resolve them. We investigate whether language models recognize these unresolved decisions before generating code, or silently adopt assumptions that may lead to incorrect results. We refer to the latter behavior as Underspecified Decision Completion (UDC). To distinguish different causes of UDC, we introduce Grounded Code Generation (GCG), a diagnostic protocol that separates the identification of unresolved decisions, their resolution using evidence, and their translation into executable code. By examining each stage separately, we can determine where the decisions responsible for incorrect results were first missed or mishandled. We evaluate this framework on BIRD-Pandas with twelve models. The results show that answering clarification questions consistently improves execution accuracy, yet substantial errors remain. Our findings suggest that the main difficulty lies not in answering clarification questions, but in recognizing which questions need to be asked in the first place.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce Grounded Code Generation (GCG) to diagnose Underspecified Decision Completion in LLMs on BIRD-Pandas, finding that models struggle more to recognize what questions to ask than to answer them.
AI.motivation: When translating ambiguous natural-language data queries into code, LLMs often silently adopt assumptions instead of recognizing unresolved computational decisions.
AI.method: They propose GCG, a diagnostic protocol separating decision identification, evidence-based resolution, and code translation, and evaluate twelve models on BIRD-Pandas.
AI.result: Answering clarification questions consistently improves execution accuracy, yet substantial errors persist because models fail to identify which clarification questions need to be asked in the first place.
AI.conclusion: Improving natural-language data querying requires teaching models to detect underspecified decisions before generating code.

title: EVA-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Evaluators for Judging Temporal Quality
summary: Video evaluators play an important role in video generation, yet they miss motion defects, limiting the quality of generated videos. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has made strong progress in mathematics and coding, where explicit verifiers provide reliable feedback on a single goal. Video evaluation poses two difficulties for RSI: it has no verifier, and it must judge many dimensions at once, such as physics, smoothness and dynamics, where a gain on one can cost another. We introduce EVA-RSI, a multi-agent framework for exploring RSI under these two constraints. We build a fixed proxy exam with construction-defined targets by applying controlled changes to videos, such as temporal reversal and frame dropping. These edits supply supervision without human annotation. A small set of human-labeled real videos anchors the exam to human judgment. Each dimension has an LLM agent that proposes improvements. A leader agent coordinates the proposals, and a Nash bargaining rule selects updates that balance progress across dimensions. Humans design the exam, review candidate changes and revise the curriculum between stages. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B, EVA-RSI improves motion evaluation, with the largest gain on smoothness, and the gains carry over to defect types never seen during the run. On the dynamics subsets of public benchmarks, our evaluator achieves the highest observed scores among 21 tested models. As an RL reward, it increases generated motion and earns human preference. A data-selection pipeline incorporating it also increases motion.

AI.tldr: The authors propose EVA-RSI, a multi-agent recursive self-improvement framework using controlled video edits and Nash bargaining that improves temporal video evaluation and downstream RL generation.
AI.motivation: Video evaluators miss motion defects, and applying recursive self-improvement to video evaluation is hard because there is no single explicit verifier and multiple quality dimensions trade off against each other.
AI.method: They build a fixed proxy exam using controlled edits (such as temporal reversal and frame dropping) anchored by human-labeled videos, where dimension-specific LLM agents propose improvements and a leader agent selects updates via Nash bargaining.
AI.result: Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B, EVA-RSI improves motion evaluation (especially smoothness), generalizes to unseen defect types, achieves the highest scores among 21 models on public dynamics benchmarks, and increases generated motion and human preference when used as an RL reward or data-selection filter.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent Nash bargaining over synthetic proxy exams enables effective recursive self-improvement for multi-dimensional video evaluation.

title: Evaluating invariance training with certified answer-changing controls in neural graph algorithms
summary: Invariance training aims to make neural algorithmic reasoners robust to answer-preserving input changes and is judged by accuracy and by how rarely such edits change predictions. We ask whether this evaluation detects lost sensitivity to answer-changing edits on minimum spanning trees of synthetic graphs, where both directions can be certified. Attaching a subgraph through one bridge provably preserves every original label. Attaching it through two edges, oracle-selected to change a label, and lowering one weight inside the graph serve as answer-changing controls; a response is a changed prediction on an edge whose label changes. A reproduced graph transformer (GDT) within its published accuracy range changes a provably fixed label on 53.3-65.9% of the 64-vertex graphs it solves exactly after a 64-vertex bridge attachment; removing the connecting edge changes little. With 16-vertex graphs and attachments, three invariance objectives lower GDT violations from 2.91% to 0.52-2.02% of pairs at essentially unchanged accuracy. Training also lowers the response to two-edge attachments from 97.6% to 66.0-79.0%, while the response to in-base weight edits stays near 99.5%. At 64 vertices accuracy also falls, but on 16-vertex bases only the attachment control reveals the loss. A message-passing network loses some attachment response at small penalty weights but gains little invariance. Running the conventionally trained GDT on each biconnected block separately removes all observed violations and keeps accuracy and both responses, so the task does not force the trade-off. Sensitivity checks for trained invariance should include certified answer-changing edits that attach material as the training edits do.

AI.tldr: The authors show that invariance training on neural graph algorithms can reduce sensitivity to answer-changing graph edits, and recommend using certified answer-changing controls alongside invariance checks.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluations of invariance training measure accuracy and invariance to answer-preserving edits, which may miss lost sensitivity to edits that actually change the answer.
AI.method: On synthetic minimum spanning trees, they pair provably answer-preserving one-bridge subgraph attachments with certified answer-changing controls (two-edge attachments and in-base weight lowering) across a graph transformer (GDT) and a message-passing network.
AI.result: Invariance objectives cut GDT violations on 16-vertex graphs from 2.91% to 0.52-2.02%, but also drop response to two-edge answer-changing attachments from 97.6% to 66.0-79.0%; running conventionally trained GDT per biconnected block removes all violations while preserving both accuracy and sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating invariance training requires certified answer-changing controls that match the structural form of the training edits.

title: Training-Free Domain Generation for One-Shot Federated Learning with Server-Side Pre-trained Diffusion Models
summary: One-shot federated learning (OSFL) has attracted increasing attention for its ability to substantially reduce communication overhead by limiting client-server interaction to a single communication round. Nevertheless, this limited interaction makes learning from heterogeneous client distributions challenging. Diffusion-based OSFL approaches seek to address this challenge by synthesizing data that approximate client distributions. However, existing diffusion-based approaches often impose substantial computational costs on clients and lack effective visual guidance to generate data aligned with client distributions. To address these limitations, we propose FedDoG, a training-free Domain Generation framework that leverages server-side pre-trained diffusion models to synthesize data aligned with client domains. FedDoG extracts compact domain representations using a frozen image encoder, substantially reducing client-side computational and communication costs. These representations are incorporated into the diffusion model through a pre-trained image-conditioning adapter, thereby providing explicit visual guidance for domain generation. To further improve the quality of synthetic data, FedDoG adapts the strength of visual conditioning according to domain concentration and filters generated samples based on class consistency and predictive entropy. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that FedDoG generates higher-quality synthetic images and outperforms existing OSFL baselines in classification accuracy. Meanwhile, FedDoG reduces client upload and computation time by 99.9% and 91.5%, respectively. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The authors propose FedDoG, a training-free one-shot federated learning framework that uses server-side pre-trained diffusion models with frozen client domain representations to boost accuracy and cut client costs.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based one-shot federated learning methods impose heavy client-side computation and lack effective visual guidance to align synthetic data with heterogeneous client domains.
AI.method: FedDoG extracts compact domain representations on clients with a frozen image encoder, feeds them into a server-side pre-trained diffusion model via an image-conditioning adapter, adapts conditioning strength by domain concentration, and filters samples by class consistency and entropy.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks, FedDoG generates higher-quality synthetic images, outperforms existing OSFL baselines in classification accuracy, and reduces client upload and computation time by 99.9% and 91.5%.
AI.conclusion: Server-side pre-trained diffusion conditioned on lightweight frozen client representations enables accurate, low-cost one-shot federated learning.

title: MLE Agents: Autonomous ML Engineering in Large-scale Recommendation Systems
summary: The typical workflow for improving large-scale ranking and recommendation models is slow and tedious: an engineer forms a hypothesis, implements it as a code change, trains a model, and evaluates it both offline and online, often relying on their own intuition and experience along the way. Autonomous LLM agents promise to speed this up by running the loop on their own, but it is still unclear whether they can do this in industry-scale systems rather than on benchmarks or small proxy tasks. We build human-on-the-loop machine learning engineer (MLE) agents that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes on large-scale search rankers. Engineers retain control over objective design, search direction, and final-model review. We identify three obstacles that make this industry setting challenging: feedback takes hours per experiment, offline metrics do not always predict online impact, and improvements saturate after the early wins. We address these with parallel training runs, an objective calibrated to match online impact, and careful context engineering. In one campaign, the system ran 1,097 completed candidate experiments and accepted 325, a 29.6\% acceptance rate compared with 15.6\% in the earlier campaign under a different objective and search constraint. Its best model increases search volume by 0.23\% in an A/B test of large scale. Several improvements were architectural changes the team had never tried, drawn from the broader industry and literature, suggesting that MLE agents can explore regions of the design space that human intuition overlooks. We find that the design of the harness around the model matters: intuition suggests that a stronger underlying model is enough, but in our experience, the design of the loop around it is just as critical. More broadly, our work shows that autonomous agents can do real machine-learning engineering in industry-scale systems.

AI.tldr: The authors deploy human-on-the-loop MLE agents on large-scale industrial search rankers, running 1,097 experiments with a 29.6% acceptance rate and lifting search volume by 0.23% in an A/B test.
AI.motivation: Improving industrial ranking models is slow, and it has been unclear whether autonomous LLM agents can perform real ML engineering in large-scale production systems rather than small benchmarks.
AI.method: They build MLE agents that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes using parallel training runs, an online-calibrated objective, and context engineering, while engineers control objectives, search direction, and final review.
AI.result: In one campaign, the agents completed 1,097 candidate experiments and accepted 325 (29.6% vs. 15.6% in an earlier campaign), with the best model increasing search volume by 0.23% in a large-scale A/B test and discovering novel architectural changes.
AI.conclusion: With proper harness design and online-calibrated objectives, autonomous MLE agents can deliver real production gains in industry-scale recommendation systems.

title: Vanguard: Knowing When to Trust the Draft in Speculative Vision-Language Agents
summary: Vision-language agents that browse websites, operate phones and act in homes reason before every action, so every step waits for a large model, a latency and cost that stand in the way of deployment. Step-level speculation lets a small model draft each step and calls the large model only on rejected drafts, but its outcome rests on the judge, and a judge that reads only a step's text cannot tell whether the step fits the screen it acts on. We find that a few samples of a small model can contain a correct step about as often as the large model gets the step right, and not always on the same steps: checked against the screen, small drafts can be not only cheaper but better. We present Vanguard, a training-free judge that leaves the draft and target models unchanged: a general decision model, with the screenshot in view, gives each candidate step a probability of being right in one forward pass; the best candidate is kept if it clears a threshold, and otherwise the large model writes the step. On web, mobile and embodied agents, a 2B draft judged by Vanguard is at least as accurate as its 8B target and significantly more accurate on Mind2Web and EB-ALFRED, while the target writes only a minority of the steps; it completes far more closed-loop episodes, and with a 27B target from another family it is both faster and more accurate. Vanguard is the most accurate judge we compare on the agent tasks; it relies on the screenshot on web and mobile tasks, its calibrated threshold transfers to unseen websites, and across model families its gain over the target grows with the draft's pass@4 relative to the target's accuracy. Vanguard composes with token-level speculative decoding and matches trained process reward models on mathematics, turning speculation from a way to save the large model's work into one that can improve on it.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce Vanguard, a training-free screenshot-aware judge for step-level speculative vision-language agents that matches or beats larger target models while calling them on only a minority of steps.
AI.motivation: Vision-language agents suffer high latency from calling large models at every step, while text-only judges in step-level speculation cannot verify whether a small draft model's action fits the current screen.
AI.method: Vanguard uses a general decision model with the screenshot in view to score candidate draft steps in one forward pass, accepting the best candidate above a calibrated threshold and falling back to the large target model otherwise.
AI.result: On web, mobile, and embodied agents, a 2B draft judged by Vanguard matches or exceeds an 8B target (and beats a 27B cross-family target in speed and accuracy) while calling the target on a minority of steps, transfers across unseen websites, and composes with token-level speculation.
AI.conclusion: Screen-grounded judging turns step-level speculation from a pure speedup technique into a way to outperform larger target models at lower cost.

title: Cardiac MRI-informed electrocardiography enables biologically grounded cardiomyopathy detection
summary: Precise myocardial phenotyping at population scale is limited by the cost and accessibility of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), whereas electrocardiography (ECG) is widely available but reflects electrical rather than structural and functional information. Here we develop MyoECG, a cross-modal representation learning framework that distils myocardial structural and functional knowledge from CMR into standard 12-lead ECGs, enabling imaging-informed cardiomyopathy detection and subtype classification from ECGs alone. MyoECG was pretrained on 45,241 paired ECG-CMR examinations from UK Biobank and a tertiary cardiovascular centre, then developed and validated across more than 1.8 million ECGs from seven independent datasets. Across internal and external datasets spanning prevalences of 0.2-54.7%, MyoECG outperformed five pretrained ECG foundation models, with AUROCs of 0.800-0.974 for cardiomyopathy detection. In a multi-reader study of six cardiologists, MyoECG assistance improved mean sensitivity by 0.109 (95% CI, 0.041-0.175; P = 0.009) and specificity by 0.056 (95% CI, 0.004-0.108; P = 0.040). In 41,128 UK Biobank participants, the MyoECG score showed genetic correlations with cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.409) and dilated cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.371), genome-wide associations at four loci, including regions mapped to NFIA and KCNQ1, and associations with 69 circulating proteins related to myocardial stress, cell adhesion, vascular biology and metabolism. The cardiomyopathy correlation attenuated to non-significance after adjustment for 27 measured CMR traits (rg = 0.131; P = 0.143), indicating that the score captures CMR-derived information rather than dataset-specific shortcuts. MyoECG offers a scalable route to CMR-informed cardiomyopathy assessment and a strategy for transferring knowledge from resource-intensive imaging to widely deployable physiological signals.

AI.tldr: The authors develop MyoECG, a cross-modal representation learning framework that distills cardiac MRI knowledge into 12-lead ECGs for scalable, biologically grounded cardiomyopathy detection.
AI.motivation: Cardiac MRI provides detailed myocardial phenotyping but is costly and limited, whereas ECG is widely accessible yet reflects electrical rather than structural and functional information.
AI.method: MyoECG is pretrained on 45,241 paired ECG-CMR exams from UK Biobank and a tertiary center to distill CMR structural and functional knowledge into ECG representations, then validated on over 1.8 million ECGs across seven datasets.
AI.result: MyoECG outperforms five ECG foundation models with AUROCs of 0.800-0.974, improves cardiologist sensitivity by 0.109 and specificity by 0.056, and shows genetic correlations with cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.409) and 69 circulating proteins that attenuate to non-significance (rg = 0.131) after adjusting for 27 CMR traits.
AI.conclusion: Cross-modal distillation from CMR into ECGs enables scalable, biologically valid cardiomyopathy detection from standard electrocardiograms.

title: Can you make models believe false facts in the prompt?
summary: Making LLMs believe false facts is useful for alignment evaluations and for building model organisms. Previous work explored doing so with Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF). But SDF requires fine-tuning one new model for each set of injected false beliefs. To enable larger scale SDF-powered alignment evaluations, we attempt to produce a single model that believes any fact placed in a <facts> tag in the prompt. To do so, we explore doing prompt-conditioned SDF: fine-tuning a model on synthetic documents covering thousands of facts, with each document conditioned on a fact presented in the prompt. We evaluate how deeply the model believes the facts provided in the prompt using evaluations from prior work and a new Jacobian lens evaluation. We find that the belief depth on unseen facts scales roughly log-linearly with the number of training facts, making this a cheap, promising avenue for making models believe false facts, though preliminary experiments on applying it to alignment audits on the small model we studied showed negative results due to these small models often already acting as if they believed facts provided in regular honeypot system prompts. Using RL to reduce the rate at which models verbalize following a false fact in the prompt, on top of prompt-conditioned SDF, generalizes to held-out evals and almost matches SDF on some evaluations. But training against one of our metrics for belief depth makes it harder to trust those evaluations.

AI.tldr: The authors explore prompt-conditioned Synthetic Document Finetuning to make a single LLM believe false facts placed in a prompt tag, finding that belief depth scales log-linearly with training facts.
AI.motivation: Standard Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF) requires training a separate model for each set of injected false beliefs, limiting its scalability for alignment evaluations and model organisms.
AI.method: They fine-tune a model on synthetic documents covering thousands of facts, each conditioned on a `<facts>` tag in the prompt, and evaluate belief depth using prior evals, a new Jacobian lens, and RL to suppress verbalization.
AI.result: Belief depth on unseen facts scales roughly log-linearly with training facts, and adding RL generalizes to held-out evals, though small models already act as if they believe honeypot system prompts and optimizing against a belief metric reduces evaluation trust.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-conditioned SDF offers a scalable path to configurable false-belief model organisms, though metric gaming and small-model baselines complicate alignment audits.

title: GLIDE: Scalable and Event-Aware Inductive Forecasting over Evolving Logistics Graphs
summary: Accurate forecasting of order volume at scale-effect hotspots (SEHs), spatially coherent groups of logistics flows that serve as distributed optimization units for real-time many-to-one dispatch, is a prerequisite for efficient order pooling in on-demand food delivery (OFD) platforms such as Meituan. However, real-world logistics networks present unique challenges that render standard spatiotemporal prediction model ineffective. (i) Dynamic Topology: Unlike static road networks, logistics graphs are ephemeral, with hotspot emerging and vanishing continuously; (ii) Scale--Volume Heterogeneity: Graph sizes vary from $10^2$ to $10^4$, while zero-inflated, long-tailed volumes create computational bottlenecks and bias predictions toward inactivity; and (iii) Event-Driven Disruption: Exogenous events (holidays, weather, academic calendars) induce systematic demand shifts that purely data-driven backbones cannot anticipate. In this paper, we present GLIDE, a production-ready framework that models evolving logistics graphs in a scalable latent space while adapting to heterogeneous demand regimes and event-driven shifts. GLIDE introduces a Graph-Guided Latent Aggregation mechanism, which dynamically projects varying physical subgraphs into a fixed-size, semantically stable latent space via a differentiable sparse assignment...

AI.tldr: The authors present GLIDE, a scalable framework for forecasting order volumes at dynamic logistics hotspots in on-demand food delivery networks.
AI.motivation: Standard spatiotemporal models fail on real-world food delivery logistics graphs because hotspots emerge and vanish dynamically, graph sizes vary from 10^2 to 10^4 with zero-inflated volumes, and exogenous events shift demand.
AI.method: GLIDE introduces a Graph-Guided Latent Aggregation mechanism that projects varying physical subgraphs into a fixed-size, semantically stable latent space via differentiable sparse assignment while adapting to heterogeneous regimes and events.
AI.result: GLIDE provides a production-ready framework capable of handling dynamic topology, scale-volume heterogeneity, and event-driven disruptions in on-demand food delivery platforms like Meituan.
AI.conclusion: Projecting evolving logistics graphs into a fixed-size latent space enables scalable, event-aware inductive forecasting for real-time order pooling.

title: SCAFFOLD: Toward Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport for Reusable LLM-Agent Skills
summary: An agent skill that succeeded yesterday may be executable today without being justified for reuse today. Tests may cover only observable contract clauses, outcome oracles may be absent, evaluations may inherit the same erroneous specification, and permissions or dependencies may change between validation and invocation. We argue that the appropriate unit of prospective trust is a Warranted Reuse Claim (WRC): a defeasible, claim-specific authorization tied to a versioned skill, target context, evidence, assumptions, and identified defeaters. The paper sharpens this position through Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport (WPET), a proposed discipline for deciding which historical evidence remains admissible after context change. It distinguishes evidence admissibility from truth of the supported safety or effectiveness claim; states a conditional preservation result and its limits; specifies three-valued applicability and asymmetric context-transfer judgments; and illustrates how provenance dependence and policy-invalidating changes alter authorization. We explicitly relate the proposal to assurance cases, contracts, and skill-library maintenance rather than claiming novelty for their ingredients. A falsifiable longitudinal evaluation would compare WRC-guided policies with strong version-aware baselines at matched coverage, utility, and review cost. This paper contributes a formalized problem statement, testable design obligations, and reporting protocol, not an implemented verifier, empirical superiority result, or proof of universal agent safety.

AI.tldr: The authors propose Warranted Reuse Claims (WRC) and Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport (WPET) to formalize when historical validation evidence remains admissible for reusing LLM-agent skills in new contexts.
AI.motivation: An agent skill that passed tests previously may not be justified for reuse after permissions, dependencies, or contexts change, especially when tests are incomplete or outcome oracles are absent.
AI.method: They formalize WRC as a defeasible, claim-specific authorization tied to versioned skills, contexts, evidence, and defeaters, and define WPET with three-valued applicability, asymmetric context-transfer judgments, and a conditional preservation result.
AI.result: The paper contributes a formalized problem statement, testable design obligations, and a longitudinal evaluation protocol comparing WRC-guided policies against version-aware baselines, rather than an implemented verifier or empirical results.
AI.conclusion: Warrant-preserving evidence transport provides a principled conceptual foundation for prospective trust in reusable LLM-agent skills.

title: Space-X: Self-Evolving Spatial Agents Weaving Clues into Evidence Chains
summary: Spatial reasoning connects visual observations, geometric estimates, and linguistic decisions into a coherent derivation. Yet tool-augmented agents often acquire evidence without clear targets, combine outputs under inconsistent object or reference-frame semantics, and misjudge evidence sufficiency. Thus, more tools or calls do not reliably improve reasoning. We introduce Space-X, a spatial-reasoning framework that self-evolves toward complete, continuous evidence-chain construction. An Execution Agent acquires, associates, and judges evidence per problem using role-specific memory. A Control Agent diagnoses evidence-chain breaks from execution traces and jointly revises tools, interfaces, skills, memory organization, and decision rules. This loop co-evolves capability and evidence use: evidence needs guide capability development; usable results guide actions. Across multiple benchmarks, Space-X yields gains with four base models. Relative to baselines, GPT-6-sol improves answer accuracy on ViewSpatial and MMSI by 50.39% and 23.07%, respectively; Gemini-3.8-Flash gains 47.50% and 25.22% on these benchmarks. This provides a unified route from fragmented spatial clues to traceable, derivable answers.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce Space-X, a self-evolving multi-agent spatial reasoning framework that constructs continuous evidence chains, boosting accuracy on ViewSpatial and MMSI by up to 50.39%.
AI.motivation: Tool-augmented spatial agents often gather evidence without clear targets, mix inconsistent reference frames, and misjudge sufficiency, so adding more tool calls fails to improve reasoning.
AI.method: Space-X pairs an Execution Agent that gathers and judges evidence using role-specific memory with a Control Agent that diagnoses evidence-chain breaks from traces and jointly revises tools, interfaces, skills, memory, and decision rules.
AI.result: Across four base models, Space-X improves accuracy over baselines, with GPT-6-sol gaining 50.39% on ViewSpatial and 23.07% on MMSI, and Gemini-3.8-Flash gaining 47.50% and 25.22%.
AI.conclusion: Co-evolving execution capabilities and evidence-chain construction turns fragmented spatial clues into traceable, accurate derivations.

title: Test-Time Symmetrization: Scaling Laws for Model-Agnostic Learning under Structure
summary: Test-time compute has emerged as a powerful way to improve the accuracy of language models at inference time, with scaling laws quantifying how accuracy improves with additional forward passes. Existing scaling laws, however, focus on repeated sampling from a fixed prompt, even though many tasks admit multiple equivalent representations of the same underlying problem. A graph does not depend on how its nodes are numbered, and a program does not depend on the names of its variables, yet language models can change their answers under such rewritings. In this paper, we study test-time symmetrization, which uses forward passes on rewritings of the input and aggregates the resulting answers over the group $G$ of rewritings. We prove that no amount of sampling and repeated decoding from a single representation can replace rewriting, while only $O(\log |G|)$ random rewritings suffice to recover the information provided by all $|G|$ rewritings. The same set of $O(\log |G|)$ rewritings provides simultaneous approximation across models, decoding rules, and sampled reasoning traces, and the logarithmic scaling is optimal in general. We validate the theory with experiments on Qwen2.5-7B, Phi-4-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen2.5-14B, with chain-of-thought reasoning, on graph reasoning, logical deduction, and multiple-choice question answering. At the same number of forward passes, spending them on rewritings of the input is substantially more accurate than spending them on repeated sampling from the original prompt whenever the model's answer depends on how the input is written, and the number of rewritings needed grows only logarithmically with the number of possible rewritings, as the theory predicts. Our results provide a principled way to enforce symmetries at inference time when they cannot be built into the model, which we call model-agnostic symmetrization.

AI.tldr: The authors study test-time symmetrization over equivalent input rewritings, proving and demonstrating empirically that O(log |G|) random rewritings suffice and outperform repeated sampling from a fixed prompt.
AI.motivation: Existing test-time scaling laws focus on repeated sampling from one prompt, overlooking that tasks like graphs and programs have equivalent representations that often change LLM answers.
AI.method: They aggregate forward passes over random rewritings from a symmetry group G, proving that no amount of single-prompt sampling can replace rewriting and that O(log |G|) rewritings suffice across models and decoding rules.
AI.result: Experiments on Qwen2.5-7B, Phi-4-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen2.5-14B across graph reasoning, logical deduction, and MCQA confirm that spending compute on rewritings is substantially more accurate than repeated sampling and scales logarithmically with |G|.
AI.conclusion: Model-agnostic test-time symmetrization offers a principled, compute-efficient way to enforce input symmetries at inference time.

title: Attention Is Not Relevance: Challenging the Causality of Attention in Autonomous Driving
summary: Attention has become one of the most widely adopted solutions for estimating the relevance of surrounding objects and interpreting an autonomous vehicle's driving decisions. However, its ability to capture the causal impact of individual input elements on an AI model's output has long been discussed in the literature, particularly in the Natural Language Processing (NLP) domain. This work brings this discussion into the autonomous driving domain by analyzing the accuracy of attention in estimating the impact of an input object on an autonomous vehicle's driving, i.e., its relevance. To this end, we compare different attention-based relevance estimation methods against a causal reference of object relevance obtained through counterfactual analysis. We perform our analysis on more than 80,000 synthetic driving scenes using an autonomous vehicle based on PlanT 2.0, a state-of-the-art Transformer-based model for object-level planning. Results show that attention provides a correlational rather than causal indication of object relevance. Attention-based relevance estimation methods do not consistently identify all relevant objects and tend to incorrectly classify as relevant objects with little or no impact on the vehicle's driving. In particular, results show that attention can effectively identify relevant objects in simple single-lane, straight-road scenarios, but its accuracy degrades in more complex settings, such as multi-lane roads and intersections. These findings highlight the limitations of attention as a proxy for object relevance, calling for novel methods able to accurately capture the causal impact of individual objects on the vehicle's driving and distinguish it from correlational associations.

AI.tldr: The authors evaluate attention-based object relevance against counterfactual causal ground truth on over 80,000 synthetic driving scenes, finding that attention is correlational rather than causal.
AI.motivation: Attention is widely used to interpret autonomous driving decisions and estimate surrounding object relevance, yet its ability to capture true causal impact has not been systematically tested in driving.
AI.method: Using PlanT 2.0 on over 80,000 synthetic driving scenes, they compare attention-based relevance estimation methods against a causal reference of object relevance derived from counterfactual analysis.
AI.result: Attention captures relevant objects in simple single-lane straight roads, but degrades on multi-lane roads and intersections, missing relevant objects and misclassifying irrelevant ones.
AI.conclusion: Attention is an unreliable proxy for causal object relevance in complex driving scenarios, motivating methods that directly capture causal impact.

title: 3D GameDev Arena: Benchmarking Coding Agents That Plan, Build, and Playtest extreme Long-Horizon Browser Games
summary: Coding agents now resolve repository issues and generate compact playable games, but whether they can build a large 3D game from scratch remains open. Such games tightly couple mechanics, scenes, assets, and interaction logic, and their quality rests on player enjoyment, which existing benchmarks rarely assess. Thus, we introduce 3D GameDev Arena, a first extreme long-horizon benchmark of 108 from-scratch game-development tasks across 14 genres. Given only a text specification and UI/UX reference images, a fully automated plan--implement--test--repair pipeline builds each task into a self-contained browser game. Runs average $\sim$1,000 LLM calls ; the longest uses 14,407 calls, 2.13B tokens, and 608 assets. Evaluation spans (1) objective code-level functional acceptance against the game specification, (2) agent-based QA and playtesting of 3D presentation and playability, and (3) blind pairwise Bradley-Terry human preference in a public arena. The preliminary findings indicate that long-horizon 3D game development remains far from solved, and code-level correctness alone does not dictate player preference. The public arena is hosted online.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces 3D GameDev Arena, a benchmark of 108 from-scratch 3D browser game-development tasks across 14 genres, and finds that long-horizon 3D game development remains far from solved and code-level correctness alone does not dictate player preference.
AI.motivation: Existing coding-agent benchmarks rarely assess whether agents can build large 3D games from scratch, where mechanics, scenes, assets, and interaction logic are tightly coupled and quality depends on player enjoyment.
AI.method: Given a text specification and UI/UX reference images, an automated plan-implement-test-repair pipeline builds each task into a self-contained browser game, evaluated via objective code-level functional acceptance, agent-based QA and playtesting, and blind pairwise Bradley-Terry human preference in a public arena.
AI.result: Runs average about 1,000 LLM calls, with the longest run using 14,407 calls, 2.13B tokens, and 608 assets; preliminary findings show that long-horizon 3D game development is far from solved and code-level correctness does not solely determine player preference.
AI.conclusion: 3D GameDev Arena provides a realistic extreme long-horizon benchmark and public arena that highlights the gap between functional code generation and player-enjoyable 3D game creation.

title: Embodied Graph: A Relational World Model for Long-Horizon Tasks
summary: Long-horizon tasks in embodied and web environments involve extended decision sequences and delayed feedback, making accurate planning crucial for success. World models tackle this by learning latent dynamics for imagination-based planning. However, existing approaches merely rely on dense pixel-level observations, which forces the model to absorb redundant information while overlooking relations among task-relevant entities. Consequently, small errors may accumulate over long imagined rollouts and gradually corrupt the predictions. In this paper, we explore world models that imagine over sparse state abstractions, which poses two key challenges: 1) how to remove redundant information and form a compact state abstraction; 2) how to incorporate the relational structure to learn reliable long-horizon dynamics. To address these challenges, we propose Embodied Graph, a relational state abstraction that supports structured dynamics modeling and long-horizon imagination, and the Relational World Model (RWM), which performs imagination directly over graph states. RWM consists of (i) a Task-Aware Embodied Graph Constructor that filters redundant details and maintains graph memory through online updates, and (ii) an Embodied Graph Recurrent State Space Model that learns node-wise latent dynamics while capturing inter-node dependencies. The imagined graph states provide predictions of action consequences to guide decision-making. Experiments on Minecraft and Crafter demonstrate the effectiveness of RWM in embodied environments. Notably, in Minecraft, RWM is the only method that obtains diamonds within the given budget. Experiments on web interaction further illustrate the applicability of relational state prediction to the decision making process of web agents.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Embodied Graph and the Relational World Model (RWM) to perform long-horizon imagination over sparse, structured graph states rather than dense pixels, outperforming baselines in Minecraft, Crafter, and web interaction.
AI.motivation: Existing world models for long-horizon tasks rely on dense pixel-level observations, absorbing redundant information and overlooking inter-entity relations, which causes small errors to accumulate over long imagined rollouts.
AI.method: RWM combines a Task-Aware Embodied Graph Constructor that filters redundant details and maintains graph memory via online updates with an Embodied Graph Recurrent State Space Model that learns node-wise latent dynamics and inter-node dependencies.
AI.result: Experiments on Minecraft and Crafter show RWM's effectiveness, with RWM being the only method in Minecraft to obtain diamonds within the given budget, and web interaction experiments further demonstrate its applicability to web agents.
AI.conclusion: Imagining over sparse relational graph abstractions enables more reliable long-horizon dynamics modeling and decision-making in both embodied and web environments.

title: Fast Bayesian Methods for Uncertainty Quantification in Sparse AI Evaluation
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 AI Measurement Science Workshop
summary: Estimating how an AI system will perform on a new benchmark need not require another large model. We use public evaluation counts to choose a weak Beta prior, then update it exactly from at most 31 revealed outcomes. The predictor uses no item semantics, pretrained weights, or inference API. Its single online evaluation in the AIMS competition returned a team-reported Brier ALC of 0.188477, a 24.6% reduction from the constant-0.5 reference. The complete submission is 7,754 bytes; a server microbenchmark measures 12.71 microseconds per prediction with 31 matching labels. We describe how source evaluations are compressed into 301 prior means and show why a concentration of two lets new evidence rapidly determine the prediction. The resulting posterior gives exact uncertainty about the modelled success rate without numerical integration or neural inference. A public evaluation covers 79 system-benchmark pairs and eight seeds, reaching Brier ALC 0.200250 for the submitted method. Accompanying code and sufficient statistics reconstruct the fitted prior byte for byte and replay all 632 evaluation trajectories. The result demonstrates how much predictive value a compact Bayesian model can extract from sparse target feedback at very low online cost.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a compact, model-free Bayesian method that uses a weak Beta prior derived from public evaluation counts and updates it exactly from up to 31 revealed outcomes to predict AI benchmark performance.
AI.motivation: Estimating how an AI system will perform on a new benchmark often relies on another large model, whereas a lightweight statistical approach could extract predictive value from sparse target feedback at minimal online cost.
AI.method: The method compresses source evaluations into 301 prior means to choose a weak Beta prior with concentration two, then updates it analytically with at most 31 revealed outcomes without item semantics, pretrained weights, or inference APIs.
AI.result: In the AIMS competition, the 7,754-byte submission achieved a team-reported Brier ALC of 0.188477 (a 24.6% reduction from the 0.5 constant reference) at 12.71 microseconds per prediction, and reached 0.200250 Brier ALC across 79 system-benchmark pairs and eight seeds in public evaluation.
AI.conclusion: A compact exact Bayesian model can provide accurate uncertainty quantification and strong predictive performance from sparse target feedback at negligible computational cost.

title: GALA: Gallery-Level Alignment for Real-Life Vision Decoding from EEG
summary: Neural decoding of visual experience from electroencephalography (EEG) has achieved strong performance in intra-subject settings, but current methods fail to generalize across individuals: on the standard 200-way benchmark THINGS-EEG-2, top-1 accuracy drops from above 80% within subjects to about 32% for an unseen subject. Adapting a pre-trained encoder to new subjects and sessions typically requires labeled data, a bottleneck whose collection time severely limits practical device deployment. In a practical Brain-Computer Interface (BCI), however, the possible outcomes are known in advance and form a gallery of candidates, and the unlabeled EEG of the user accumulates as soon as the device is used. We propose a new setting, incremental transductive calibration, in which the decoder is calibrated regularly on all the unlabeled EEG received so far and on the known gallery, without any labels. This setting is closer to the conditions of a deployed BCI than the zero-shot and batch evaluations in current use. We evaluate it with a protocol in which queries arrive one at a time, with unknown and possibly unequal frequencies, and each query is decoded before it is used for calibration. In this setting, we introduce GALA : GAllery-Level Alignment, a label-free calibration method which registers the unlabeled EEG embeddings onto the gallery through shrinkage whitening, hubness correction and a Sinkhorn--Procrustes alignment with query frequencies estimated from the buffer, updated after every query. On THINGS-EEG-2, with a gallery of 200 images, it raises the top-1 accuracy on a new subject from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes of use. Across 60 evaluation settings that vary the gallery size, the query frequencies and the number of repetitions averaged per query, GALA is the most accurate label-free method in every setting, 6.6 points above the best competing method on average at the end of the stream.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces incremental transductive calibration for EEG-based visual decoding and proposes GALA, a label-free calibration method that raises cross-subject top-1 accuracy on THINGS-EEG-2 from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes of use.
AI.motivation: Cross-subject EEG visual decoding suffers severe accuracy drops (from over 80% within-subject to about 32% on unseen subjects on THINGS-EEG-2), and collecting labeled calibration data for new users is a major bottleneck for practical BCIs.
AI.method: GALA registers unlabeled EEG embeddings onto a known candidate gallery using shrinkage whitening, hubness correction, and Sinkhorn-Procrustes alignment with query frequencies estimated from the buffer, updated after every incoming query.
AI.result: On THINGS-EEG-2 with a 200-image gallery, GALA improves new-subject top-1 accuracy from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes of use, and ranks as the most accurate label-free method across all 60 evaluation settings, averaging 6.6 points above the best competing method.
AI.conclusion: Incremental transductive calibration with GALA enables practical, label-free adaptation of EEG visual decoders to unseen subjects under realistic deployment conditions.

title: Learning to Coordinate: LLM-Guided Workflow Evolution for Token-Efficient Red Teaming
summary: Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. Moreover, a target model's response indicates the outcome of a test without identifying which collaboration decision should change. We present Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves an executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case. L2C represents agent responsibilities, execution dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph, and associates each graph with records of the information actually delivered and produced. A controller trained through supervised fine-tuning integrates these records with target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain the workflow, refine instructions, restructure collaboration, or lock further editing. This design connects feedback to explicit changes in subsequent execution while allowing a useful organization to continue without repeated controller intervention. The evaluation protocol covers HarmBench with three execution backbones and two target models, together with component ablations, dataset transfer, and evaluator checks. Across the six executor-target configurations, L2C improves ASR over EvoSynth by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%. L2C connects adaptive collaboration to the resource requirements of automated security evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves executable multi-agent workflows per red-teaming case, improving attack success rate while cutting online token usage by over 35%.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent automated red teaming can be expensive due to repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective routing, and target model responses do not directly indicate which collaboration decision should change.
AI.method: L2C represents agent responsibilities, dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph paired with execution records, and uses an SFT-trained controller to retain, refine, restructure, or lock workflows based on target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget.
AI.result: Across six executor-target configurations on HarmBench, L2C improves attack success rate (ASR) over EvoSynth by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%.
AI.conclusion: Adapting multi-agent collaboration structures based on execution feedback makes automated LLM red teaming both more effective and more token-efficient.

title: From Points to Trajectories: Rethinking Multimodal Alignment for Physical Events
summary: Advancing physical artificial intelligence (Physical AI) requires moving beyond static object recognition to ground how real-world mechanics (e.g., impact, friction, and force transfer) unfold over time. While multimodal aligners seek to capture these interactions by matching multi-sensor streams, prevailing architectures compress each temporal sequence into a single pooled embedding. We show that this paradigm fails on twin events: distinct physical executions recorded under identical task conditions. Collapsing the temporal dimension averages out transient cross-modal dynamics, effectively reducing physical event alignment to static scene recognition. Formally, we prove that as sequence length increases, any temporally pooled representation converges to the stationary recording condition. Consequently, as windows grow, no choice of loss function or embedding geometry can disambiguate twin events from pooled features alone. Instead, we show that physical events are uniquely identified by the event gap, namely the instantaneous, synchronous co-fluctuations across modalities that are erased by pooling and accumulate only along unpooled trajectories. To recover this signal, we introduce CounterPoint, a lightweight plug-in module that strips out each modality's temporal mean to score frame-level cross-modal agreement. Integrated across four state-of-the-art (SOTA) multimodal aligners, CounterPoint shifts representations from coarse condition matching to fine-grained physical event alignment, consistently outperforming existing temporal alignment methods.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that temporally pooled multimodal aligners cannot disambiguate twin physical events and introduces CounterPoint, a lightweight plug-in that recovers frame-level cross-modal co-fluctuations.
AI.motivation: Prevailing multimodal aligners compress temporal sequences into a single pooled embedding, which averages out transient cross-modal dynamics and reduces physical event alignment to static scene recognition, failing on twin events recorded under identical conditions.
AI.method: The authors prove that temporally pooled features converge to stationary recording conditions as sequence length grows, and propose CounterPoint, a plug-in module that strips out each modality's temporal mean to score frame-level cross-modal agreement along unpooled trajectories.
AI.result: Integrated across four state-of-the-art multimodal aligners, CounterPoint shifts representations from coarse condition matching to fine-grained physical event alignment and consistently outperforms existing temporal alignment methods.
AI.conclusion: Preserving unpooled trajectory co-fluctuations rather than relying on temporal pooling is essential for grounding physical interactions in Physical AI.

title: Beyond Corpus-Driven Imitation: Evolving Musical Mindsets in the Agentic Orchestra via Quantum Reinforcement Learning
comment: This is the accepted, prepublication version of a paper forthcoming in Computer Music Journal, MIT Press. Beyond routine editorial and typesetting amendments, the content remains subject to further revision before final publication
summary: This paper presents a framework for computer-aided music composition and performance based on quantum reinforcement learning and multi-agent interaction. We introduce the agentic orchestra, where musical agents evolve distinct mindsets through trial-and-error engagement with a musical environment, rather than through training on large datasets. The agents are implemented as parameterised quantum circuits. They evolve distinct compositional behaviours, referred to as mindsets. This enables the exploration of musical decision spaces using quantum superposition and entanglement within a hybrid quantum-classical loop. We present two complementary agent architectures: atomistic agents, which process pitch and rhythm independently, and holistic agents, which handle pitch and duration as unified note events. Mindsets are shaped through musically grounded reward functions, which can be combined and weighted to develop different mindsets across agents. The resulting system positions quantum computing agents less as autonomous composers and more as adaptive musical partners, each developing its own musical personality through interaction rather than imitation. Demonstrations show how agents generalise their learned behaviour to previously unseen material, operating in interactive and offline batch modes using MIDI-encoded music. While quantum computers are still in development, experiments conducted on IBM quantum hardware confirmed that musically meaningful learning is achievable with existing quantum computers. For composers and performers, the agentic orchestra opens new possibilities for emergent, process-oriented musical creativity, offering a scalable foundation for quantum computer-aided music composition as quantum computing technology continues to advance.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an agentic orchestra framework using quantum reinforcement learning, where parameterized quantum circuit agents evolve distinct musical mindsets through interaction rather than training on large corpora.
AI.motivation: Traditional computer-aided music composition relies on corpus-driven imitation, whereas interactive, process-oriented creativity could emerge from agents developing distinct musical personalities through trial-and-error engagement.
AI.method: The framework implements atomistic agents (processing pitch and rhythm independently) and holistic agents (handling pitch and duration as unified note events) as parameterized quantum circuits trained in a hybrid quantum-classical loop with weighted, musically grounded reward functions.
AI.result: Demonstrations on MIDI-encoded music in interactive and offline batch modes show generalization to unseen material, and experiments on IBM quantum hardware confirm that musically meaningful learning is achievable on existing quantum computers.
AI.conclusion: The agentic orchestra establishes a scalable foundation for quantum computer-aided music composition where quantum agents act as adaptive musical partners.

title: KnowledgeClaw: Towards Agentic Knowledge Engineering via Omnimodal Hypergraphs
summary: Knowledge engineering (KE) turns raw files into a reasoning-ready knowledge base, a task now within reach of LLM agents. KE has progressed from chunk and graph retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to memory agents, agentic KE and multimodal KE. However, a live knowledge base needs omnimodality, a closed-loop lifecycle and multi-granular application at once, yet existing systems meet at most two and no benchmark measures all three. We formalize Omnimodal Knowledge Engineering (OmniKE) and release OmniKE-Bench, six tasks with 1,829 model-free items over 3,960 real files in five modalities. We further propose KnowledgeClaw, an agentic system that builds an omnimodal typed hypergraph, keeps it current with a closed-loop lifecycle agent and routes each query to the granularity it needs. Against 30 baselines, it ranks first on all six tasks with an overall OKE of 55.9, +14.6 over the strongest baseline. Our software and data are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes Omnimodal Knowledge Engineering (OmniKE), releases OmniKE-Bench, and proposes KnowledgeClaw, an agentic system using an omnimodal typed hypergraph that ranks first across all six benchmark tasks.
AI.motivation: A live knowledge base requires omnimodality, a closed-loop lifecycle, and multi-granular application simultaneously, yet existing knowledge engineering systems meet at most two of these requirements and no benchmark evaluates all three.
AI.method: KnowledgeClaw constructs an omnimodal typed hypergraph, maintains it via a closed-loop lifecycle agent, and routes each query to the appropriate granularity, evaluated on OmniKE-Bench (six tasks, 1,829 model-free items over 3,960 real files in five modalities).
AI.result: Against 30 baselines on OmniKE-Bench, KnowledgeClaw ranks first on all six tasks and achieves an overall OKE score of 55.9, outperforming the strongest baseline by 14.6 points.
AI.conclusion: Combining omnimodal typed hypergraphs with closed-loop lifecycle management and granularity-aware routing advances agentic knowledge engineering.

title: OpenKAGE: Open-Ended Lifelong Learning in the Open World via Knowledge-Sharing Agent-Group Evolution
summary: Building autonomous agents that continually explore open worlds and acquire new capabilities through experience is a long-standing aspiration in artificial intelligence. Existing research often pursues lifelong learning within predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. We introduce OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning. Within this framework, agents autonomously explore open worlds and continually acquire new capabilities by accumulating and reusing knowledge from their own interactions and the experience of others. OpenKAGE builds on two key mechanisms: (1) a two-layer knowledge representation, with a memory layer for situated memories and an experience layer for transferable experience and skills that retains the applicability conditions needed for reuse; and (2) a knowledge-sharing mechanism that semantically consolidates textual experience into a continuously evolving shared knowledge graph, while executable skills are shared verbatim. In Minecraft, OpenKAGE supports open-ended lifelong learning, enabling agent groups to sustain exploration and reach advanced technological milestones. Furthermore, the accumulated knowledge can be transferred to a newly initialized agent group on a different backbone model, improving its survival and exploration progress.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning that enables agents in Minecraft to share situated memories, transferable experiences, and executable skills.
AI.motivation: Existing lifelong learning research typically focuses on predefined tasks or curricula and confines self-improvement to individual agents rather than collective open-ended exploration.
AI.method: OpenKAGE uses a two-layer knowledge representation (a memory layer for situated memories and an experience layer for transferable experience and skills with applicability conditions) and shares knowledge by consolidating textual experience into a shared knowledge graph while sharing executable skills verbatim.
AI.result: In Minecraft, OpenKAGE enables agent groups to sustain open-ended exploration and reach advanced technological milestones, and accumulated knowledge transfers to newly initialized agent groups on different backbone models to improve survival and exploration progress.
AI.conclusion: Collective knowledge consolidation and skill sharing across agent groups provide an effective mechanism for open-ended lifelong learning in complex open worlds.

title: Benchmarking LLM abilities on postdoc-level natural science problems
summary: Scientific problems have no answer key, so evaluating an agent means deciding what counts as a better solution before any agent is run. Existing benchmarks either match a symbolic answer against a key or, where they require executable work, score it by unit tests, by a rubric, or by position on a competition leaderboard. None of these is the criterion by which a field decides that one published method beats another. STEMBench adopts that criterion directly. Each of its twelve research problems in high-energy physics, astrophysics and neuroscience is scored by its own field's figure of merit, and each comes with two measured anchors: a submission that uses no domain knowledge, and an expert reference reproducing a published method, both obtained by running code shipped with the benchmark. The interval between them states how much of a problem is crossed by scientific insight rather than by engineering. Across eight frontier models, task-level wins and domain-level leadership dissociate: a model that wins five of the twelve tasks leads no domain mean. In the high-effort cross-model comparison, at least one model's mean score exceeds the expert anchor on seven of twelve tasks. The remaining five span uncertainty estimation, latent and causal inference, and cross-site clinical classification. Numerical scores and official-submission validity capture different aspects of performance and are reported separately. We release the tasks, graders, anchors and harness.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces STEMBench, a benchmark of 12 postdoc-level natural science problems scored by each field's own figure of merit with no-domain-knowledge and expert anchors, revealing that task-level wins dissociate from domain-level leadership.
