AI.tldr: This paper establishes nearly tight almost sure convergence rates and matching lower bounds for the last iterate of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) on convex objectives.
AI.motivation: Characterizing the almost sure convergence rate of the last iterate of SGD for convex objectives has remained an important theoretical question.
AI.method: The authors analyze deterministic, anytime stepsize policies for SGD on smooth and nonsmooth convex objectives and derive matching lower bounds.
AI.result: For smooth convex objectives, the last-iterate optimization error converges almost surely at rate k^(-1/3) when a stationary minimizer exists and k^(-1/4) otherwise (up to polylogarithmic factors), with k^(-1/4) extending to nonsmooth convex objectives; matching lower bounds show both exponents are optimal up to polylogarithmic factors.
AI.conclusion: The results resolve the almost sure last-iterate convergence rates of SGD for convex optimization up to polylogarithmic factors.

title: TableControl: Gesture Interaction Through Surface Vibrations
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures, accepted as demo paper on the ACM ISS
summary: Integrating gesture sensing into furniture offers a way to interact with digital applications and physical devices through familiar surfaces. We present TableControl, an interactive demonstration of continuous surface-vibration-based gesture recognition with the complete processing pipeline running on a microcontroller. Using four concealed piezoelectric sensors, the system combines signal acquisition and preprocessing with neural event detection and gesture classification. The resulting labels for knock, swipe-up, and swipe-down gestures are transmitted to a host computer without streaming the underlying sensor signals. Visitors explore two example applications through hands-on interaction: an endless runner game and a physical table lamp with on/off and brightness control. A dashboard displays recognized gestures, class probabilities, and processing times.

AI.tldr: This paper presents TableControl, an interactive demonstration of continuous surface-vibration-based gesture recognition running end-to-end on a microcontroller.
AI.motivation: Integrating gesture sensing into everyday furniture enables natural interaction with digital applications and physical devices through familiar surfaces.
AI.method: Using four concealed piezoelectric sensors, TableControl runs signal acquisition, preprocessing, neural event detection, and gesture classification (knock, swipe-up, swipe-down) entirely on a microcontroller, transmitting only gesture labels to a host computer.
AI.result: The demonstration showcases hands-on control of an endless runner game and a physical table lamp (on/off and brightness) alongside a dashboard displaying recognized gestures, class probabilities, and processing times.
AI.conclusion: TableControl demonstrates practical, privacy-preserving on-device gesture interaction on furniture surfaces without streaming raw sensor signals.

title: ViLFlow: Parallel Vision-Language Generation with Continuous Latent Flows
summary: Vision-language generation has predominantly relied on autoregressive and discrete diffusion models. Autoregressive models generate tokens sequentially, while discrete diffusion models typically predict tokens independently within each denoising step. We propose ViLFlow (Vision-Language Flow), a continuous-flow vision-language model that combines joint modeling of output embeddings with parallel token decoding. ViLFlow adapts pretrained continuous language generation to visual question answering and image captioning through learned image guidance and prediction-aware token decoding. A visually adapted teacher provides image-guided predictions as additional denoising supervision. The denoiser learns to reproduce these predictions directly, retaining one image-conditioned prediction per generation step. We train the token decoder on denoiser predictions and paired reference text to improve the conversion of continuous outputs into words. The decoder can be adapted independently, improving answering and captioning without further denoiser training. For captioning, it also supplies text feedback during late denoising, allowing decoded words to inform subsequent refinement. ViLFlow outperforms autoregressive and masked-diffusion baselines by up to 8.46 percentage points on VQAv2 and 4.50 points on GQA without GQA training. On COCO Karpathy test, it improves CIDEr by 16.25 over masked diffusion and 17.81 over sampled autoregression.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ViLFlow, a continuous-flow vision-language model that combines joint output embedding modeling with parallel token decoding for VQA and image captioning.
AI.motivation: Vision-language generation relies mainly on sequential autoregressive models or discrete diffusion models that predict tokens independently per denoising step.
AI.method: ViLFlow adapts pretrained continuous language generation via learned image guidance from a visually adapted teacher and a prediction-aware token decoder that can be adapted independently and provide text feedback during late denoising for captioning.
AI.result: ViLFlow outperforms autoregressive and masked-diffusion baselines by up to 8.46 percentage points on VQAv2 and 4.50 points on GQA (without GQA training), and improves CIDEr on COCO Karpathy test by 16.25 over masked diffusion and 17.81 over sampled autoregression.
AI.conclusion: Continuous latent flows with image guidance and prediction-aware decoding offer a strong parallel alternative to autoregressive and discrete diffusion vision-language generation.

title: RespCCT and FreqCCT: Compact, Explainable and Cost-Aware Convolutional Transformers for Multi-Class Respiratory Disease Classification
comment: 22 pages. Manuscript to be submitted to Biomedical Signal Processing and Control
summary: Chest auscultation depends on the listener, and software that classifies lung sounds could give a second reading where trained listeners are scarce. The most accurate published classifiers fine-tune large pretrained networks, and their accuracy is rarely reported with running cost or paired statistics. This study makes three contributions. (i) It proposes RespCCT and FreqCCT, two compact convolutional transformers of 173,187 and 124,999 parameters that learn from random initialization on mel, constant-Q and cepstral images of 5 s frames from three public databases, ICBHI, KAUH and RD@TR, with 1,665 audio files in seven classes. (ii) It compares both models with five ImageNet-pretrained networks and larger distilled variants on one test set, using paired bootstrap intervals. (iii) It measures the cost of every pipeline stage on one CPU thread, tests whether attribution maps depend on the trained weights, and probes whether the learned features reveal the recording source. On the test fold, RespCCT reaches an accuracy of 98.13% and a macro F1 of 0.970, and FreqCCT reaches 97.58% and 0.951. Over five folds, RespCCT with three seeds reaches 97.65% and 0.959, and FreqCCT with one seed reaches 96.95% and 0.941. The two strongest pretrained networks reach a macro F1 of 0.984, whereas RespCCT needs 2.0 to 64.6 times less weight storage. Computing the three input images takes longer than running either model, and a linear probe identifies the source database with 0.958 accuracy. A team can weigh accuracy against storage and time before device testing.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes RespCCT and FreqCCT, two compact convolutional transformers trained from scratch for multi-class respiratory disease classification from lung sounds, and benchmarks their accuracy, storage, and CPU cost.
AI.motivation: Accurate lung sound classifiers typically fine-tune large pretrained networks without reporting running cost or paired statistics, limiting deployment assessment where trained listeners or compute are scarce.
AI.method: The authors train RespCCT (173,187 parameters) and FreqCCT (124,999 parameters) from random initialization on mel, constant-Q, and cepstral images of 5 s frames across 1,665 audio files in seven classes from ICBHI, KAUH, and RD@TR, comparing against five ImageNet-pretrained networks and larger distilled variants using paired bootstrap intervals and single-thread CPU profiling.
AI.result: On the test fold, RespCCT reaches 98.13% accuracy (0.970 macro F1) and FreqCCT reaches 97.58% (0.951 macro F1), with 2.0x to 64.6x less weight storage than the strongest pretrained networks (0.984 macro F1); input image computation takes longer than model inference, and a linear probe identifies the source database with 0.958 accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Compact convolutional transformers trained from scratch achieve near-pretrained accuracy with dramatically smaller storage, enabling teams to weigh accuracy against storage and CPU time before device deployment.

title: Exploring Daily Emotional Well-Being through Personalized Data Analysis
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: This project analysed daily emotional well-being from a personalized perspective using records of emotional states and contextual information derived from daily life. It was based on the idea that well-being is not a fixed value, but varies from day to day, and can be better understood in relation to individual context and behaviour. The work is framed within the field of Data Science and focuses on emotional states at an individual level. The project focused on constructing an integrated daily dataset from multiple personal data sources and analysing emotional states. The distributions of emotional variables, their temporal evolution and the differences between users were studied, together with their variability over time. Personality and well-being questionnaires were also incorporated as stable references to better contextualize daily emotional results. A simple personalized recommendation approach was then developed by comparing similar days within each user, exploring how past contextual conditions relate to differences in the user's emotional state. Finally, machine learning techniques were used to evaluate whether daily contextual information contains signals that help distinguish between different types of days relative to a person's usual well-being. The project adopted an applied approach, with an exploratory scope focused on understanding patterns rather than building a fully predictive system. The results showed that emotional well-being is very personal and changes from day to day. General models had limited value, while personalized approaches captured these differences much better, highlighting the importance of analysing each person on their own terms.

AI.tldr: This exploratory Data Science project analyzes daily emotional well-being using integrated personal and contextual data, finding that personalized models capture day-to-day emotional variations much better than general models.
AI.motivation: Emotional well-being varies from day to day in relation to individual context and behavior rather than remaining a fixed value, motivating personalized analysis.
AI.method: The project integrates multiple personal data sources, daily emotional states, contextual information, and personality/well-being questionnaires, then builds a simple personalized recommendation approach comparing similar days within each user and evaluates machine learning models to distinguish day types.
AI.result: General models showed limited value, whereas personalized approaches captured individual differences and day-to-day emotional variations much better.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of analyzing emotional well-being on an individualized basis rather than relying solely on general population models.

title: Harmonic Circuit: Chord Progression Lies in a Sparse Principal Information Flow in Symbolic Music Models
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpretability for Discovery. 12 pages, 6 figures
summary: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) seeks to decode neural network computations into human-understandable logic. A core methodology in MI is circuit discovery: identifying the information flow in sub-networks that drive specific model behaviors. While circuit discovery has matured within Natural Language Processing (NLP), the interpretable circuits in music models remain largely unexplored. In this work, we identify a music-functional circuit within two symbolic music generative models: ChatMusician and MuPT. The music function we consider is the prediction of the terminal tonic root in a classical harmonic progression pattern $I \ldots V \rightarrow I$. We use the Auto-Emergence algorithm to extract a principal sparse sub-network as the identified circuit. Validation via causal intervention confirms that this identified circuit is a primary driver of harmonic progression behaviors in the symbolic music models. To our knowledge, this represents the first systematic circuit-discovery study conducted within the music domain. Our demo page is available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systematic circuit-discovery study in symbolic music models, identifying a sparse principal information-flow circuit that drives harmonic progression prediction.
AI.motivation: While mechanistic interpretability and circuit discovery have matured in NLP, interpretable functional circuits in symbolic music generative models remain largely unexplored.
AI.method: Using the Auto-Emergence algorithm, the authors extract a sparse principal sub-network in ChatMusician and MuPT for predicting the terminal tonic root in classical harmonic progressions (I ... V -> I) and validate it via causal intervention.
AI.result: Causal intervention confirms that the extracted sparse circuit is a primary driver of harmonic progression behavior in both symbolic music models.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes circuit discovery in the music domain, showing that harmonic progression behavior in symbolic music models is governed by a sparse principal information flow.

title: Cooperative UAV and Ground Station for Robust MEC of Dynamic Aquatic IoT: A Generative AI-Enhanced Approach
summary: The increasing aquatic Internet of Things (AIoTs) require computational support and coverage in applications such as maritime search and rescue. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can offer low-cost, flexible aerial services, and ground stations (GSs) can provide powerful supports, which can cooperate to help the AIoTs in complex scenarios. However, the collaboration between UAVs and GSs for AIoTs faces challenges of task uncertainties, AIoTs trajectory uncertainties, heterogeneities, and limited computational resources. To address these issues, we propose a cooperative UAV and GS based robust multi-access edge computing (MEC) framework to assist AIoTs in completing computational tasks. Specifically, we formulate the optimization problem of joint task offloading and UAV trajectory to minimize the total execution time, which is in the form of mixed integer nonlinear programming and NP-hard to tackle. Therefore, we propose the algorithm of generative artificial intelligence-enhanced heterogeneous agent proximal policy optimization (GAI-HAPPO). The proposed algorithm integrates GAI models to enhance the actor network ability to model complex environments and extract high-level features, thereby allowing the algorithm to predict uncertainties and adapt to dynamic conditions. Additionally, GAI stabilizes the critic network, addressing the instability of multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches. Finally, extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms the existing benchmark methods, thus highlighting the potentials in tackling intricate, cross-domain issues in the considered scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a generative AI-enhanced multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithm (GAI-HAPPO) for cooperative UAV and ground-station multi-access edge computing (MEC) in dynamic aquatic IoT scenarios.
AI.motivation: Cooperative UAV and ground-station MEC for aquatic IoT faces task uncertainties, trajectory uncertainties, heterogeneity, and limited compute, leading to an NP-hard mixed integer nonlinear programming problem.
AI.method: The authors formulate joint task offloading and UAV trajectory optimization to minimize total execution time and propose GAI-HAPPO, which integrates generative AI models to enhance actor feature extraction/uncertainty prediction and stabilize the critic network.
AI.result: Extensive simulations demonstrate that GAI-HAPPO outperforms existing benchmark methods in handling dynamic, cross-domain aquatic IoT scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Integrating generative AI into heterogeneous-agent proximal policy optimization improves stability and performance for cooperative UAV-GS edge computing.

title: Every Query Routes Itself: Accelerating Video Diffusion Transformers with Per-Query Routed Sparse Attention
summary: Self-attention over long token sequences dominates the inference cost of video diffusion transformers. Clustering-based sparse attention clusters both queries and keys and lets all queries in a cluster share one selection of key clusters. We show that this sharing limits accuracy: with key clusters and density fixed, attention grows more accurate as the query clusters are refined, and is most accurate when each query selects on its own, which needs no query clustering at all. We therefore propose Per-Query Routed Sparse Attention (PQRS), a training-free method that clusters only keys, lets each query select its own key clusters, and compensates for the unselected ones with their centroids. Per-query selections leave no query tile with a shared key list, so PQRS traverses key clusters instead of queries, buckets queries with identical selections into dense tasks, and merges their partial results in one pass under a fixed softmax offset carried from the previous denoising step. On four text-to-video and image-to-video models from the Wan and HunyuanVideo families, PQRS is the fastest of all the sparse attention methods we evaluate and the closest to the dense output, reaching $28.9$ dB PSNR on Wan2.1-T2V and $35.4$ dB on HunyuanVideo at $1.66$--$2.10\times$ end-to-end speedup.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Per-Query Routed Sparse Attention (PQRS), a training-free sparse attention method for video diffusion transformers that lets each query route itself to key clusters, achieving 1.66x to 2.10x end-to-end speedup.
AI.motivation: Clustering-based sparse attention shares one key-cluster selection across all queries in a query cluster, which limits attention accuracy compared to per-query selection.
AI.method: PQRS clusters only keys, lets each query select its own key clusters while compensating for unselected ones with centroids, traverses key clusters instead of queries, buckets queries with identical selections into dense tasks, and merges partial results in one pass using a fixed softmax offset from the previous denoising step.
AI.result: Across four text-to-video and image-to-video models from the Wan and HunyuanVideo families, PQRS is the fastest and closest to dense output among evaluated sparse attention methods, reaching 28.9 dB PSNR on Wan2.1-T2V and 35.4 dB on HunyuanVideo at 1.66x to 2.10x end-to-end speedup.
AI.conclusion: Eliminating query clustering in favor of per-query key-cluster routing with key-cluster traversal enables both higher accuracy and faster inference in video diffusion transformers.

title: Taming the Tails of Stochastic Gradient Descent in the Interpolation Regime
summary: In this paper, we study stochastic gradient descent in the smooth interpolation regime, where the population objective shares a common minimizer with the sample losses. In contrast to prior work, which has largely focused on in-expectation analysis, we obtain high-probability convergence guarantees under the same assumptions. In the convex case, we prove a fast rate of order $\log(\beta^{-1}) \cdot n^{-1}$ after $n$ iterations, with failure probability at most $\beta$. In the strongly convex case, we derive a family of moment-based bounds of order $\beta^{-p} \cdot \exp(-\mathcal{O}(p \cdot n))$ for $p \in (0,1]$, and complement them with a matching lower bound showing that the corresponding deterioration in the exponential rate is essentially unavoidable. In both settings, our theoretical results are unified across a broad class of step-size schedules. Building on this analysis, we extend our results to a low-noise regime and to nonconvex objectives satisfying the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes high-probability convergence guarantees for stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in the smooth interpolation regime across convex, strongly convex, low-noise, and Polyak-Lojasiewicz nonconvex settings.
AI.motivation: Prior analyses of SGD in the smooth interpolation regime have largely focused on in-expectation bounds rather than high-probability convergence guarantees.
AI.method: The authors derive high-probability convergence bounds unified across a broad class of step-size schedules, using moment-based bounds and matching lower bounds in the strongly convex case, and extend the analysis to low-noise and Polyak-Lojasiewicz nonconvex regimes.
AI.result: In the convex case, SGD achieves a fast rate of log(1/beta) * n^(-1) after n iterations with failure probability at most beta; in the strongly convex case, moment-based bounds of order beta^(-p) * exp(-O(p * n)) for p in (0, 1] are matched by a lower bound showing the exponential-rate deterioration is essentially unavoidable.
AI.conclusion: The work provides tight high-probability guarantees for SGD in interpolation and near-interpolation regimes across diverse step-size schedules.

title: Surrogate Modeling and Reduced-Order Methods in Gravitational-Wave Physics and Numerical Relativity: From Spectral Representations to Adaptive Compression
summary: The rapid expansion of gravitational-wave astronomy and high-precision numerical relativity has created an acute computational bottleneck: direct numerical integration of the Einstein field equations and high-dimensional Bayesian parameter estimation require millions of waveform evaluations that cannot be sustained by traditional solvers alone. Reduced-order modeling (ROM) and surrogate techniques have emerged as foundational tools to bridge this gap, compressing high-fidelity solution manifolds into compact, rapidly evaluable representations without sacrificing physical accuracy. This perspective reviews the mathematical pillars of projection-based reduced-order modeling---including Proper Orthogonal Decomposition, greedy basis selection, and the Empirical Interpolation Method---and traces their operational impact in gravitational-wave data analysis through surrogate waveform families and Reduced-Order Quadratures. We then examine the fundamental approximation barriers posed by slow Kolmogorov n-width decay in non-stationary, transient, and strongly nonlinear regimes, showing how adaptive hp-greedy domain partitioning and multi-scale spectral compression overcome these limits. Finally, we discuss how combining certified reduced-order structures with modern scientific machine learning and sensitivity-aware quantization provides a rigorous blueprint for next-generation detectors such as LISA, Einstein Telescope, and Cosmic Explorer.

AI.tldr: This perspective reviews projection-based reduced-order modeling (ROM) and surrogate techniques for gravitational-wave physics and numerical relativity, from spectral representations to adaptive compression.
AI.motivation: Direct numerical integration of Einstein's field equations and high-dimensional Bayesian parameter estimation require millions of waveform evaluations, creating an acute computational bottleneck for traditional solvers.
AI.method: The perspective reviews mathematical pillars of projection-based ROM (Proper Orthogonal Decomposition, greedy basis selection, Empirical Interpolation Method), surrogate waveform families, Reduced-Order Quadratures, and adaptive hp-greedy domain partitioning with multi-scale spectral compression to address slow Kolmogorov n-width decay.
AI.result: It traces the operational impact of these methods in gravitational-wave data analysis and outlines how combining certified reduced-order structures with scientific machine learning and sensitivity-aware quantization supports next-generation detectors.
AI.conclusion: Certified reduced-order structures paired with scientific machine learning provide a rigorous blueprint for waveform modeling in next-generation detectors such as LISA, Einstein Telescope, and Cosmic Explorer.

title: Sex Differences in the Detection of Parkinson's Disease from Speech
summary: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease in the world, and 70\% to 75\% of PD patients suffer from speech disorders at some stage. Since PD affects men more frequently than women, previous publications tend to rely on unbalanced datasets that potentially introduce sex biases into trained models. This study investigates sex differences in PD detection from speech using deep learning and traditional machine learning approaches. We evaluated speech-based PD detection using embeddings from three pre-trained speech models, combined with handcrafted acoustic features and different classifiers. Sex-specific experiments were conducted on balanced subsets of four sustained phonation datasets, controlling for sex, disease status, and, where possible, age. All recordings were obtained during a sustained phonation task. Results show that female speakers were more accurately classified than male speakers in the larger dataset. Sex-specific results show that when the models are trained on one sex, they fail to generalize to the other one. Our results highlight the importance of including sex as a variable in the development of PD detection systems.

AI.tldr: This study investigates sex differences in Parkinson's disease (PD) detection from speech on balanced datasets, finding that models trained on one sex fail to generalize to the other.
AI.motivation: Because PD affects men more frequently than women, prior speech-based PD detection studies rely on unbalanced datasets that can introduce sex biases into trained models.
AI.method: The authors evaluate PD detection using embeddings from three pre-trained speech models combined with handcrafted acoustic features and various classifiers on sex-, disease-, and age-controlled balanced subsets of four sustained phonation datasets.
AI.result: Female speakers are more accurately classified than male speakers in the larger dataset, and models trained on one sex fail to generalize when tested on the other sex.
AI.conclusion: Sex must be explicitly included as a variable when developing speech-based PD detection systems to avoid bias and cross-sex generalization failure.

title: Cross-Vehicle Transferability of Lateral Velocity Estimation on Production Vehicles through Input Selection and Data Augmentation
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to Control Engineering Practice
summary: Lateral velocity is safety-critical for vehicle-dynamics control but cannot be measured with production sensors. Model-based estimators such as Kalman filters are established, whereas data-driven estimators are more accurate within the training regime but suspected to lose accuracy beyond it. Their transfer to a structurally different vehicle has rarely been tested. We record real-world test drives of three series-production vehicles, train a neural-network estimator on production CAN signals of a compact car, and evaluate it zero-shot on an SUV and a van against a GNSS-aided inertial reference. On the unseen vehicles, the network's error exceeds that on the training vehicle by an order of magnitude, a gap not quantified on production vehicles before. A systematic comparison of input sets from ten production CAN signals identifies a five-signal set that transfers most robustly. To narrow this gap, we introduce three physically motivated augmentations of training data. Two improve generalization, namely exploiting the vehicle's left-right symmetry and emulating accelerometer bias. Combined, they reduce the error on the validation maneuvers of the SUV and van by 13% and 15%. Contrary to common expectation, on the SUV the data-driven estimator trained with both augmentations matches a model-based estimator tuned on the same training data.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates cross-vehicle transferability of neural-network lateral velocity estimators on production vehicles and shows that input selection and physics-based data augmentation significantly narrow the generalization gap.
AI.motivation: Data-driven lateral velocity estimators are more accurate than model-based estimators within their training regime, but their zero-shot transfer to structurally different production vehicles has rarely been tested.
AI.method: The authors train a neural-network estimator on production CAN signals from a compact car, evaluate it zero-shot on an SUV and a van against a GNSS-aided inertial reference, select a robust five-signal input set from ten CAN signals, and apply physically motivated augmentations (left-right symmetry and accelerometer bias emulation).
AI.result: Zero-shot error on unseen vehicles exceeds training-vehicle error by an order of magnitude; combining both augmentations reduces error on validation maneuvers of the SUV and van by 13% and 15%, matching a tuned model-based estimator on the SUV.
AI.conclusion: Careful CAN input selection and physically motivated data augmentation substantially improve cross-vehicle transferability of data-driven lateral velocity estimators.

title: Learning the Anyon Atlas
summary: We extend our previous search for the modular data of topological quantum field theories in 2+1 dimensions from 22 to 42 anyons, identifying 150,679 new modular data. We do so by adding to our algorithm three rejection gates, two of them based on logistic regression, that discard representations of $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ unlikely to yield modular data. We estimate that roughly 80% of the modular data between ranks 23 and 42 has been identified after closing under known constructions. With this data, we find counterexamples to a conjecture of Geiko and Moore that the reality of the higher Gauss sums suffices for time-reversal symmetry in Chern-Simons theories, and propose a refined criterion. We demonstrate the scalability of this gated implementation by identifying prime modular data at rank 100 that is not realized by any Chern-Simons theory. The identified data through rank 42 has been made available at this https URL, to which further data will be added as it is found.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the search for modular data of (2+1)-dimensional topological quantum field theories from rank 22 to 42 using machine-learning-gated rejection, identifying 150,679 new modular data and refuting a conjecture by Geiko and Moore.
AI.motivation: Searching for modular data of topological quantum field theories at higher ranks is computationally expensive due to representations of SL(2, Z) that do not yield valid modular data.
AI.method: The authors add three rejection gates, including two based on logistic regression, to discard unlikely SL(2, Z) representations, scaling the search to rank 42 (and testing prime modular data at rank 100).
AI.result: The search identifies 150,679 new modular data between ranks 23 and 42 (estimated ~80% coverage after closure), finds counterexamples to Geiko and Moore's conjecture on higher Gauss sums and time-reversal symmetry, proposes a refined criterion, and identifies prime modular data at rank 100 not realized by any Chern-Simons theory.
AI.conclusion: Machine-learning-gated search scales modular data discovery to high ranks and yields new mathematical insights into time-reversal symmetry and Chern-Simons realizations.

title: Training-free motion statistics match self-supervised behavior encoders
comment: 10 pages, 7 tables, 1 figure. Code will be released with the conference version
summary: Self-supervised encoders for animal behavior are often trained on, or fed, hand-built movement features. We ask whether they beat those ingredients when compared fairly. A training-free representation, made of generic per-frame measurements summarized over fixed time windows and reduced with PCA, is compared with retrained and released encoders (BAMS, hBehaveMAE) under a preregistered protocol: frozen representations of equal size and one shared classifier. On CalMS21 it reaches 85.8 macro F1 against 82.4 for the best encoder, ties with four labelled videos, and leads when the annotator changes or new behaviors must be learned from a few videos; the reading holds for encoders retrained with three seeds. On the MABe22 mouse triplets it scores 83.7 against 80.3 for the released hBehaveMAE (gap +3.4, 95% interval +2.1 to +4.7). On a second species, the MABe22 fly groups, the same recipe scores 51.6 mean F1 over 50 tasks against 48.2 for BAMS, the best published method. On Shot7M2, the synthetic basketball benchmark built by hBehaveMAE's authors, it scores 68.8 against 64.7 for hBehaveMAE, the best method in that paper, though hBehaveMAE remains better on the shortest movements. Short time windows carry most of the result. Raw keypoints in each body's own frame, summarized over the same windows, already match or beat the encoders on both mouse datasets and on Shot7M2; on the fly groups they fall short, and the measurements add 5.3 points. On these benchmarks, current behavior encoders have yet to beat the hand-built features they learn from, and such baselines should be reported alongside them.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that a training-free representation of motion statistics matches or outperforms self-supervised animal behavior encoders (BAMS, hBehaveMAE) across four benchmarks under a preregistered protocol.
AI.motivation: Self-supervised animal behavior encoders are often trained on or fed hand-built movement features, raising the question of whether they actually outperform those ingredients under fair comparison.
AI.method: Under a preregistered protocol with frozen equal-size representations and one shared classifier, the authors compare a training-free representation (generic per-frame measurements summarized over fixed time windows and reduced with PCA) against retrained and released BAMS and hBehaveMAE encoders.
AI.result: The training-free representation scores 85.8 vs 82.4 macro F1 on CalMS21, 83.7 vs 80.3 on MABe22 mouse triplets, 51.6 vs 48.2 mean F1 on MABe22 fly groups, and 68.8 vs 64.7 on Shot7M2 (though hBehaveMAE leads on the shortest movements).
AI.conclusion: Current self-supervised behavior encoders have yet to surpass the hand-built motion features they learn from, which should be reported as baselines.

title: Kaer: Security-Aware Replanning for Multi-Agent Systems
summary: One popular architecture for multi-agent systems (MAS) relies on an orchestrator that generates an initial plan, coordinates its execution, and dynamically revises the plan based on agent feedback when tasks cannot be fully specified in advance. This dynamic replanning introduces a critical vulnerability: malicious agents can embed instructions within their feedback to hijack the replanning process. Existing defenses focus exclusively on per-tool access control or static, pre-execution policy enforcement, leaving the replanning phase unsecured. We introduce Kaer, a multi-agent framework featuring security-aware replanning. Kaer shields the planner from untrusted agent feedback by conveying diagnostics to the replanning procedure strictly through abstract templates. Plan revisions are restricted to a set of deterministic repair operators, and all modified plans must satisfy preset policies. We create Cintra, a benchmark of simulated user tasks requiring replanning paired with adversarial objectives targeting the replanning phase. Using Cintra, we evaluate both task completion rates and system vulnerability to replanning exploits by malicious agents. Evaluating Kaer on Cintra against Magentic-One (an undefended MAS) and ControlValve (the state-of-the-art defense) demonstrates that Kaer achieves higher robustness than both systems while maintaining comparable utility to ControlValve. Although abstract failure templates slightly constrain utility on select tasks, Kaer enables MAS to perform secure, dynamic plan revisions without exposing the orchestrator to untrusted agent feedback.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Kaer, a security-aware replanning framework for multi-agent systems, and Cintra, a benchmark for evaluating replanning exploits.
AI.motivation: Dynamic replanning in orchestrator-based multi-agent systems allows malicious agents to embed instructions in feedback to hijack the replanning process, a phase left unsecured by existing static or per-tool defenses.
AI.method: Kaer shields the planner by conveying diagnostics strictly through abstract templates, restricts plan revisions to deterministic repair operators, and enforces preset policies on all modified plans; the authors also build the Cintra benchmark with simulated tasks and adversarial replanning objectives.
AI.result: On Cintra, Kaer achieves higher robustness than both Magentic-One (undefended) and ControlValve (state-of-the-art defense) while maintaining comparable utility to ControlValve, with minor utility constraints from abstract templates on select tasks.
AI.conclusion: Abstract diagnostic templates, deterministic repair operators, and policy enforcement enable secure dynamic replanning in multi-agent systems.

title: Does the Action Matter? Probing Action-Conditioned Semantic Forecasting as a World Model for Autonomous Driving
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Accepted at the WAM-AD Workshop, WACV 2027. Code: this https URL
summary: World models are increasingly used in autonomous driving to predict how a scene evolves under the ego vehicle's actions, supporting counterfactual reasoning and model-based planning. However, existing evaluations focus on prediction fidelity and planning performance, and rarely verify that the predictions depend on the conditioning action. In this paper, we study action dependence in action-conditioned semantic forecasting, which predicts future semantic segmentation from past segmentations and the ego action. We compare a forecaster with feature-wise and input-level action conditioning against an identical model without action input, and measure action dependence with test-time action interventions scored by standard segmentation metrics. The evaluation is validated in a synthetic environment with known action-dependent dynamics and applied to Cityscapes and BDD100K, both within each dataset and across the two vehicle platforms. Experiments show that the executed action improves mid-term mIoU by at most 2.5 points on Cityscapes and 0.6 points on BDD100K, whereas a wrong action reduces it by up to 23.2 and 7.0 points, below the model without action input. On real data, feature-wise conditioning depends 1.6 times more on the action than input-level conditioning at similar accuracy, whereas both depend on it equally in the synthetic environment, where the history does not determine the action. These results show that an accuracy gain indicates that a driving world model uses its action, but not how strongly its forecasts depend on it. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper probes action dependence in action-conditioned semantic forecasting for autonomous driving, showing that accuracy gains alone do not reveal how strongly world-model forecasts depend on the conditioning action.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of driving world models focus on prediction fidelity and planning performance, rarely verifying whether forecasts actually depend on the conditioning ego action.
AI.method: The authors compare forecasters with feature-wise and input-level action conditioning against an identical action-free baseline using test-time action interventions in a synthetic environment, Cityscapes, and BDD100K.
AI.result: Executed actions improve mid-term mIoU by at most 2.5 points on Cityscapes and 0.6 points on BDD100K, while wrong actions reduce it by up to 23.2 and 7.0 points; on real data, feature-wise conditioning depends 1.6x more on the action than input-level conditioning at similar accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Test-time action interventions are necessary alongside accuracy metrics to measure true action dependence in driving world models.

title: Learning to Interact in Multi-Agent Self-Play for Controllable Autonomous Driving Scenario Generation
summary: Large-scale, multi-agent self-play trains robust driving policies effectively in simulation, but controlling these models to generate specific, safety-critical edge cases remains a key challenge. Existing goal-conditioned self-play frameworks rely primarily on static map-location goals and fail to reliably produce complex agent interactions such as aggressive tailgating or adversarial cut-offs. These agent interactions are necessary for rigorous autonomous vehicle (AV) testing. To address this, we present an extended multi-agent self-play framework that introduces agent-relative dynamic goals. By conditioning policies on this extended goal representation, our framework enables targeted, controllable scenario synthesis. We demonstrate that our approach successfully generates interactive driving behaviors that static-goal baselines cannot simulate, providing a flexible tool for long-tail scenario generation in AV testing.

AI.tldr: This paper extends multi-agent self-play with agent-relative dynamic goals to enable controllable generation of interactive, safety-critical autonomous driving scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing goal-conditioned self-play frameworks rely on static map-location goals and fail to reliably produce complex agent interactions such as aggressive tailgating or adversarial cut-offs needed for autonomous vehicle testing.
AI.method: The authors introduce agent-relative dynamic goals into a multi-agent self-play framework to condition driving policies on interactive objectives.
AI.result: The framework successfully generates interactive driving behaviors that static-goal baselines cannot simulate.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning multi-agent self-play on agent-relative dynamic goals provides a flexible tool for controllable long-tail scenario generation in autonomous vehicle testing.

title: Enhancing Active Learning Performance with Initial Data Selection Based on Foundation Models
summary: In active object detection, selecting the initial labeled pool is essential, especially in complex datasets with expensive labeling and low resource budget. This study presents an active learning framework designed to optimize the initial training cycle of active learning for the object detection task. Our approach diverges from traditional methods by utilizing feature-based clustering from the YOLO-World model and refining images based on objectness scores rather than relying on uncertainty sampling in the initial cycle. This approach focuses on finding samples with various features and emphasizes training in areas where the foundation model is most confident. Doing so helps the model better understand different types of objects. For subsequent cycles, we employ a consistency-based sampling technique to maintain the robustness of the training process. To evaluate our method, we use two complex datasets called Aquarium and NWPU VHR-10, which are well known for their diverse object sizes and challenging conditions. In the NWPU dataset, our method increases mAP50 by an average of 6.6% in image-based evaluation. Moreover, the image refinement method shows an improvement of approximately 11% in object-based evaluation. The results show improvements in model performance and labeling time, demonstrating the advantages of using foundation models in early cycles of active learning. An implementation of the algorithm is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an active object detection framework that uses YOLO-World feature clustering and objectness-based image refinement for initial pool selection, improving mAP50 on NWPU VHR-10.
AI.motivation: Selecting the initial labeled pool in active object detection is critical under low resource budgets and complex datasets, where traditional uncertainty sampling can be suboptimal.
AI.method: The framework uses YOLO-World feature-based clustering and objectness-score image refinement for the initial cycle, followed by consistency-based sampling in subsequent cycles.
AI.result: Evaluated on Aquarium and NWPU VHR-10, the method increases mAP50 by an average of 6.6% in image-based evaluation on NWPU, while image refinement improves object-based evaluation by approximately 11%.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging foundation models for initial data selection and refinement improves both object detection performance and labeling efficiency in active learning.

title: Keeping Shielded Data-Driven Controllers Safe Under System Evolution via Model Consistency
summary: Cyber-physical systems (CPS) increasingly contain data-driven controllers, which raise safety concerns given their black-box nature. A common mitigation is to enforce system safety via a shield around the controller, which restricts the inputs based on assumptions about the physical system. However, these assumptions are usually fixed and may become invalid as the system evolves (during development or due to component degradation), possibly leading to unsafe behavior. We address this limitation in a model-driven approach that treats both the data-driven controller and safety shield as first-class models that are integrated into a virtual single underlying model (V-SUM) alongside system models. We describe system evolution as changes in the associated models, such that consistency checking yields a continuous assessment of safety guarantees. In case of inconsistencies, consistency-preservation rules automatically update the models and restore a valid safety shield. We evaluate our approach on a reach-avoid task for a unicycle system. The results show that consistency-driven evolution effectively maintains safety guarantees under system changes and provides a principled basis for evaluating and restoring performance.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a model-driven approach that integrates data-driven controllers, safety shields, and system models into a virtual single underlying model (V-SUM) to maintain safety under system evolution.
AI.motivation: Fixed assumptions in safety shields around data-driven controllers can become invalid as cyber-physical systems evolve or degrade, leading to unsafe behavior.
AI.method: Both the data-driven controller and safety shield are treated as first-class models in a V-SUM alongside system models, where consistency checking detects evolution-induced violations and consistency-preservation rules automatically update models to restore a valid shield.
AI.result: Evaluated on a reach-avoid task for a unicycle system, consistency-driven evolution maintains safety guarantees under system changes.
AI.conclusion: Integrating controllers, shields, and system models via consistency-driven evolution provides a principled way to preserve safety in evolving cyber-physical systems.

title: Let a Small Model Read First: Faster Prefill for Long Interleaved Image-Text Inputs
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer questions about long interleaved inputs, such as documents of many pages and collections of hundreds of images, but they are slow to start: on inputs of about 100K tokens, the prefill takes most of the wait for the first output token. A common approach prunes the input by scoring its tokens with the target model itself or with a small model of the same family that first writes an answer. However, this scoring takes much of the time that pruning saves. We find that the evidence for a question lies in a few whole units (images or paragraphs), and that a small hybrid model finds them with one attention head of an early layer, even at half image resolution. Based on these findings, we propose SkimPrefill, which lets the small hybrid model read the whole input first, up to that early layer, with images at half resolution. Most layers of the small hybrid model (Qwen3.5-0.8B) run in linear time, so this pass is short. SkimPrefill then ranks every unit with that head and gives the target the top units as an ordinary shorter prompt. One untrained selector serves targets of different model families. Extensive experiments on MMLongBench at 128K tokens, with 19 datasets of five task types, show the effectiveness of SkimPrefill. With 10% of the input tokens kept, SkimPrefill speeds up the prefill of Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-4-12B and Qwen3-VL-32B by 3.7 times, 11.6 time and 8.2 times while maintaining their average accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SkimPrefill, a prefill acceleration method that uses a small hybrid model's early-layer attention head at half image resolution to select top evidence units, achieving 3.7x to 11.6x prefill speedup at 128K tokens.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models have slow prefill on ~100K-token interleaved image-text inputs, and existing token-pruning methods spend too much time scoring tokens with the target model or a small model generating an answer.
AI.method: SkimPrefill runs a small hybrid model (Qwen3.5-0.8B) up to an early layer with half-resolution images, uses one attention head to rank whole units (images or paragraphs), and passes only the top units to the target model as a shorter prompt.
AI.result: Across 19 datasets on MMLongBench at 128K tokens, keeping 10% of input tokens speeds up prefill for Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-4-12B, and Qwen3-VL-32B by 3.7x, 11.6x, and 8.2x while maintaining average accuracy, with one untrained selector serving different model families.
AI.conclusion: Early-layer unit selection by a small linear-time hybrid model dramatically accelerates VLM prefill on long interleaved inputs without losing accuracy.

title: Mitigating fix reversal: Counterfactual constraints for function-level vulnerability detection
summary: Function-level vulnerability detectors often exhibit fix reversal, assigning a higher vulnerability probability to a fixed version than to its vulnerable counterpart. Fixes usually lengthen functions, and larger length increases are associated with more severe reversal. Code-transformation experiments indicate that fix reversal mainly stems from a length shortcut: vulnerability probability increases with function length when content is fixed. We propose CFVul to address this problem. Sliding-window encoding covers complete functions, retaining fix information beyond the truncation boundary. During training, a content constraint encourages the vulnerable version to receive a higher vulnerability probability under a common length input. During inference, a length constraint averages vulnerability probabilities over fixed reference lengths, reducing the influence of actual length changes. On PrimeVul, CFVul achieves a fix-pair ranking metric, PairRank, of 59.4\%, exceeding the existing methods compared. For fixes that increase function length by more than 15\%, PairRank rises from CodeBERT's 25.8\% to 48.4\%. PairRank also improves in experiments with four additional models and three additional datasets. By weakening the length shortcut, CFVul reduces cases in which fixed versions receive higher vulnerability probabilities than vulnerable versions. It requires only existing fix pairs and applies to multiple pretrained code models, facilitating adoption in existing detectors.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes CFVul, a counterfactual constraint framework that mitigates fix reversal in function-level vulnerability detection caused by a function-length shortcut.
AI.motivation: Function-level vulnerability detectors often exhibit fix reversal—assigning higher vulnerability probability to fixed functions than vulnerable ones—because fixes lengthen functions and detectors rely on a length shortcut.
AI.method: CFVul uses sliding-window encoding to cover complete functions, a training-time content constraint encouraging higher vulnerability probability for vulnerable versions at a common length, and an inference-time length constraint averaging probabilities over fixed reference lengths.
AI.result: On PrimeVul, CFVul achieves 59.4% PairRank (exceeding compared methods) and raises PairRank from CodeBERT's 25.8% to 48.4% on fixes that lengthen functions by over 15%, with consistent gains across four additional models and three datasets.
AI.conclusion: Weakening the length shortcut with counterfactual constraints reduces fix reversal and is readily applicable to existing pretrained code vulnerability detectors.

title: Probing agent overeagerness in realistic settings with continuation audits
comment: Presented at NeurIPS Workshops: (1) Third Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond, and (2) The 1st Workshop on Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB) at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Frontier coding agents increasingly exhibit overeagerness, taking surprising, sometimes reckless actions beyond a user's mandate --- reported in recent system cards from frontier model developers. These cases are surfaced through internal deployment monitoring, which requires private traffic and is out of reach for open-weight models and independent evaluators. Automated alignment audits are the natural alternative, but capable models increasingly recognise the synthetic setup and adjust their behaviour. We introduce Continuation Audits, a pipeline that grounds the auditor on a prefix drawn from a real coding-agent transcript and directs it to continue the trajectory toward a seeded behaviour. Because the prefix is drawn from a real session, the auditor only needs to maintain a realistic setting rather than manufacturing it. We validate the method on SWE-Chat prefixes: on a paired subset of 90 audits a judge cannot reliably distinguish continuations from their source sessions (realism win rate 0.42 vs.\ 0.43), and across all 900 audits verbalized eval-awareness does not exceed the rate observed in the unaudited real sessions. Applying the pipeline to three recent models across three seeds, we find each model leads a different seed --- DeepSeek~V4~Pro on colleague-credentials misuse, GPT-5.6~Terra on file-permission bypasses, and Kimi~K3 on treating diagnostic questions as instructions. Kimi~K3 additionally continues to bypass file-permission protections after an explicit this http URL prohibition while the other two stop entirely, corroborating Moonshot's own report of excessive proactiveness.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Continuation Audits, an automated alignment auditing pipeline that grounds an auditor on real coding-agent transcripts to probe overeagerness without triggering evaluation awareness.
AI.motivation: Frontier coding agents exhibit overeagerness beyond user mandates, but internal deployment monitoring is inaccessible to open-weight evaluators and existing synthetic alignment audits are increasingly recognized by capable models.
AI.method: Continuation Audits draws prefixes from real coding-agent transcripts and directs an auditor to continue the trajectory toward a seeded behavior, maintaining a realistic setting rather than manufacturing one from scratch.
AI.result: Validated on SWE-Chat prefixes, a judge cannot distinguish continuations from source sessions (realism win rate 0.42 vs. 0.43 across 90 paired audits) and verbalized eval-awareness across 900 audits does not exceed real sessions; across three seeds, DeepSeek V4 Pro leads on colleague-credentials misuse, GPT-5.6 Terra on file-permission bypasses, and Kimi K3 on treating diagnostic questions as instructions while continuing to bypass file-permission protections after an explicit prohibition.
AI.conclusion: Grounding automated audits in real session prefixes enables realistic, stealthy probing of agent overeagerness in open-weight and third-party evaluations.

title: Harvesting Expert-Parallel Bubbles for Fine-Tuning
summary: GPUs are expensive, yet latency-critical large language model (LLM) inference leaves part of them idle. Colocation reclaims this capacity by running best-effort work, such as fine-tuning, alongside serving. Many leading LLMs now use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which adds a new source of idle time. Under expert parallelism, MoE experts are spread across GPUs, and because the router sends uneven numbers of tokens to each GPU, lightly loaded GPUs wait for the most loaded one. Even after applying load balancing solutions, such bubbles still take 8--13% of prefill time. We present BubbleTea, the first colocation system that leverages expert-parallel bubbles for fine-tuning. Unlike existing colocation systems, which make one scheduling decision for all GPUs per forward pass, BubbleTea predicts each GPU's bubble at every layer from the router's token assignment, and fills it with short chunks of fine-tuning work that reuse the weights already loaded for serving. We also introduce compiler passes that automatically derive these chunks from the served LLM as-is, without porting each model architecture to a separate training engine. Our evaluation on three MoE models, served on four A100 GPUs, shows that fine-tuning throughput with BubbleTea is 1.9--6.2$\times$ faster than with LLMStation, a state-of-the-art colocation system. BubbleTea keeps p90 inference latency within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads, compared to 44 for LLMStation. On bursty production traces, BubbleTea trains 3.3$\times$ faster than LLMStation and 14$\times$ faster than a stock trainer colocated under CUDA MPS, with p90 inference latency staying within 7% of serving alone.

AI.tldr: The paper presents BubbleTea, a colocation system that harvests idle GPU time from expert-parallel bubbles in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM serving to run fine-tuning work.
AI.motivation: Expert-parallel MoE serving leaves lightly loaded GPUs waiting for the most loaded GPU (8-13% of prefill time even with load balancing), and existing colocation systems make only one coarse scheduling decision per forward pass for all GPUs.
AI.method: BubbleTea predicts each GPU's per-layer bubble from the router's token assignment and fills it with short fine-tuning chunks that reuse already-loaded serving weights, using compiler passes to derive chunks directly from the served LLM without porting to a separate training engine.
AI.result: Evaluated on three MoE models across four A100 GPUs, BubbleTea achieves 1.9-6.2x faster fine-tuning throughput than LLMStation while keeping p90 inference latency within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads (vs. 44 for LLMStation); on bursty production traces it trains 3.3x faster than LLMStation and 14x faster than stock training under CUDA MPS, with p90 latency within 7%.
AI.conclusion: Per-layer, per-GPU bubble harvesting enables high-throughput MoE fine-tuning alongside latency-critical serving without sacrificing tail latency.

title: BaseRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of a Base Vision-Language Model via Training-Free Harness Internalization
summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is moving from the harness of prompts and tools around a base model toward the model itself. However, existing RSI still faces key challenges, including harness-bound gains that stay outside the base model, black-box supervision that reads only the model's outputs, and imprecise edits whose site and strength are fixed in advance. To address these challenges, we propose BaseRSI, a new paradigm of Recursive Harness Internalization: the base model improves its harness, then writes what the harness adds into its own weights through training-free edits, round after round on its own responses. To support this paradigm, we introduce ReGap, a mechanism that supervises every transformer block with the high-dimensional activation difference that the harness makes at that block alone, and updates the block's weights along this signal in a low-dimensional subspace. Building on this mechanism, we further propose ReKey, an algorithm that writes this signal by regression into a few key-value neurons of every block, and measures the site and strength of each edit on the model's own responses. Moreover, the base model fills every role of this recursion with forward passes alone, and its edits, written at different sites, compose in one checkpoint without refitting. Experimental results on ten visual reasoning benchmarks show that BaseRSI consistently improves a base vision-language model both in distribution and on held-out benchmarks. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes BaseRSI, a recursive self-improvement paradigm that internalizes harness-level gains directly into a base vision-language model's weights through training-free edits.
AI.motivation: Existing recursive self-improvement methods keep gains bound to external prompts and tools, rely on black-box output supervision, and use imprecise edits with fixed sites and strengths.
AI.method: BaseRSI uses ReGap to supervise each transformer block with the high-dimensional activation difference induced by the harness, and ReKey to regress this signal into a few key-value neurons per block while measuring edit site and strength on the model's own responses using only forward passes.
AI.result: Across ten visual reasoning benchmarks, BaseRSI consistently improves a base vision-language model both in distribution and on held-out benchmarks, with edits at different sites composing in a single checkpoint without refitting.
AI.conclusion: Training-free harness internalization offers a scalable mechanism for base vision-language models to recursively absorb external reasoning improvements into their own parameters.

title: Negotiating Control and Accountability among Stakeholders in High-Risk AI Use Cases: Development and Evaluation of the Method ALIGN
summary: Characteristics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) severely restrict human control. This creates new challenges for socio-technical systems design especially in safety-critical domains, where control over risks is essential along with the accountability for any harm caused. Drawing from human factors and AI governance literature, expert interviews and participant observation in a complex high-risk AI use case from the railways, we developed ALIGN, a scenario-based method that supports the governance of and stakeholder involvement in AI development and implementation in three ways: raising awareness for potential accountability-control misalignments in socio-technical systems and their negative consequences, offering a structured approach to assessing the alignment between accountability and control for stakeholders in a given use case, and supporting effective design decisions to mitigate AI risks. We describe the iterative development and evaluation of ALIGN and discuss how this method promotes AI governance by highlighting the relevance of control-accountability alignment throughout the AI life cycle.

AI.tldr: The paper develops and evaluates ALIGN, a scenario-based method for negotiating control and accountability among stakeholders in high-risk AI socio-technical systems.
AI.motivation: AI characteristics restrict human control, creating governance challenges in safety-critical domains where risk control and harm accountability must align across stakeholders.
AI.method: Drawing on human factors, AI governance literature, expert interviews, and participant observation in a high-risk railway AI use case, ALIGN provides a scenario-based approach to raise awareness of control-accountability misalignments, structure alignment assessments, and support risk-mitigating design decisions.
AI.result: The authors describe the iterative development and evaluation of ALIGN in the railway domain, demonstrating how it surfaces misalignments and guides stakeholder involvement.
AI.conclusion: ALIGN promotes effective AI governance by foregrounding control-accountability alignment throughout the AI life cycle in safety-critical systems.

title: H3Remover: Reinforcing Video Object Removal without Paired Data
comment: Project page: this https URL , code at: this https URL
summary: Pretrained video editors possess rich removal and completion priors, yet may retain targets or alter unrelated content. We present H3Remover, which reinforces MiniMax-H3 Base Ref2VA for video object removal without paired object-free training targets. To discourage superficial edits such as recoloring, a target-removal reward favors calibrated depth changes consistent with revealing farther content. To limit unintended scene changes, a background-geometry reward encourages preservation of relative depth ordering. To preserve background appearance without retaining unwanted shadows or reflections, an appearance reward constrains RGB changes in source-derived protected regions while exempting targets and estimated effects. Frozen HPSv3 complements these constraints with perceptual-quality feedback for synthesized content. Evaluation regions remain fixed across candidates, and DiffusionART optimizes LoRA adapters with the backbone frozen. Experiments show substantial reconstruction gains over original H3, with qualitative comparisons demonstrating more effective object removal and better preservation of surrounding scene content.

AI.tldr: The paper presents H3Remover, a reinforcement learning approach that adapts MiniMax-H3 Base Ref2VA for video object removal without requiring paired object-free training videos.
AI.motivation: Pretrained video editors have strong removal and completion priors but often retain target objects or alter unrelated scene content, while paired object-free training data is scarce.
AI.method: H3Remover freezes the backbone and optimizes LoRA adapters via DiffusionART using four rewards: a target-removal reward favoring calibrated depth changes, a background-geometry reward preserving relative depth ordering, an appearance reward constraining RGB changes in protected regions while exempting targets and estimated shadows/reflections, and frozen HPSv3 for perceptual quality.
AI.result: Experiments show substantial reconstruction gains over the original H3 model, with qualitative comparisons demonstrating more effective object removal and better preservation of surrounding scene content.
AI.conclusion: Depth- and appearance-aware reward signals enable effective video object removal with pretrained video editors without paired ground-truth data.

title: Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge
summary: Continual learning (CL) enables neural networks to adapt to non-stationary data streams by mitigating catastrophic forgetting, offering a path to robust, private, and adaptable edge devices. Yet, porting CL to real-world edge devices remains challenging for two reasons: (i) online operation, where sensor data arrives one sample at a time and the device must adapt on-the-fly, and (ii) the low footprint of edge devices, which makes traditional error backpropagation training prohibitive. Inspired by the brain's wake and sleep cycles, the former for rapid adaptation with minimal resources and the latter for long-term consolidation, we introduce Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase platform for efficient CL at the edge. In the wake phase (e.g., daily operation), Hypnos relies on a low-footprint system-on-chip with a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) targeting efficient inference and supporting lightweight gradient-free prototype updates. In the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), where wall-plug energy and larger memory budgets are available, a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates for consolidation. Deployed on a ZCU104 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, Hypnos is benchmarked on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol. It sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% for edge CL systems, with an on-device latency of 7.79s-10.54s per sample depending on activation precision, and requires $3.8\times$ fewer learning steps and $22\times$ less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase edge continual learning platform inspired by wake-sleep cycles that combines online gradient-free updates with offline rehearsal-based consolidation.
AI.motivation: Deploying continual learning on edge devices is hindered by online single-sample data streams and tight resource budgets that make standard backpropagation prohibitive.
AI.method: During the wake phase, Hypnos uses a low-footprint RISC-V MCU SoC for efficient inference and lightweight gradient-free prototype updates; during the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient consolidation.
AI.result: Deployed on a ZCU104 FPGA and synthesized in a 28-nm process on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol, Hypnos achieves 78.6%-81.6% accuracy with 7.79s-10.54s per-sample latency, requiring 3.8x fewer learning steps and 22x less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.
AI.conclusion: Separating fast gradient-free wake adaptation from energy-rich sleep consolidation enables scalable, state-of-the-art continual learning on resource-constrained edge hardware.

title: LLM-Guided Cyber-Physical Attack Path Identification in Smart Grids
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Accepted at IEEE IECON 2026
summary: Identifying high-impact attack paths in cyber-physical power systems is critical for improving grid resilience. Existing methods typically rely on either structural topology analysis or simulation-based cascading-failure models. Topology-based approaches capture connectivity but lack adversarial reasoning, while simulation-driven methods are primarily suited for offline analysis and are less effective for rapid evaluation of evolving attack scenarios. As a result, identifying realistic attack paths that jointly capture topology, threat semantics, and physical impact remains challenging. This paper presents a physics-grounded framework for identifying cyber-physical attack paths using large language models (LLMs), with cascading-failure-derived impact rankings used as physics-grounded references. The framework integrates system topology, LLM-guided STRIDE and MITRE ATT&CK threat modeling, and three baseline strategies for comparison: topology-driven, threat-driven, and fusion-based. Evaluation is performed using (i) critical-node overlap between LLM-inferred top-K rankings and cascading-failure-based ground truth; (ii) node-level similarity between LLM-inferred and reference paths; and (iii) path-level alignment capturing agreement in complete attack sequences. Results show that structured LLM-based threat modeling substantially improves alignment with physics-grounded references. In the cyber layer, critical-node overlap@3 increases from approximately 33% to as high as 100%, while node-level similarity reaches up to 65% and path-level alignment reaches up to 48%. In addition, the proposed framework reduces runtime by approximately 75--85% compared to the fusion-based baseline in the IEEE 14-bus system. These results suggest that LLM-guided attack path identification is a promising approach for efficient and impact-aware cyber-physical security analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a physics-grounded framework that uses large language models (LLMs) with STRIDE and MITRE ATT&CK threat modeling to identify high-impact cyber-physical attack paths in smart grids.
AI.motivation: Topology-based grid analysis lacks adversarial reasoning, while simulation-based cascading-failure models are slow and ill-suited for rapid evaluation of evolving attack scenarios.
AI.method: The framework integrates system topology with LLM-guided STRIDE and MITRE ATT&CK threat modeling, evaluated against cascading-failure-derived impact rankings and compared with topology-driven, threat-driven, and fusion-based baselines.
AI.result: On the IEEE 14-bus system, structured LLM threat modeling increases cyber-layer critical-node overlap@3 from roughly 33% to up to 100%, reaches up to 65% node-level similarity and 48% path-level alignment, and reduces runtime by 75-85% compared to the fusion-based baseline.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLM threat reasoning with physics-grounded cascading-failure references enables fast, impact-aware cyber-physical attack path identification in smart grids.

title: Isabelle Pool Server: a pooled verification service for prover training and multi-agent proving
summary: Isabelle Pool Server (IPS), a verification service with a pool of warm headless Isabelle sessions behind an HTTP API, with session leasing and reclamation, memory-aware admission control, and a time budget on every call. Its verification interface spans single-step execution, block-level proof checking and whole-theory builds, with checkpoints for cheap branching and backtracking, and a build from scratch as the final arbiter. The service runs as a single container with monitoring and is accessible via a Python client, two MCP servers and a raw HTTP API. In our measurements IPS is level with PIDE MCP, a PIDE frontend for agents, at one worker and ahead of it at eight, at its commit of October 2026 (the tool is now PIDE AI). Once its sessions are up it scales to 32 concurrent workers on one host at 24 times the single-worker rate, and under memory pressure it refuses new sessions rather than losing existing ones. IPS is free software and publicly available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Isabelle Pool Server (IPS), a containerized verification service managing a pool of warm headless Isabelle sessions behind an HTTP API for prover training and multi-agent proving.
AI.motivation: Automated theorem proving and multi-agent systems need fast, concurrent, and resource-safe Isabelle verification across single steps, proof blocks, and full theories.
AI.method: IPS provides session leasing and reclamation, memory-aware admission control, per-call time budgets, checkpoints for branching and backtracking, and from-scratch theory builds, accessible via Python client, two MCP servers, and raw HTTP API.
AI.result: IPS matches PIDE MCP at one worker, outperforms it at eight workers, and scales to 32 concurrent workers on a single host at 24x the single-worker rate while refusing new sessions under memory pressure rather than dropping active ones.
AI.conclusion: Pooled warm Isabelle sessions with admission control provide a reliable, high-throughput verification backend for prover training and agentic proving.

title: Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning
summary: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has attracted increasing interest as a possible route to construct feature representations that are difficult to reproduce with classical models. However, near-term QML architectures based on trainable parametrized quantum circuits remain affected by limited hardware resources, noise, and severe optimization difficulties such as barren plateaus. In this work we propose Soft-MoQE, a Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts architecture that replaces variational quantum training with the input-dependent selection and combination of fixed quantum feature maps. The model is composed of a heterogeneous pool of non-trainable quantum circuits, each defining a distinct embedding, and a classical gating network that learns how to weight these embeddings for each data point. We benchmark Soft-MoQE on three PCA-reduced tasks: MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST. Soft-MoQE outperforms the single best expert, the uniform average of all experts and a linear baseline, achieving task-dependent performance comparable to that of a trainable quantum neural network, without optimizing any quantum parameter and with a quantum training cost that is lower by orders of magnitude. The analysis of the class- conditioned expert usage shows that the learned routing combines a few experts for each input, with a selection that depends on the class. These results support the learned routing among fixed quantum circuits as a trainability-aware design principle for hybrid QML.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Soft-MoQE, a hybrid quantum-classical architecture that replaces variational quantum circuit training with a classical gating network routing over fixed quantum feature maps.
AI.motivation: Near-term quantum machine learning based on trainable parametrized quantum circuits suffers from hardware noise, limited resources, and optimization issues such as barren plateaus.
AI.method: Soft-MoQE pairs a heterogeneous pool of non-trainable fixed quantum circuits with a classical gating network that learns input-dependent weights to combine their embeddings for each data point.
AI.result: On PCA-reduced MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST tasks, Soft-MoQE outperforms the single best expert, uniform averaging, and a linear baseline, matching trainable quantum neural networks at orders-of-magnitude lower quantum training cost while exhibiting class-conditioned expert routing.
AI.conclusion: Learned classical routing over fixed quantum feature maps offers a trainability-aware, barren-plateau-free design principle for hybrid quantum-classical learning.

title: LAaDT-DSS: decision support for non-experts on rooftop PV, incentive and grid simulations under Turkish tariff rules
comment: 51 pages, 10 figures. Code, scripts and results: this https URL
summary: Rooftop photovoltaics raise three questions: should a household invest, which incentive costs the state least, and does the feeder stay within limits? Those who ask are rarely modellers. We present LAaDT-DSS, decision-support software that answers all three under Turkish tariff rules from one simulation core. Non-experts reach it by clicking a house on a 3D map or by asking in plain words; a language model is asked to call the simulation tools, not to compute. Each entry of its 125-entry parameter registry is marked as sourced or estimated. Case studies test the system. Its PV yield lies within $\pm$3.6% of two independent tools at equal losses. Across 2,048 draws of its estimated inputs, the answer for PV alone held in all but one; with a battery, it changed in 31-41% of the draws. Four scripted chat scenarios ran end to end; no user study was run.

AI.tldr: The paper presents LAaDT-DSS, a decision-support software for non-experts to evaluate rooftop photovoltaic (PV) investment, state incentives, and feeder limits under Turkish tariff rules.
AI.motivation: Households, policymakers, and grid operators need answers on rooftop PV economics, incentives, and feeder constraints, yet those asking are rarely energy modellers.
AI.method: LAaDT-DSS wraps a unified simulation core behind a 3D map interface and a natural-language chat interface where an LLM calls simulation tools rather than computing, backed by a 125-entry parameter registry distinguishing sourced from estimated inputs.
AI.result: Its PV yield agrees within plus or minus 3.6% of two independent tools; across 2,048 draws of estimated inputs, PV-only decisions held in all but one draw while battery decisions changed in 31-41% of draws, and four scripted chat scenarios ran end to end (with no user study conducted).
