AI.conclusion: Tool-calling LLMs paired with a transparent parameter registry and unified simulation core can make complex rooftop PV and grid analyses accessible to non-experts.

title: Agentic Harness Engineering Beta: Requirement-Centered Evolution of Agent Harnesses
summary: Real-world harness engineering is driven by explicit and implicit user requirements, which guide development and validation. However, existing harness evolution methods often overlook implicit requirements and interaction needs, while using a single evolution agent to modify the harness and benchmark scores to select changes. This process often produces narrow patches and leads to benchmark-specific local optima. We introduce Agentic Harness Engineering Beta (AHE-Beta), a requirement-centered loop that brings real-world engineering practices into harness evolution. The loop consists of three steps: (1) User-driven evaluation lets simulated users raise their requirements as issues while they work with the harness over multiple turns. (2) Team-based modification implements those requirements as generalizable changes rather than task-specific patches. (3) Requirement-driven selection merges a change only when it resolves a verified requirement and passes review. Empirically, on held-out tasks, AHE-Beta raises pass@1 from 21.9% to 33.3% while using 40.8% fewer tokens than Base Harness, and achieves higher pass@1 than Claude Code, Meta-Harness, and AHE. In a blind human A/B test, real users prefer AHE-Beta in 31 of 48 valid pairs and rate it higher on all five dimensions, matching the directional preference of the user simulator. The human A/B results show that AHE-Beta achieves its goal of aligning harness evolution with real-world user requirements. Without further evolution, the gains transfer to GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with pass@1 improvements of 15.8% and 5.3% over Base Harness. Together, these results show that requirement-centered harness evolution is a more general method for improving agent capabilities.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Agentic Harness Engineering Beta (AHE-Beta), a requirement-centered evolutionary loop that improves agent harnesses using simulated user feedback and team-based modifications.
AI.motivation: Existing harness evolution methods rely on a single agent and benchmark scores, which overlooks implicit user requirements and leads to narrow, benchmark-specific patches.
AI.method: AHE-Beta iterates through three steps: multi-turn user-driven evaluation where simulated users raise issues, team-based modification implementing generalizable changes, and requirement-driven selection that merges changes only after requirement verification and review.
AI.result: On held-out tasks, AHE-Beta raises pass@1 from 21.9% to 33.3% with 40.8% fewer tokens than Base Harness, outperforming Claude Code, Meta-Harness, and AHE; in a blind human A/B test it is preferred in 31 of 48 valid pairs, and transfers without further evolution to GLM-5.3 (+15.8% pass@1) and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (+5.3% pass@1).
AI.conclusion: Requirement-centered, multi-turn harness evolution produces generalizable agent improvements that align better with real-world user needs.

title: Mapping the AI Supply Chain: Dependencies, Vulnerabilities, and Market Concentration in the AI Ecosystem
summary: AI systems are built across many organizations that contribute models, data, compute, capital, talent, and other assets. While the layers of the AI stack are relatively well understood, the relationships between actors and components across layers remains sparsely documented. In this work, we focus on the organizations that make up the AI supply chain: the complex network of actors that contribute to the development and deployment of AI. We motivate the examination of the organizational AI supply chain---highlighting concerns about concentration, power, chokepoints, cascading failures, fragmented accountability, and risk---then describe our pipeline for mapping the AI supply chain. Our pipeline yields our main contribution: a multilayered, large-scale dataset of actors and relationships in the AI ecosystem, annotated with dates, descriptions, types, tags, and more. This work takes a step toward systematically mapping and measuring the AI supply chain and its properties, cataloging how models, data, chips, infrastructure, capital, and even talent flow between organizations. This data enable critical examinations of industry relationships and yield insights into the political economy of AI development and concentration. We provide several illustrative analyses, including studying the most central actors, analyzing network concentration, and identifying communities and chokepoints. While our dataset is fairly comprehensive, it is also necessarily incomplete: public documents omit private deals, and coverage is shaped by search design. Together, the approach, data, and findings aim to serve as a resource for studying the AI ecosystem. The dataset is publicly available at this https URL and can be explored interactively at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper maps the organizational AI supply chain by constructing a large-scale, multilayered dataset of actors and relationships across models, data, compute, capital, and talent.
AI.motivation: While technical layers of the AI stack are well understood, organizational dependencies, concentration, chokepoints, and accountability gaps across those layers remain sparsely documented.
AI.method: The authors build a pipeline to extract and annotate a multilayered dataset of organizations and their relationships—including dates, descriptions, types, and tags—tracking flows of models, data, chips, infrastructure, capital, and talent.
AI.result: Illustrative analyses of the publicly released dataset reveal central actors, network concentration, communities, and supply-chain chokepoints, while noting incompleteness due to private deals and search design.
AI.conclusion: The dataset and mapping pipeline provide an empirical foundation for studying market concentration, systemic risk, and political economy in the AI ecosystem.

title: OCLDA-GS: Object-Centric Local Deformation-Aware Gaussian Streaming
summary: Streaming 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) allows for online reconstruction of dynamic scenes from multi-view videos for Free Viewpoint Video (FVV). Current time and storage efficient methods rely on selecting a subset of anchor Gaussians and neighborhood interpolation for fast streamable 3DGS. However, these methods can overlook object-specific motion and introduce inconsistencies near object boundaries. We propose OCLDA-GS, an object-centric streaming framework that dynamically reallocates object and motion-aware Gaussian anchors to allocate anchor Gaussian support for objects undergoing large motion while at the same time, restricting the gaussian neighborhood within object groups for more precise object boundaries. Furthermore, it estimates object-wise rigid transformations (e.g. a hand moving) and leverages these estimates to learn per-anchor local deformation correction for small deformations (e.g. wrinkles on a shirt). Then, we conduct experiments on three dynamic multi-view video datasets and demonstrate improvements over the previous baselines alongside improved quality between refinement timesteps. Under matched refinement budgets, our method improves PSNR over Instant Gaussian Stream (IGS) by 0.169 dB on N3DV, 0.202 dB on Meeting Room and +0.199 on Google Immersive, while reducing the mean PSNR drop between refinement timesteps by 9.2% and 13.8% in N3DV and Meeting Room, respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes OCLDA-GS, an object-centric streaming 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that handles large object motion and local deformations for Free Viewpoint Video.
AI.motivation: Existing streamable 3DGS methods use uniform anchor selection and neighborhood interpolation, which overlook object-specific motion and cause artifacts near object boundaries.
AI.method: OCLDA-GS dynamically reallocates Gaussian anchors to objects with large motion, restricts Gaussian neighborhoods within object groups for sharper boundaries, and estimates object-wise rigid transformations combined with per-anchor local deformation corrections.
AI.result: Under matched refinement budgets, OCLDA-GS improves PSNR over Instant Gaussian Stream by 0.169 dB on N3DV, 0.202 dB on Meeting Room, and 0.199 dB on Google Immersive, while reducing mean PSNR drop between refinement timesteps by 9.2% on N3DV and 13.8% on Meeting Room.
AI.conclusion: Object-aware anchor allocation, grouped neighborhoods, and rigid-plus-local deformation modeling improve dynamic 3DGS streaming quality and temporal stability.

title: Autoregressive View Model
summary: We present the Autoregressive View Model (AVM), which generates a scene as a stream of views without constructing an explicit 3D representation. Through a unified in-context interface, AVM conditions on images or videos to generate short clips along a requested camera path. Visual context grounds reconstruction and interpolation, while a learned prior enables extrapolation into unseen regions. AVM retrieves relevant views from inputs and generated history to form a bounded active context. We fine-tune a pretrained bidirectional video diffusion transformer with flow matching in an N-in-1-out formulation. We then tune a causal model on its own rollouts to improve photorealism, reduce denoising steps, and limit long-horizon drift. We scale training to approximately 8M scenes and video clips. We evaluate generation capacity and scene persistence across benchmarks for camera control, text control, visual quality, dynamics, sparse and 4D reconstruction, and long-horizon consistency. The results demonstrate that AVM adapts to diverse input and output settings through one in-context interface.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the Autoregressive View Model (AVM), a video-diffusion-based model that generates scenes as a stream of views along a camera path without an explicit 3D representation.
AI.motivation: Synthesizing consistent, photorealistic views across long camera trajectories from diverse image or video inputs remains challenging without building explicit 3D geometry.
AI.method: AVM fine-tunes a pretrained bidirectional video diffusion transformer with flow matching in an N-in-1-out formulation, retrieves relevant views from inputs and history into a bounded active context, and tunes a causal model on its own rollouts over ~8M scenes and clips.
AI.result: Evaluations across camera control, text control, visual quality, dynamics, sparse and 4D reconstruction, and long-horizon consistency benchmarks show that AVM adapts to diverse input-output settings through one unified in-context interface.
AI.conclusion: Autoregressive view generation with bounded active context and rollout tuning enables persistent, controllable scene synthesis without explicit 3D reconstruction.

title: Bits, Not Boxes: Label-Free Layer Selection for Visual Localization in VLMs
summary: Attention maps cheaply show where a vision-language model (VLM) looks, but attention sinks make them unreliable for localization. Contrasting the question with a generic prompt suppresses sinks, yet only some layers localize the queried object. Existing methods find these layers with box annotations or fixed rules. We show that attention itself can identify them. A question changes how much a head attends to the image and where this attention goes. The two effects separate exactly, and the second, measured in bits on unlabeled questions, indicates which layers localize. WhereBits turns these where-to-look bits into a layer prior and combines it with per-head contrastive scores. Its three design constants were fixed once on labeled COCO data, and a new model or resolution needs only unlabeled questions. Across eight VLMs, WhereBits matches the pointing accuracy of box-tuned layers on COCO and RefCOCO and ranks target tokens better. This advantage holds on a held-out model family and at higher resolutions. Its COCO pointing accuracy is 0.72, against 0.22 for mean attention. In training-free zoom-in, its crops raise V* accuracy by 6.0 points under forced-choice evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces WhereBits, a label-free method that identifies which VLM layers localize queried objects by measuring how much a question shifts attention distribution in bits.
AI.motivation: Contrastive attention maps suppress attention sinks, but only specific VLM layers localize objects, and existing methods require box annotations or fixed rules to find them.
AI.method: WhereBits separates how much a head attends to the image from where attention goes, converts the where-to-look bits on unlabeled questions into a layer prior, and combines it with per-head contrastive scores using three constants fixed once on COCO.
AI.result: Across eight VLMs, WhereBits matches box-tuned layer pointing accuracy on COCO and RefCOCO (0.72 COCO pointing accuracy vs. 0.22 for mean attention), generalizes to a held-out model family and higher resolutions, and improves V* forced-choice accuracy by 6.0 points via training-free zoom-in.
AI.conclusion: Information-theoretic measurement of question-induced attention shifts provides a simple, label-free way to select localizing layers in VLMs.

title: TransFIRA+: Transfer Learning for Biometric Recognizability Assessment
summary: Biometric recognition in surveillance, video, and web imagery must contend with extreme variation in pose, blur, illumination, occlusion, and distance, where visual quality metrics fail to predict whether inputs are recognizable to the deployed encoder. Existing face image quality assessment methods rely on visual heuristics, curated annotations, or costly generative pipelines, leaving their predictions detached from the encoder's decision geometry. We introduce TransFIRA, a lightweight framework that grounds recognizability directly in embedding space. TransFIRA derives class-center similarity (CCS) and class-center angular separation (CCAS) from a pretrained encoder's embeddings and learns to predict them from images without quality annotations. Using predicted CCS for template weighting and CCAS>0 as a natural filtering threshold yields state-of-the-art face verification performance on BRIAR, raising TAR at $10^{-6}$ FMR from 0.085 with uniform averaging to 0.598. The predicted scores also reveal how image degradations affect encoder-specific recognizability. TransFIRA+ extends this framework to cross-camera multimodal person identification in untrimmed surveillance video. In this setting, body recognizability scores saturate within a narrow range, making direct weighting effectively uniform. We introduce a post-hoc sigmoid calibration that transforms these saturated scores into informative weights without retraining. After calibration, the BRIAR-trained TransFIRA predictor improves fused face and body identification on two unseen multi-camera datasets, outperforming detector-confidence weighting and uncalibrated CCS-rank weighting. Together, TransFIRA and TransFIRA+ demonstrate that encoder-grounded recognizability generalizes across biometric modalities and recognition settings.

AI.tldr: The paper presents TransFIRA and TransFIRA+, lightweight frameworks that predict biometric recognizability directly from a pretrained encoder's embedding geometry without quality annotations.
AI.motivation: Visual quality heuristics and curated annotations fail to reflect whether degraded surveillance or web images are recognizable to a specific deployed biometric encoder.
AI.method: TransFIRA predicts class-center similarity (CCS) and class-center angular separation (CCAS) from images to weight and filter templates; TransFIRA+ adds post-hoc sigmoid calibration without retraining to address score saturation in cross-camera body identification.
AI.result: On BRIAR face verification, TransFIRA raises TAR at 10^-6 FMR from 0.085 (uniform averaging) to 0.598; after calibration, TransFIRA+ improves fused face-and-body identification on two unseen multi-camera datasets over detector-confidence and uncalibrated CCS-rank weighting.
AI.conclusion: Grounding recognizability assessment in encoder embedding geometry with lightweight calibration generalizes effectively across biometric modalities and surveillance settings.

title: mmTherm: Absolute 3D Human Pose Estimation from Low-Resolution Thermal Images and mmWave Radar
summary: Absolute 3D human pose estimation (HPE) aims to recover both a person's body pose and their global position in 3D space. Privacy-preserving millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar provides distance and direction measurement capabilities, but its sparse point clouds make HPE under-constrained. Low-resolution thermal imaging can provide complementary observations of body direction and structure. However, our evaluation shows that a strong feature-level fusion baseline loses much of its localization and HPE advantage when generalizing to unseen subjects, with radial localization becoming less accurate than a radar-only baseline. Motivated by this finding, we introduce mmTherm, a lightweight framework that explicitly incorporates the complementary geometric properties of thermal imaging and mmWave radar. It combines body structure and joint directions estimated from thermal images with range information from radar to localize the body and reconstruct its 3D pose. Experiments on OctoNet show that mmTherm reduces cross-user absolute joint error by 33% and root localization error by 38% relative to the strongest corresponding baselines, while requiring substantially fewer parameters and less computation at inference.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces mmTherm, a lightweight framework for absolute 3D human pose estimation that fuses low-resolution thermal images with millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar.
AI.motivation: mmWave radar point clouds are too sparse for accurate 3D pose estimation alone, while naive feature-level fusion with thermal images degrades cross-user localization accuracy below a radar-only baseline.
AI.method: mmTherm explicitly exploits complementary geometric properties by combining body structure and joint directions estimated from thermal images with range measurements from mmWave radar to localize the body and reconstruct 3D pose.
AI.result: On OctoNet, mmTherm reduces cross-user absolute joint error by 33% and root localization error by 38% compared to the strongest baselines, while requiring substantially fewer parameters and less inference computation.
AI.conclusion: Explicit geometric fusion of thermal directionality and radar range overcomes cross-user generalization failures in privacy-preserving 3D human pose estimation.

title: Reference-Guided Data Curation for 3D Medical Vision-Language Pretraining
comment: Accepted at WACV 2027. Code: this https URL
summary: Training 3D vision-language models (VLMs) on large medical imaging datasets collected across institutions is constrained by data quality. Vast, uncurated pools of image-report pairs are characterized by redundancy, class imbalance, and cross-institutional heterogeneity. We address this challenge of data curation for improving 3D VLM pretraining by proposing an offline, training-free, reference-guided data curation recipe. Our approach leverages a small, high-quality reference set to independently extract quality signals for each modality of a large, uncurated pool and merges them through a rank-aggregation step into a single ranking that guides sample selection. We validate this method on datasets comprising 35k 3D abdominal CT volume-report pairs from two institutions and 58k 2D chest X-ray image-report pairs. On 3D CT, using our reference-guided data curation strategy, our curated model matches the zero-shot disease classification performance of a state-of-the-art baseline (Merlin) while using $3.3\times$ less training data and a reference set of 5k samples. On 2D chest X-rays, our method yields a curated model that matches or exceeds the zero-shot disease classification performance of a model trained on the full pool while using up to $10\times$ less training data and a reference set of only 74 samples. Ablations show that the selection is stable under resampling of the reference, that smaller reference sets still outperform random sampling, and that label rebalancing does not improve performance. To support reproducibility, we release our code.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an offline, training-free, reference-guided data curation recipe for 3D medical vision-language pretraining.
AI.motivation: Large, uncurated medical image-report datasets suffer from redundancy, class imbalance, and cross-institutional heterogeneity that degrade 3D VLM pretraining.
AI.method: The method uses a small, high-quality reference set to independently score each modality in an uncurated pool and merges them via rank aggregation to select training samples.
AI.result: Evaluated on 35k 3D abdominal CT volume-report pairs and 58k 2D chest X-rays, the curated model matches Merlin's zero-shot disease classification on 3D CT with 3.3x less data (5k reference set) and matches or exceeds full-pool 2D X-ray performance with up to 10x less data (74 reference samples).
AI.conclusion: Training-free rank aggregation guided by a small reference set substantially improves data efficiency for medical vision-language pretraining.

title: GRID-UAV: Geometry and Ray-depth Integrated Decision-making for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) encode images with 2D encoders that capture little 3D structure. A common approach is to feed the policy estimated depth, but a UAV chooses its own altitude, must judge distances tens of meters away, where monocular depth is less reliable, and must relate its forward and downward views. On long aerial routes, adding depth features directly brings no significant gain (42.5% vs. 42.6% success), so we study how 3D information should be given to the policy. Analyzing flight failures, we find that two forms of 3D grounding fail in opposite ways: explicit 3D lifting of depth collides less on the way but more often fails to finish at the target, while implicit alignment with a 3D geometry model finishes more often but collides more. We propose GRID, which combines both: (1) it lifts monocular depth into ray-corrected 3D positions in the UAV's frame for both cameras, and (2) during training only, it aligns its visual features with a frozen multi-view geometry model, at no inference cost. GRID adding explicit lifting to implicit alignment significantly increases how often the policy reaches the target ($61.5\% \rightarrow 69.5\%$, $p<0.001$), and adding implicit alignment to explicit lifting significantly increases how often it completes the task once there ($57.7\% \rightarrow 61.4\%$, $p<0.05$). On TravelUAV (3,005 test episodes), GRID achieves the best success rate on every split, with relative gains over the state of the art of 9.5% (seen), 17.1% (unseen objects) and 25.4% (unseen map).

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GRID, a 3D grounding framework for UAV vision-language-action (VLA) models that combines explicit ray-corrected depth lifting with training-time implicit geometric alignment.
AI.motivation: 2D encoders in VLAs lack 3D structure, and simply adding monocular depth fails on long aerial routes (42.5% vs. 42.6% success) because explicit lifting and implicit alignment fail in opposite ways (task completion vs. collision).
AI.method: GRID lifts monocular depth into ray-corrected 3D positions in the UAV frame for forward and downward cameras, and aligns visual features with a frozen multi-view geometry model during training only at zero inference cost.
AI.result: Combining both components significantly increases target reaching (61.5% to 69.5%) and task completion (57.7% to 61.4%); on TravelUAV (3,005 test episodes), GRID achieves the best success rate on every split with relative gains over SOTA of 9.5% (seen), 17.1% (unseen objects), and 25.4% (unseen map).
AI.conclusion: Integrating explicit ray-corrected 3D lifting with implicit geometric feature alignment resolves complementary failure modes in aerial VLA navigation.

title: MedHarness: A Unified Budgeted Runtime for Reliable Medical Imaging Agents
summary: Medical imaging agents already return answers on heterogeneous imaging surfaces, yet deployment still faces a limited verification budget where each wrong accept can harm clinical trust. When a thin check and a deeper evidence pass disagree on the same case, deciding when to stop, open more evidence, repair, or reject without a shared controller remains ill-posed. Tool-using workflows often lock a surface-specific evidence order per dataset, or a private always-open full-depth verification path; those pipelines stay costly, leave many wrong accepts, and cannot share one controller across modalities. We present MedHarness, a registered multi-surface runtime reliability layer that reformulates post-answer control as shared decision-object attachment after a proposer's initial prediction. Under Shared Decision Object, Minimum-Sufficient Verification, and Intermediate Repair, one shared policy with surface recipe adapters lets a new imaging surface join the same stop / open-evidence / repair / reject controller by recipe registration. On a 512-case live pool, MedHarness cuts wrong accepts versus a full-verification baseline by about 47% and raises accepted accuracy to 83.2% vs. 72.9% at 86.1% coverage versus full release under that baseline. On a failure-enriched multi-surface stress ranking, the same controller cuts estimated remote service calls per case by about 71% versus that baseline under a matched context-load setting. A held-out three-surface check and an alternate language-model transfer keep the same control ordering. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper presents MedHarness, a unified budgeted runtime reliability layer that manages post-answer verification, repair, and rejection across heterogeneous medical imaging agents.
AI.motivation: Medical imaging agents face limited verification budgets and heterogeneous modalities, making it ill-posed to decide when to stop, gather more evidence, repair, or reject when initial checks disagree.
AI.method: MedHarness reformulates post-answer control as shared decision-object attachment after an initial prediction, using surface recipe adapters so one shared stop/open-evidence/repair/reject controller works across modalities under Minimum-Sufficient Verification and Intermediate Repair.
AI.result: On a 512-case live pool, MedHarness cuts wrong accepts by ~47% versus a full-verification baseline and raises accepted accuracy from 72.9% to 83.2% at 86.1% coverage; on a stress ranking it cuts estimated remote service calls by ~71% and preserves control ordering on held-out surfaces and an alternate LLM.
AI.conclusion: A shared, recipe-registered verification controller improves clinical reliability and reduces verification cost across multi-surface medical imaging agents.

title: Trust the Ray, Not the Depth: Ray-Lateral Agreement for Multi-View 3D Human Pose Fusion
summary: Put a monocular mesh estimator behind every camera of a calibrated rig, and the reconstructed bodies land a meter or more apart. The cause is geometric: each estimate sits at the depth implied by a focal length the network assumed, not the one the camera has. Its error therefore points almost entirely along its own viewing ray, and the calibration tells us that direction exactly. To address this, we introduce the Ray-Lateral Agreement (RLA), which follows one rule: trust the ray, not the depth. RLA first slides every estimate along its own rays, which removes the depth bias and leaves the shape untouched. It then fuses the views one point at a time, under a Gaussian error whose precision follows each viewing ray. The maximum-likelihood solution is closed-form, interpolates between averaging and midpoint triangulation, and stays well conditioned where triangulation is singular. Robustness is the harder half, because correct views also disagree along their rays. Any weight built on the full residual therefore punishes good views together with bad ones. Ray-lateral agreement instead scores every view, at every point, by its residual across that view's own ray alone. We evaluated RLA on multi-camera public benchmark datasets. Across two, three, and four cameras and three per-view pose estimators, RLA consistently achieves lower worst-case error than all triangulation baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Ray-Lateral Agreement (RLA), a closed-form, robust multi-view 3D human pose fusion method that trusts viewing rays rather than monocular depth estimates.
AI.motivation: Monocular mesh estimators placed behind calibrated cameras suffer from depth errors along their viewing rays due to assumed focal lengths, while full-residual weighting in fusion punishes correct views that only disagree along their rays.
AI.method: RLA slides each per-view estimate along its own viewing rays to remove depth bias without altering shape, fuses points via closed-form maximum-likelihood under ray-aligned Gaussian precision, and weights views per point using only the residual lateral to each view's own ray.
AI.result: Evaluated across two, three, and four cameras and three per-view pose estimators on public multi-camera benchmarks, RLA consistently achieves lower worst-case error than all triangulation baselines.
AI.conclusion: Separating ray-lateral agreement from depth uncertainty yields well-conditioned, robust multi-view 3D human pose fusion.

title: ORGANIC3D: Grounding 3D CT Vision Language Models in Organ Level Image Text Coupling
summary: Vision language models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in 3D computed tomography (CT) classification, but high accuracy does not reflect whether their predictions rely on the correct anatomical evidence. We introduce ORGANIC3D, a framework for evaluating and improving organ level image text alignment through controlled anatomical interventions. Our benchmark assesses 12 vision encoder checkpoints and 7 generative VLMs using matched patient comparisons, organ erasure, lesion replacement, and laterality perturbations, revealing substantial alignment failures even among top performing models. To learn organ level image text correspondence, ORGANIC3D aligns each finding sentence with the anatomy aware image features and trains on edited scans to anchor this alignment in the organ's image evidence. We further extend this framework to generative VLMs, promoting evidence dependent question answering and report generation. Trained exclusively on public data, ORGANIC3D achieves SOTA classification AUROC on CTRATE, Merlin, and the heldout RADChestCT dataset and reaches 77% laterality accuracy, compared with at most 66% for prior models. Its generative VLM matches or exceeds all evaluated publicly released VLMs on visual question answering, achieves the highest report accuracy, and retracts 96 to 99% of target organ findings after organ removal, versus a maximum of 69% for other models. Together, these results establish ORGANIC3D as a framework for testing whether 3D CT vision language models ground their predictions in anatomical evidence and for improving organ level alignment alongside predictive accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ORGANIC3D, a benchmark and training framework for evaluating and improving organ-level image-text alignment in 3D CT vision-language models.
AI.motivation: High classification accuracy on 3D CT scans does not guarantee that VLMs rely on the correct anatomical evidence rather than spurious correlations.
AI.method: ORGANIC3D benchmarks 12 vision encoders and 7 generative VLMs via matched patient comparisons, organ erasure, lesion replacement, and laterality perturbations, and trains models by aligning finding sentences with anatomy-aware image features on edited scans.
AI.result: Trained solely on public data, ORGANIC3D achieves SOTA classification AUROC on CTRATE, Merlin, and held-out RADChestCT, reaches 77% laterality accuracy (vs. at most 66% prior), and its generative VLM retracts 96-99% of target organ findings after organ removal (vs. at most 69% for others).
AI.conclusion: Controlled anatomical interventions and anatomy-aware sentence alignment ground 3D CT VLMs in genuine organ-level visual evidence.

title: Layer-Matched Sparse Attention for Low-Redundancy 3D Reconstruction
summary: VGGT reconstructs cameras and geometry from unposed images in one pass, but its global attention grows quadratically with the number of views. Training-free accelerators thin this attention and work well on redundant video, but lose pose accuracy when views share little geometry. This paper traces these losses to two kinds of cross-view information that a uniform sparse approximation can fail to preserve together: diffuse layers aggregate distributed context, whereas matching layers depend on query-specific interactions that carry little attention mass. A per-layer statistic measures the log-mass missed by a mean token. Its row-free proxy is the logit variance, and it selects the estimator for each layer. Diffuse layers use shared, importance-sampled hub keys, with log-weights that make the softmax numerator and denominator unbiased. Matching layers stay exact: every aggressive thinning tested cost accuracy. At equal cost, the selected layers outperform the four shifted windows tested. On 13 unseen low-redundancy scenes with 32 views, LMSA stays within 1.4 AUC@5 of dense attention, compared with 10.3 for AVGGT and 4.5 for SAF3R; its difference from contemporaneous GPA-VGGT is not significant, and only its gains over AVGGT pass both scene-level tests. With 100 views, it stays within 1.9 AUC@5 while its aggregator runs $2.0\times$ faster. Used post hoc to choose the layers GPA-VGGT protects, the statistic improves it by 1.2 AUC@5 for 5% more FLOPs. Applied untuned to $\pi^3$, it beats AVGGT but remains further from dense accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Layer-Matched Sparse Attention (LMSA) to accelerate VGGT global attention on low-redundancy 3D reconstruction without losing camera pose accuracy.
AI.motivation: Training-free sparse attention accelerators work on redundant video but degrade pose accuracy on low-redundancy views because uniform sparsity cannot preserve both diffuse context layers and query-specific matching layers.
AI.method: LMSA uses logit variance as a row-free proxy to classify layers: diffuse layers use shared importance-sampled hub keys with unbiased log-weights, while matching layers remain exact.
AI.result: On 13 unseen low-redundancy 32-view scenes, LMSA stays within 1.4 AUC@5 of dense attention (vs. 10.3 for AVGGT and 4.5 for SAF3R); at 100 views it stays within 1.9 AUC@5 while running its aggregator 2.0x faster, and its layer-selection statistic also improves GPA-VGGT by 1.2 AUC@5 for 5% more FLOPs.
AI.conclusion: Distinguishing diffuse layers from exact matching layers enables fast, accurate sparse attention for low-redundancy multi-view 3D reconstruction.

title: DOCK: Dual-Stream-Inspired Self-Supervised Object-Centric Representations Grounded in Robot Kinematics
summary: Latent-space planners select actions by comparing the embedding of a predicted future image with that of a goal image. This assumes that distance in the embedding reflects how far the scene is from the goal. We profile this assumption with simulator-executed futures, which removes prediction error. For six frozen DINO and V-JEPA encoders, feature distance barely tracks the object's distance to its goal: the rank correlation is at most 0.11, against 0.87 for object-mask centroids. It is dominated by background and robot patches, and frozen-feature readouts capture the arm far better than the object. Inspired by the ventral (what) and dorsal (where/how) visual streams, we propose DOCK, which learns an object representation whose changes agree with measured physical motion. A grasped object moves with the gripper, so forward kinematics on the joint angles gives a proxy for the object's displacement without annotation. From 9,951 held-object transport trajectories in 21 simulated kitchen scenes, we mine 404K displacement pairs and train three components: an object token pooled from patch features (what), a spatial ruler that makes differences of readout coordinates equal to measured displacements (where), and a dynamics predictor over object tokens (how). Used as a planning cost, the learned representation places the object in 15 of 21 tasks, as many as an oracle that reads the true object position, while mask geometry reaches 10 and frozen feature distance 9. It still solves the most tasks when the unseen robot arm is visible, and its ranking transfers to held-out layouts with unseen object instances and categories without any adaptation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DOCK, a self-supervised object-centric representation learning method grounded in robot forward kinematics for latent-space planning.
AI.motivation: Frozen DINO and V-JEPA embeddings fail to track object-to-goal distance (rank correlation at most 0.11 vs. 0.87 for mask centroids) because they are dominated by background and robot arm patches.
AI.method: Using 404K displacement pairs mined from 9,951 simulated kitchen transport trajectories where gripper kinematics proxy object motion, DOCK trains a pooled object token (what), a spatial ruler matching readout differences to physical displacements (where), and a dynamics predictor (how).
AI.result: Used as a planning cost, DOCK places objects in 15 of 21 tasks—matching an oracle with true object positions and outperforming mask geometry (10) and frozen features (9)—and transfers zero-shot to unseen robot arms, layouts, and object categories.
AI.conclusion: Grounding visual representations in robot kinematics yields object-centric embeddings that accurately reflect physical task progress for planning.

title: VIBRA: Backward-Compatible Cross-Modal Retrieval with Consensus Barycenters
summary: Backward-compatible retrieval enables a new encoder to query the gallery that an old model has already encoded, so that a cross-modal retrieval system can be upgraded without re-encoding billions of items. Existing compatible methods either fit the old query and stay near the accuracy of the old model, or run the old and the new encoder for every query. We propose VIBRA, which matches relevance on the old gallery, corrects the errors of a single model with the barycenter of several views, which is itself a query in the old space, and trains the new encoder to inherit this consensus, so that models absent at deployment still shape every query. We show that the barycenter gains margin over the average of its views exactly when their hardest irrelevant items differ, and we characterize the share of this gain that one encoder can reach. On five benchmarks with five upgrades among six CLIP, MetaCLIP and SigLIP2 backbones, VIBRA is the best compatible method in all 50 settings, improving Recall@1 by up to 5.6 points over the strongest baseline and by up to 18.0 points over the old model, while adding less than 1 ms to the latency of the new encoder.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VIBRA, a backward-compatible cross-modal retrieval method that trains a new encoder to match the consensus barycenter of multiple views in an old gallery space.
AI.motivation: Upgrading cross-modal retrieval without re-encoding billions of gallery items requires backward compatibility, yet existing methods either cap accuracy at the old model or require running both old and new encoders at query time.
AI.method: VIBRA forms a query in the old space from the barycenter of multiple views to correct single-model errors and trains the new encoder to inherit this consensus, eliminating the need for the old encoder at deployment.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks and five upgrades among six CLIP, MetaCLIP, and SigLIP2 backbones, VIBRA ranks best in all 50 settings, improving Recall@1 by up to 5.6 points over the strongest baseline and 18.0 points over the old model while adding under 1 ms latency.
AI.conclusion: Distilling multi-view consensus barycenters into a new encoder enables high-accuracy, low-latency backward-compatible retrieval upgrades.

title: PRISM: Profiling and Representation of Individual Stereotypical Motion
summary: An anatomical pose provides interpretable joint structure, but no fixed set of physical landmarks can fully specify a person's movement. We introduce PRISM, a complementary representation that characterizes repetitive movement using tracked masks and dense optical flow. Torso-relative flow measures intensity, frame-wise mask variation measures spatial extent, signed-flow recurrence estimates frequency, and persistent sliding-window geometry describes the rhythmicity of the movement. Across 1,890 synthetic conditions, the measurements recover controlled speed, amplitude, and frequency while exposing observation limits. An idealized hand-motion experiment demonstrates variation omitted by identical exact COCO-17 trajectories; controlled corruption experiments separately examine measurement sensitivity. Audits of two pose methods on the same data cohort and 36,930 external skeleton clips document incomplete observation and dependence on processing choices. In 1,404 annotated complex stereotypical motor movement bouts from six autistic participants, total flow converges with pose motion, while matched-coordinate examples and repeated-session profiles show differences in intensity, extent, frequency, and rhythmicity within behavior labels. A separate VLM comparison evaluates quantitative frequency estimation, and a profile-conditioned decoder links the measurements to illustrative skeletal movements. PRISM connects numerical profiles to visible examples, providing an interpretable way to compare how the same behavior is expressed beyond its label or event count.

AI.tldr: The paper presents PRISM, a representation using tracked masks and dense optical flow to profile intensity, spatial extent, frequency, and rhythmicity of repetitive stereotypical movements.
AI.motivation: Fixed anatomical pose landmarks miss subtle movement variations and depend heavily on pose-estimation processing choices when characterizing repetitive behaviors.
AI.method: PRISM computes torso-relative optical flow for intensity, frame-wise mask variation for spatial extent, signed-flow recurrence for frequency, and persistent sliding-window geometry for rhythmicity, paired with a profile-conditioned decoder for visual illustration.
AI.result: Across 1,890 synthetic conditions, PRISM recovers controlled speed, amplitude, and frequency; across 1,404 annotated stereotypical movement bouts from six autistic participants, it reveals within-label differences in movement expression that identical pose trajectories omit.
AI.conclusion: Optical-flow and mask-based profiling complements skeletal pose to provide an interpretable, fine-grained characterization of stereotypical motor behaviors.

title: LightSEAD: Lightweight SE(3)-Aware Keypoint Detector through Selective Knowledge Distillation
summary: The pursuit of improved performance in deep learning has often been accompanied by increasing architectural complexity and computational demands. We explore an alternative direction: achieving more with less through structured supervision. We introduce LightSEAD, a lightweight SE(3)-aware keypoint detector initialised with calibrated Harris pseudo-labels and enriched through viewpoint-aware and appearance-aware supervision and selective knowledge distillation. LightSEAD comprises only six convolutional layers and 84,289 learnable parameters, achieving competitive repeatability across HPatches, KITTI 06 and 4Seasons while demonstrating its downstream applicability to relative pose estimation on MegaDepth-1500. Further optimised for mixed-precision inference, LightSEAD Coarse achieves approximately 909 FPS on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 and 139 FPS on a Jetson Orin Nano Super.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LightSEAD, a lightweight SE(3)-aware keypoint detector trained via structured supervision and selective knowledge distillation.
AI.motivation: Deep keypoint detectors increasingly rely on heavy architectures and high compute, limiting their deployment on resource-constrained edge hardware.
AI.method: LightSEAD uses only six convolutional layers (84,289 parameters), initialized with calibrated Harris pseudo-labels and trained with viewpoint-aware, appearance-aware supervision and selective knowledge distillation.
AI.result: LightSEAD achieves competitive repeatability on HPatches, KITTI 06, and 4Seasons and strong relative pose estimation on MegaDepth-1500, while LightSEAD Coarse reaches ~909 FPS on an RTX 4090 and 139 FPS on a Jetson Orin Nano Super with mixed-precision inference.
AI.conclusion: Structured supervision and selective distillation enable a compact convolutional keypoint detector to match heavier models at high edge frame rates.

title: EyeDiT: Anatomy-Grounded Multi-Modal Eye Generation and Simulation
summary: Synthetic eye data are critical for rapid development of eye tracking (ET) in AR/VR applications. However, existing synthetic eye generators are largely image-centric and lack a high-quality underlying 3D anatomy of the eye, which limits their control mainly to the gaze and provides no anatomical labels. To address this problem, we propose EyeDiT, an anatomy-grounded, multi-modal 3D eye generation and simulation model trained with optical coherence tomography (OCT), labeled anatomy point clouds and near-eye images. Our pipeline first trains a Multi-Modal Anatomy Variational Autoencoder (VAE), which encodes an anatomy-aware latent representation from all input modalities. Then, our Eye Latent DiT is trained to generate latent samples conditioned on the optical axis, the pupil position and radius, and the subject identity. Together with Gaussian decoders for novel-view simulation, our model enables control over the pupil, subject identity and viewpoint for data synthesis. We show that our model outperforms previous eye image synthesis models in novel-view synthesis (24.9 against 21.8 dB PSNR from a single view), and that a public ET neural network trained on our synthetic data shows a smaller sim-to-real gap than when trained on data from other generators (3.5$^\circ$ vs. 8.4$^\circ$ gaze error), approaches a network trained on real data, and further improves ET performance when combined with real data (2.3$^\circ$ vs. 2.6$^\circ$). More information is available on the project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes EyeDiT, an anatomy-grounded multi-modal 3D eye generation and simulation model for AR/VR eye tracking data synthesis.
AI.motivation: Existing synthetic eye generators are image-centric and lack underlying 3D eye anatomy, limiting control to gaze direction and omitting anatomical labels.
AI.method: EyeDiT trains a Multi-Modal Anatomy VAE on OCT, labeled anatomy point clouds, and near-eye images, then trains an Eye Latent DiT conditioned on optical axis, pupil position/radius, and subject identity, paired with Gaussian decoders for novel-view rendering.
AI.result: EyeDiT outperforms prior eye synthesis models in novel-view synthesis (24.9 vs. 21.8 dB PSNR from a single view), reduces sim-to-real gaze error for a public ET network (3.5 deg vs. 8.4 deg), and improves real-data training when combined (2.3 deg vs. 2.6 deg).
AI.conclusion: Grounding generative eye synthesis in multi-modal 3D anatomy improves both controllability and downstream eye-tracking generalization.

title: Image-Condition-Controlled Diffusion Network with Large-Scale CT Pretraining for CT-Free Attenuation Correction in Dynamic Cardiac PET
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Radiation and Plasma Medical Sciences
summary: Positron emission tomography (PET) provides quantitative information on myocardial perfusion. In dynamic PET, tracer kinetics are tracked through a series of reconstructed time frames. Reliable attenuation correction is essential for accurate measurements. Clinical attenuation maps ($\mu$-maps) are typically derived from computed tomography (CT), which adds radiation exposure and may introduce PET-CT misregistration due to respiratory and cardiac motion. Moreover, supervised CT-free methods rely on paired non-attenuation-corrected (NAC) PET and CT data, which are scarce, whereas large-scale unpaired CT data are more readily available. To address these challenges, we propose Large-scale Unpaired CT-Informed Diffusion (LUCID), a framework that transfers anatomical priors learned from 10,000 chest CT volumes in the public CT-RATE dataset to $\mu$-map synthesis for dynamic cardiac $^{82}$Rb PET. First, a convolutional neural network (CNN) predicts an initial $\mu$-map from each NAC PET frame. Second, the CT-pretrained diffusion backbone refines a low-noise perturbation of the CNN prediction through a single denoising step, conditioned on the corresponding NAC PET frame via ControlNet. Finally, frame-wise predictions are averaged voxel-wise to obtain the final $\mu$-map. We further introduce the voxel-wise temporal standard deviation (TSD) to quantify inter-frame variability without requiring a reference $\mu$-map. We evaluated LUCID on an in-house dataset of 102 patients and found that it achieved the best quantitative accuracy while maintaining competitive inter-frame consistency. Ablation studies showed that refinement with a diffusion backbone pretrained on in-house CT data from the training patients was less accurate than the CNN prediction alone, highlighting the importance of large-scale CT pretraining.

AI.tldr: The paper presents LUCID, a diffusion framework pretrained on 10,000 unpaired chest CT volumes to synthesize attenuation maps for dynamic cardiac PET without CT scans.
AI.motivation: CT-derived attenuation maps add radiation and suffer from motion misregistration, while supervised CT-free methods require scarce paired non-attenuation-corrected (NAC) PET and CT data.
AI.method: A CNN predicts an initial mu-map from each NAC PET frame, which a CT-pretrained diffusion backbone refines in a single denoising step conditioned on the NAC PET frame via ControlNet before voxel-wise temporal averaging; inter-frame consistency is measured via temporal standard deviation (TSD).
AI.result: Evaluated on 102 patients, LUCID achieves the best quantitative accuracy with competitive inter-frame consistency, whereas ablations show that a diffusion backbone pretrained only on in-house training CT underperforms the CNN alone.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale unpaired CT pretraining is essential for diffusion-based, CT-free attenuation correction in dynamic cardiac PET.

title: Learning What to Degrade: A Recoverability-Aware Curriculum for Reliable Smart-Glasses Super-Resolution
summary: Degradations in smart-glasses images obscure small text and fine-grained structures needed by vision-language models (VLMs) for visual assistance. We introduce an high-resolution (HR)-referenced semantic evaluation protocol that compares VLM outputs on restored images with those on corresponding HR references. Our evaluation reveals two failure modes: generative SR can synthesize misleading details, whereas restoration-oriented SR can leave critical evidence blurred or ambiguous. These findings motivate improving faithful detail recovery in restoration-oriented SR, where a key training challenge is to provide sufficiently difficult inputs while retaining recoverable visual information. We propose ReDiC (Recoverability-Difficulty Curriculum), which combines a model-independent recoverability proxy with model-relative restoration difficulty to adapt training degradation severity. ReDiC increases severity when inputs are recoverable and restoration is easy, maintains challenging but recoverable conditions, and reduces severity when estimated recoverability is low. It modifies only training degradation generation, leaving the SR architecture and reconstruction objective unchanged. Across NAFNet, SwinIR, and MambaIR, ReDiC improves average PSNR by approximately 2.5 dB and HR-referenced semantic scores by about 3 points over the corresponding baselines on synthetic benchmarks, with further gains confirmed by LLM-based and human evaluations on 200 real smart-glasses captures.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ReDiC, a recoverability-difficulty curriculum for training restoration-oriented super-resolution (SR) models on degraded smart-glasses images.
AI.motivation: Smart-glasses degradations obscure small text and details needed by VLMs; generative SR hallucinates misleading details while restoration SR leaves evidence blurred when training degradations are poorly calibrated.
AI.method: ReDiC combines a model-independent recoverability proxy with model-relative restoration difficulty to dynamically adjust training degradation severity, leaving the SR architecture and reconstruction loss unchanged.
AI.result: Across NAFNet, SwinIR, and MambaIR, ReDiC improves average PSNR by ~2.5 dB and HR-referenced semantic scores by ~3 points on synthetic benchmarks, with gains confirmed by LLM and human evaluations on 200 real smart-glasses captures.
AI.conclusion: Adapting training degradation severity to both input recoverability and model difficulty improves faithful detail recovery for VLM-assisted smart glasses.

title: What Do Learned 3D Models Add to Localization from Posed References?
summary: Localizing a query from a few posed reference images avoids building a 3D point map. We ask what the camera predictions of learned 3D models add to geometric estimation from the same references, and where failures arise. Across eight learned models and variants and five test sets, we compare reference budgets, swap pose components, and intervene on the references a model sees. At fine pose-error thresholds, geometric estimation with one additional reference is significantly more accurate than every model on two references on Cambridge and NAVER B1 and never significantly worse, alone or as a fallback behind a shared acceptance gate; with the same three references, the more accurate approach depends on the scene. The gain from the learned translation magnitude depends on reference selection: it improves seven of the eight models on 12-Scenes with the spread-out pairs we select, but none of the five we test with the two top-ranked retrieved references. Where retrieval also returns references from other locations, at NAVER Gangnam Station, models fail at different stages. A robust alignment brings Pi3X and MapAnything within 3.3 pp of adding references as needed. In controlled tests, aligning on the nearby references largely restores VGGT, Pi3X and MapAnything but not Depth Anything 3, and pose-conditioned Pi3X recovers only if the far poses are masked and left out of its input-pose normalization.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates what camera predictions from learned 3D models add to classical geometric estimation when localizing a query image from a few posed references.
AI.motivation: Learned 3D models are increasingly used for few-reference localization, but it is unclear when they outperform classical geometric estimation or how reference selection affects their failure modes.
AI.method: Across eight learned models and five test sets, the authors compare reference budgets, swap pose components, and intervene on reference sets, including robust alignment and pose-masking tests.
AI.result: At fine pose-error thresholds, geometric estimation with one extra reference beats every model on two references on Cambridge and NAVER B1; learned translation magnitude helps 7 of 8 models on spread-out 12-Scenes pairs but none with top-2 retrieved references, while robust alignment brings Pi3X and MapAnything within 3.3 pp on NAVER Gangnam Station.
AI.conclusion: Classical geometry remains competitive with more references, and learned 3D models depend heavily on reference selection and robust alignment against outlier references.

title: A Hardware-Aware Comprehensive Study of Edge Vision Deployment with A Unified Hardware-Model-Runtime Mapping Framework
summary: The rapid growth of deep learning has driven the deployment of computer vision directly on resource-constrained edge devices. However, the extreme heterogeneity of edge hardware architectures poses major challenges in selecting and designing suitable vision models. This survey bridges the gap between edge hardware constraints, model architectures, and deployment software toolchains. We establish a comprehensive taxonomy classifying edge hardware into three distinct tiers: mid-range devices (GPUs and dedicated NPUs or TPUs), dedicated embedded MPU or SoC processors, and microcontrollers (MCUs). We aggregate and analyze multi-source benchmark results for image classification and object detection across the computing spectrum, spanning from tens of watts down to milliwatt-scale bare-metal MCUs. Based on these empirical findings, we propose a two-tiered hardware-to-model mapping framework that provides concrete model selection matrices across performance priorities (Speed, Balanced, Accuracy) and actionable architectural design principles (peak SRAM budgeting, resolution-first scaling, and algorithm-compiler co-design). Finally, we highlight critical deployment challenges including toolchain fragmentation, operator incompatibility, and Vision Transformer feasibility, and outline promising future research directions in on-device adaptation and sustainable Edge AI.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a hardware-aware survey and unified hardware-model-runtime mapping framework for deploying computer vision models on edge devices.
AI.motivation: Extreme heterogeneity across edge hardware—from mid-range GPUs/NPUs to milliwatt microcontrollers—makes selecting and designing suitable vision models challenging.
AI.method: The authors classify edge hardware into three tiers, aggregate multi-source classification and detection benchmarks, and propose a two-tiered hardware-to-model mapping framework with selection matrices and design principles (peak SRAM budgeting, resolution-first scaling, algorithm-compiler co-design).
AI.result: The survey synthesizes empirical trade-offs across Speed, Balanced, and Accuracy priorities and identifies key bottlenecks including toolchain fragmentation, operator incompatibility, and Vision Transformer feasibility.
AI.conclusion: Aligning model architecture choices with hardware-tier constraints and compiler toolchains is critical for practical, sustainable Edge AI deployment.

title: CoScan: Multi-Scale Content-Adaptive Space-Filling Scans for Causal State-Space Image Restoration
summary: Selective state-space models (SSMs) have recently shown strong potential for efficient image restoration. A central difficulty, however, is that a 2D feature map typically needs to be linearized into a 1D token sequence for causal state-space updates, making restoration performance highly sensitive to the imposed scan order. Existing deterministic scans follow space-filling principles but remain fixed and content-agnostic, and can yield fragmented or semantically inconsistent contexts under degradations. We propose \textbf{CoScan}, a \textbf{co}ntent-adaptive \textbf{scan}-order design for causal vision SSMs. CoScan learns image-dependent space-filling traversals via differentiable proxy supervision driven by \textbf{scan-quality objectives} that \textit{encourage short-range coherence and causal predictability, while preserving spatial adjacency}. To support hierarchical restoration backbones, we introduce an \textbf{efficient multi-scale scan construction by coarsening a fine-level minimum spanning tree}, producing coherent scans across feature resolutions. In addition, a \textbf{frequency-guided start selection strategy} is designed to \textit{place informative structures early in the sequence prefix to strengthen causal context formation}. Plugged into existing Mamba-based backbones, CoScan yields consistent improvements across several restoration benchmarks with minimal overhead and shows promising results on high-level vision tasks. Code will be released at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CoScan, a content-adaptive, multi-scale space-filling scan-order method for causal state-space image restoration models.
AI.motivation: Causal vision state-space models (SSMs) linearize 2D feature maps into 1D sequences, and existing fixed space-filling scans produce fragmented or semantically inconsistent contexts under image degradations.
AI.method: CoScan learns image-dependent traversals via differentiable proxy supervision for short-range coherence and causal predictability, constructs multi-scale scans by coarsening a fine-level minimum spanning tree, and uses frequency-guided start selection to place informative structures early.
AI.result: Integrated into existing Mamba-based backbones, CoScan consistently improves performance across several image restoration benchmarks with minimal overhead and shows promising results on high-level vision tasks.
AI.conclusion: Content-adaptive, multi-scale scan ordering strengthens causal context formation in state-space image restoration.

title: GTA: Generative Tower of Agents for Scalable Holonic Scene Generation
summary: Scalable world modeling requires coordinating scene-wide goals with fine-grained objects and dynamic characters under limited time and context budgets. We introduce GTA (Generative Tower of Agents), which represents every unit at every level of an adaptive scene hierarchy as a holon, both a self-contained construction task and a composable scene unit. Parallel agents recursively plan the hierarchy top-down, generate assets, and assemble and refine them bottom-up. Uniform interfaces carry scene-wide requirements down the hierarchy, guiding local construction so that each holon fits into the larger one. GTA accelerates scalable world modeling through high-throughput parallel execution while preserving well-structured layouts and fine-grained asset details. GTA then populates the assembled environments with dynamic human characters whose appearance and motion are guided by the scene, yielding realized 4D worlds. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GTA (Generative Tower of Agents), a hierarchical multi-agent framework for scalable 3D and 4D world generation.
AI.motivation: Scalable world modeling must coordinate global scene-wide goals with fine-grained object details and dynamic characters under tight time and context budgets.
AI.method: GTA models every scene unit as a holon, using parallel agents to recursively plan the hierarchy top-down, generate assets, and assemble/refine them bottom-up via uniform interfaces, then populates environments with scene-guided dynamic human characters.
AI.result: GTA accelerates scalable world modeling through high-throughput parallel execution while preserving structured layouts, fine-grained asset details, and dynamic 4D character motion.
AI.conclusion: Holonic hierarchical decomposition with parallel agent execution enables scalable, coherent 4D scene generation.

title: GaussLearner: 3D Gaussian Primitives as Self-Regulating Continual Learners
summary: Continual learning of 3D Gaussian fields aims to maintain faithful reconstructions of the evolving world. However, directly fine-tuning an existing Gaussian field on new observations can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously reconstructed content. To address this challenge, existing methods employ selective local optimization, replay, or parameter regularization, yet still struggle to balance adaptation to scene changes with preservation of still-valid content. Our key insight is to view 3D Gaussian primitives themselves as self-regulating continual learners. Based on this insight, we introduce GaussLearner, which equips each Gaussian with a closed continual-learning loop connecting observation, self-regulation, and adaptation at the primitive level. At each novel state, GaussLearner first attributes pixel-wise inconsistencies in current observations to their contributing Gaussians. Each Gaussian then self-regulates through a learning weight that balances current observations against cross-state reliability. This weight governs both Gaussian parameter adaptation and optimizer memory refresh. As current inconsistencies are resolved, the adaptation outcome renews each Gaussian's reliability for future states. The resulting field is a globally coupled population of locally self-regulating learners. Across scenes from CL-Splats, WAT, and our CL-3D dataset, GaussLearner improves average PSNR by 3.41 dB over the strongest baseline. On CL-3D, it achieves the best reconstruction quality on both changed and unchanged views.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GaussLearner, a continual 3D Gaussian Splatting framework where individual Gaussian primitives act as self-regulating continual learners.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning 3D Gaussian fields on new observations causes catastrophic forgetting, and existing replay or regularization methods struggle to balance adaptation with preserving unchanged content.
AI.method: GaussLearner attributes pixel-wise observation inconsistencies to contributing Gaussians, computes a per-Gaussian learning weight balancing current observations against cross-state reliability to govern parameter updates and optimizer memory refresh, and updates reliability after adaptation.
AI.result: Across CL-Splats, WAT, and the new CL-3D dataset, GaussLearner improves average PSNR by 3.41 dB over the strongest baseline and achieves the best reconstruction quality on both changed and unchanged views on CL-3D.
AI.conclusion: Primitive-level self-regulation enables 3D Gaussian fields to adapt to local scene changes while preserving previously learned geometry and appearance.

title: ACUS: An Angular Calibrated Uncertainty Score for Incomplete-View CT
summary: Sparse-view and limited-arc computed tomography (CT) are commonly treated as projection completion: a network fills an unmeasured view, and the result is ranked by similarity to one ground-truth image. That score can be high even when the query angle is far from every acquired measurement, because a learned prior may invent anatomy the scan never constrained. Existing protocols therefore leave a basic question unanswered: how does predictive reliability change with distance from the acquired views? We propose the Angular Calibrated Uncertainty Score (ACUS) to answer that question. ACUS is the Winkler interval score of a nominal 90% predictive interval on held-out projections, binned by distance to the nearest acquired view. It charges interval width and adds a large miss penalty when a held-out pixel falls outside the interval, so a narrow band helps only when coverage holds. We use collapse on acquired angles as a necessary consistency check on the predictor. On chest and dental cone-beam orbits, interval width grows with the angular gap. Empirical coverage ranges from 77% to 92%, and the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of the point estimate falls as the width rises. Nearest-neighbor, interpolation, and point completion, each given one residual scale, have zero reported far coverage and incur outside-distance penalties. ACUS exposes gap-dependent overconfidence that a point-estimate PSNR alone does not measure.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Angular Calibrated Uncertainty Score (ACUS) to evaluate how predictive reliability degrades with angular distance in incomplete-view CT.
AI.motivation: Standard projection-completion metrics (e.g., PSNR against one ground-truth image) can score high even far from acquired views where learned priors hallucinate unconstrained anatomy.
AI.method: ACUS computes the Winkler interval score of a nominal 90% predictive interval on held-out projections binned by angular distance to the nearest acquired view, penalizing both interval width and out-of-interval misses, with collapse on acquired angles as a consistency check.
AI.result: On chest and dental cone-beam orbits, interval width grows with angular gap while coverage ranges from 77% to 92% and point-estimate PSNR drops; nearest-neighbor, interpolation, and point completion baselines yield zero far coverage and incur miss penalties.
AI.conclusion: ACUS exposes gap-dependent overconfidence in incomplete-view CT that point-estimate metrics alone fail to capture.

title: Detect What You Need: Chain-of-Causal Reasoning for 3D Intent Grounding
summary: Accurately matching human intentions in 3D space is an important goal of artificial intelligence. Recently, 3D Intention Grounding (3D-IG) has emerged, aiming to localize target 3D objects given a natural-language intent. Unlike conventional visual grounding with descriptive referring expressions, 3D-IG intents are abstract and non-descriptive, making object localization substantially more challenging. This requires inferring latent functional requirements from non-descriptive intents and aligning them with object-level 3D representations. However, existing methods largely rely on implicit intent-object matching, leading to logical gaps and limited interpretability, robustness, and generalization. To address these challenges, we propose Chain-of-Causal Reasoning (CoCR), a causality-inspired functional dependency reasoning framework that explicitly bridges abstract intentions and candidate objects through intermediate functional requirements. Specifically, CoCR progressively decomposes complex intents into ordered functional requirements, thereby forming an explicit intent-function-object reasoning chain that links abstract intentions to object suitability. Building on this chain, we construct a causality-inspired functional dependency graph to model requirement-attribute relationships and introduce a causal-visual alignment module that aligns function-aware representations with the geometric-semantic features of 3D point clouds, enabling bidirectional verification between structured functional reasoning and visual evidence. Extensive experiments on 3D Intention Grounding and 3D Visual Grounding demonstrate that our method enhances intent-aware object localization. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Chain-of-Causal Reasoning (CoCR), a framework that bridges abstract natural-language intents and 3D objects through intermediate functional requirements for 3D Intention Grounding.
AI.motivation: Unlike descriptive 3D visual grounding, 3D Intention Grounding uses abstract, non-descriptive intents, and existing implicit matching methods suffer from logical gaps and poor interpretability.
AI.method: CoCR decomposes intents into ordered functional requirements (intent-function-object chain), builds a functional dependency graph, and uses a causal-visual alignment module to bidirectionally verify function-aware representations against 3D point cloud features.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 3D Intention Grounding and 3D Visual Grounding benchmarks demonstrate that CoCR improves intent-aware object localization.
AI.conclusion: Explicit causal-functional reasoning chains enhance interpretability, robustness, and accuracy in 3D intention grounding.

title: Mean Curvature Minimizing Foliations Of A Vector Field
summary: Streamline patterns are ubiquitous in nature. Prominent examples include white matter fibre tracts in the mammalian brain and arrangements of elongated cells, such as cardiomyocytes in the heart wall. It has been posited that such organisations foliate into locally smooth surfaces to optimise function. However, the recovery of these foliations from a single vector field aligned with the local orientation of the underlying sheets remains an open problem. We address this challenge by introducing a mathematical model of a sheet and developing an algorithm for sheet inference, from measurements of the oriented structures. Given an input vector field, our model estimates a second vector field that is orthonormal to it, while also requiring the Lie bracket of the two to vanish. To balance sheet likelihood against low surface area, we also reduce the mean curvature of the recovered local surface. We compute the first variation of an associated energy and provide a numerical method which admits an efficient, parallel implementation for sheet estimation. We demonstrate our approach on both synthetic and biological examples, motivated by applications to medical imaging. These include white matter fibre tracts from a brain atlas and confocal microscopy images of cleared heart wall tissue. For the latter we are able to reconstruct sheets aligned with local cardiomyocyte directions at unprecedented (micrometre) scale.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a mathematical model and parallel numerical algorithm to infer smooth local surface foliations from a single oriented 3D vector field.
AI.motivation: Recovering sheet-like biological structures such as brain white matter tracts or cardiac myocyte sheets from a single orientation vector field remains an open problem.
AI.method: Given an input vector field, the model estimates an orthonormal second vector field with vanishing Lie bracket and minimizes an energy balancing sheet likelihood against surface area and mean curvature via its first variation.
AI.result: Applied to synthetic data, a brain atlas white matter tractography field, and confocal microscopy of cleared heart wall tissue, the method reconstructs cardiomyocyte sheets at micrometre scale.
AI.conclusion: Mean-curvature-minimizing foliation inference provides an efficient, parallelizable tool for reconstructing sheet-like biological architectures from medical imaging vector fields.

title: Keep the Reasoning, Read the Image: On-Demand Visual KV for Multi-Turn Reasoning VLMs
summary: Reasoning vision-language models (VLMs) think for thousands of tokens before they answer, and retention policies keep the KV cache affordable by pruning it as the reasoning grows. We find that this pruning sacrifices the image in multi-turn conversations: the image and the reasoning share one budget, so the growing reasoning crowds the visual entries out. A chart question that loses 8 points to the full cache when asked first loses 24 points when asked after a round of reasoning. Protecting a small visual reserve from eviction recovers most of this loss, while adding the same slots to the shared budget recovers considerably less. The image therefore lacks protection, not capacity. Based on this finding, we propose ShelfKV, a training-free method that works on top of existing retention policies. It keeps every visual entry in CPU memory and, at each decoding step, swaps the visual entries that the current query scores highest into the attention slots of the text entries it scores lowest. The image is never evicted, yet it occupies attention slots only while it is read. We evaluate ShelfKV on four benchmarks, three of them conversational, with two retention policies and two reasoning VLMs. In conversations, it improves the strongest existing policy, DBTrimKV, by up to 20.3 points at matched GPU memory, and still leads by 8.7 points when DBTrimKV uses twice the memory. It also consistently outperforms a fixed visual reserve of matched GPU memory in these settings, without hurting accuracy on standalone questions. These results show that the image should be protected from the reasoning but read only on demand.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ShelfKV, a training-free KV cache method that offloads visual entries to CPU memory and swaps relevant ones into GPU attention slots on demand during multi-turn reasoning.
AI.motivation: In reasoning VLMs, long chains of thought share a single KV cache budget with image tokens, causing pruning policies to evict visual entries and drop multi-turn chart accuracy by 24 points (vs. 8 points on first-turn questions).
AI.method: ShelfKV keeps all visual KV entries in CPU memory and, at each decoding step, swaps the highest-scoring visual entries into the GPU attention slots of the lowest-scoring text entries.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks, two retention policies, and two reasoning VLMs, ShelfKV outperforms the strongest policy (DBTrimKV) by up to 20.3 points at matched GPU memory and 8.7 points even when DBTrimKV uses twice the memory, without hurting standalone question accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Protecting visual KV entries in CPU memory and reading them on demand prevents reasoning chains from crowding out visual context in multi-turn VLMs.

title: DetectViT: Test-time Backdoor Detection for Vision Transformers via Inter-Head Attention Discrepancy
summary: Vision Transformers (ViTs) now underpin the visual encoders of most multimodal models, but this success comes at a cost: relying on third-party pretrained checkpoints leaves these systems open to backdoor attacks. Existing test-time detection methods rely on either the predicted label or intermediate embeddings, limiting their applicability across diverse tasks and incurring substantial computational overhead. In this work, we study how backdoor triggers affect the multi-head attention mechanism of ViTs and identify two distinct anomalous patterns: $\textit{complete attention hijacking}$, causing the attention to exhibit abnormally high inter-head spatial overlap, and $\textit{partial attention hijacking}$, causing an abnormally large variance in the concentration of the attention distribution. Motivated by these findings, we propose $\textbf{DetectViT}$, a test-time backdoor detection method that requires neither training data, model outputs, nor any prior knowledge of the trigger. DetectViT quantifies the two hijacking phenomena via an inter-head consistency score and an inter-head entropy variance score, with thresholds estimated from a small out-of-distribution (OOD) calibration set drawn from an arbitrary source. Across four representative attacks, diverse architectures (DeiT, CLIP, and LLaVA), and downstream tasks (image classification and captioning), DetectViT substantially outperforms all baselines with as few as 64--128 OOD calibration samples, achieving a true positive rate of $100\%$ and a false positive rate of $0.17\%$ on BadCLIP. Notably, it introduces negligible additional overhead by relying solely on attention weights already computed during inference. Code is available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DetectViT, a training-free test-time backdoor detection method for Vision Transformers based on inter-head attention discrepancy.
AI.motivation: Third-party ViT checkpoints are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, and existing test-time detectors rely on predicted labels or intermediate embeddings, limiting task generality and adding compute overhead.
AI.method: DetectViT detects complete and partial attention hijacking using an inter-head consistency score and an inter-head entropy variance score computed from existing inference attention weights, calibrated on 64-128 arbitrary out-of-distribution samples.
AI.result: Across four attacks, DeiT, CLIP, and LLaVA architectures, and classification and captioning tasks, DetectViT outperforms all baselines—achieving 100% TPR and 0.17% FPR on BadCLIP—with negligible overhead.
AI.conclusion: Inter-head attention statistics provide a fast, task-agnostic, and label-free signal for test-time backdoor detection in Vision Transformers.

title: When accuracy hides risk: risk-controlled confirmation of the critical view of safety under expert disagreement
