Across both hybrid and pure-attention VLMs, dependence on the video is concentrated early in the response. On Qwen3.6-27B, writing notes preserves accuracy better than free reasoning at the same withdrawal step. Replacing them with another video's notes harms accuracy, whereas keeping the video visible alongside the model's own notes adds no significant benefit. Without additional training, LookAway nearly matches full-video thinking accuracy at 0.12-0.13 times its modeled decode cost. To shorten this initial look, we fine-tune the model on its own correct LookAway responses. Reinforcement learning then rewards correct answers while penalizing KV reads. The trained model puts the video away after a median of 66-68 tokens. Across three held-out benchmarks, it writes more tokens than an identically trained full-video model yet reads only 27-35% as many KV positions at matched accuracy.

AI.tldr: LookAway lets thinking VLMs write timestamped notes on a long video and then hide the video's KV cache, matching full-video accuracy while reading only 27–35% as many KV positions.
AI.motivation: Thinking VLMs re-read the entire long-video KV cache at every decoding step, even though dependence on visual tokens is concentrated early in the response.
AI.method: In LookAway, the model writes timestamped notes relevant to the question and closes them, after which the inference engine hides the video KV cache; fine-tuning on correct LookAway traces and RL with a KV-read penalty further shorten the initial look.
AI.result: Without extra training, LookAway nearly matches full-video accuracy on Qwen3.6-27B at 0.12–0.13x modeled decode cost; after RL, it puts the video away after a median of 66–68 tokens and reads only 27–35% as many KV positions at matched accuracy across three held-out benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Externalizing visual evidence into brief timestamped notes and dropping the video KV cache drastically cuts long-video reasoning decode cost without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Look Closer, Look Back, or Wait for Agentic Streaming Video Understanding
summary: Streaming video models must answer questions about a live video under strict memory and latency limits. Feeding only the latest few frames keeps present perception sharp, whereas adding past frames dilutes attention on the current scene and triggers hallucinations. Recent cascade methods retrieve past frames when uncertain, but they still fail when current frames are blurry or when decisive future clues have not appeared yet. We introduce ActiveForager, a streaming video agent that maintains a clean short working window and gathers extra evidence only on demand. For each query, the agent either answers directly, zooms into high-resolution recent frames, recalls past events from memory, or waits for upcoming frames. When recalling history, a shared-weight sub-agent verifies candidate clips in isolation and returns a compact evidence summary. A stream-decoupled attention mask then keeps historical evidence from interfering with present visual tokens. We train this policy using counterfactual information gain, which rewards a tool call only when the gathered evidence makes the true answer more likely and prevents tool collapse across all actions. Across Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B on OVO-Bench, ActiveForager improves real-time perception, historical recall, and proactive response at once, lifting overall accuracy on Qwen3-VL-8B from 47.6% to 65.9%. It also doubles zero-shot accuracy on the multi-hop Video-Holmes benchmark while adding minimal visual tokens per query.

AI.tldr: ActiveForager is a streaming video agent that keeps a short working window and selectively zooms, recalls history via a sub-agent, or waits, lifting Qwen3-VL-8B accuracy on OVO-Bench from 47.6% to 65.9%.
AI.motivation: Streaming video models face strict memory and latency limits where adding past frames dilutes attention on the present, while cascade retrieval fails on blurry current frames or when future clues have not yet arrived.
AI.method: ActiveForager decides per query to answer directly, zoom into recent high-res frames, recall past clips via a shared-weight sub-agent behind a stream-decoupled attention mask, or wait for upcoming frames, trained using counterfactual information gain rewards.
AI.result: On OVO-Bench, ActiveForager lifts overall accuracy on Qwen3-VL-8B from 47.6% to 65.9% (with gains across Qwen2.5-VL-7B as well) and doubles zero-shot accuracy on Video-Holmes with minimal added visual tokens.
AI.conclusion: Counterfactual information-gain training and stream-decoupled memory retrieval enable accurate, low-overhead agentic streaming video understanding.

title: Semantic Guidance for Joint Infrared-Visible Video Fusion and Frame Interpolation
summary: Infrared and visible video fusion at high frame rates requires recovering missing observations when camera rates differ or fall below the desired output rate. Cascading interpolation and fusion can accumulate errors and cause brightness fluctuations. Motion and occlusion further complicate content selection, particularly when missing visible frames also remove direct semantic guidance. We propose SAFI, which uses semantics at the target time to guide joint interpolation and fusion. When the visible frame rate exceeds the infrared rate, available visible frames provide semantic context directly. At times without visible observations, motion guides local matching, and propagation recovers semantics from neighboring frames. Semantic context complements aligned image features at the target time, while matching confidence helps select reliable infrared and visible information. Reconstruction and fusion share source selection within each scale, allowing supervision on missing frames to guide fusion. To preserve visible appearance and reduce flicker, we bound thermal enhancement and penalize brightness inconsistencies across frames while accounting for changes in thermal contrast. Experiments on three datasets show improved visual quality with less computation than cascaded baselines and consistent temporal gains when input rates differ. SAFI maintains strong downstream tracking performance despite missing frames. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: SAFI uses target-time semantic guidance and bounded thermal enhancement for joint infrared-visible video fusion and frame interpolation, improving visual quality and tracking with less compute than cascaded baselines.
AI.motivation: Cascading interpolation and fusion for mismatched-rate infrared-visible videos accumulates errors and causes brightness flicker, while missing visible frames remove direct semantic guidance under motion and occlusion.
AI.method: SAFI uses available visible frames or motion-propagated neighbor semantics to guide target-time alignment and shared-scale source selection, while bounding thermal enhancement and penalizing cross-frame brightness inconsistencies.
AI.result: Experiments on three datasets show improved visual quality, consistent temporal gains under differing input frame rates, lower computation than cascaded baselines, and strong downstream tracking despite missing frames.
AI.conclusion: Jointly supervising reconstruction and fusion with target-time semantics and temporal brightness constraints resolves error accumulation in multi-rate infrared-visible video.

title: CROMPT: Adapting CLIP via Cross-Modal Prompting for Robust Zero-Shot Generalization under Adverse Weather
summary: Domain adaptation for semantic segmentation is challenging when target-domain images are unavailable during training. Zero-shot domain adaptation addresses this by adapting models using only textual descriptions of the target domain. However, existing prompt-learning methods are not well suited for ResNet-based CLIP vision backbones or pixel-level cross-modal feature alignment. We propose CROMPT, a prompt-learning framework for zero-shot domain adaptation in semantic segmentation. CROMPT introduces Cross-Modal Feature Augmentation (CROMA), combining Random Visual Prompting with Hybrid Textual Prompting (HTP) to jointly adapt visual and textual representations. We further propose CROMA-VL, which leverages vision-language models to generate domain-conditioned prompts, and a progressive easy-to-hard adaptation strategy for improved domain invariance. Experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines and state-of-the-art methods, achieving 1.63-2.63% mIoU gains while maintaining inference-time complexity. These results establish CROMPT as an effective and efficient framework for zero-shot multi-domain semantic segmentation. OpenReview: this https URL

AI.tldr: CROMPT is a cross-modal prompt-learning framework for zero-shot domain adaptation in semantic segmentation under adverse weather, achieving 1.63–2.63% mIoU gains without extra inference cost.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt-learning methods for zero-shot domain adaptation struggle with ResNet-based CLIP vision backbones and pixel-level cross-modal feature alignment when target-domain images are unavailable.
AI.method: CROMPT introduces Cross-Modal Feature Augmentation (CROMA) combining Random Visual Prompting and Hybrid Textual Prompting, alongside CROMA-VL for VLM-generated domain-conditioned prompts and a progressive easy-to-hard adaptation strategy.
AI.result: Across two benchmark datasets, CROMPT improves over strong baselines and prior SOTA by 1.63–2.63% mIoU while preserving inference-time complexity.
AI.conclusion: Jointly augmenting visual and textual prompts with progressive adaptation provides an efficient path to zero-shot multi-domain semantic segmentation.

title: AnchorUp: Anchoring Feature Upsampling on a Classical Interpolation
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. Code: this https URL
summary: Vision foundation models produce semantically strong features on a coarse patch grid, and dense prediction needs them at pixel resolution. Existing learned upsamplers close that gap by regressing the high-resolution feature map from the low-resolution one, typically through cross-attention driven by the input image. We observe that most of what they regress needs no learning: plain bilinear interpolation already reproduces the smooth regions of the target, and recent benchmarks even report bilinear and bicubic on par with several learned upsamplers. The rest is mostly edges and fine details, which suggests that these learned upsamplers spend much of their capacity re-computing the smooth content that classical interpolation provides. We therefore introduce AnchorUp, which stops predicting the high-resolution feature map and predicts only its correction from the interpolation. It keeps a parameter-free classical upsampler as an anchor, obtains a second prediction from a small guidance network, and blends the two through a single learnable scalar gate. Because the anchor supplies the smooth content, the guidance network only has to correct what remains. An analysis of the learned correction confirms that it concentrates on edges and fine details, and so the network can be small: AnchorUp uses 167,425 parameters, a quarter of the budget of the strongest baseline, NAF, and runs at 64% of its latency. Trained once on DINOv3 with only the first of NAF's two training stages, and evaluated on that backbone plus six held-out ones, it is already on par with NAF trained through both stages on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes. Our method surpasses it on DAVIS-2017 video object segmentation; the gain holds on every backbone and is larger in contour accuracy F. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: AnchorUp anchors feature upsampling on parameter-free classical interpolation and learns only a lightweight residual correction, matching NAF with a quarter of the parameters and 64% of the latency.
AI.motivation: Learned feature upsamplers spend substantial capacity re-computing smooth content that plain bilinear or bicubic interpolation already reproduces accurately.
AI.method: AnchorUp keeps a classical upsampler as a parameter-free anchor, predicts a correction with a small guidance network (167,425 parameters), and blends them via a single learnable scalar gate.
AI.result: Trained once on DINOv3 using only NAF's first stage, AnchorUp matches two-stage NAF on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes across DINOv3 and six held-out backbones, and surpasses it on DAVIS-2017 video object segmentation (especially contour accuracy F) at 64% of NAF's latency.
AI.conclusion: Predicting only the edge and detail residual over classical interpolation yields fast, compact, and generalizable feature upsampling.

title: Pixel2Perspective: A Benchmark for Multi-Modal and Multi-View Generalization in Vision-Language Models
summary: Embodied AI systems, such as drones and autonomous vehicles, improve navigation by enhancing perception in environments containing unseen objects. While Visual Language Models (VLMs) offer strong image understanding, their real-world application is underexplored. For effective deployment, open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) models, leveraging models like CLIP to assign pixel-level labels from text, must be robust to outdoor conditions, adverse weather, and varying viewpoints. Despite their potential, these models encounter significant challenges in cross-domain generalization, hindering their practical use in embodied AI applications. In this work, we present Pixel2Perspective, a benchmark for multi-angle object localization and open-vocabulary segmentation across both aerial and ground perspectives. This benchmark supports thorough evaluation across different viewpoints and sensor modalities. We assess foundational models like CLIP and advanced OVSS models using a curated dataset that spans varied outdoor conditions, sim-to-real scenarios, and multiple sensors, including infrared, to support the development of robust and generalizable perception systems. We also present a novel framework, Multi-Source RGB-IR Uncertainty Quantification (MSRIQ), which jointly models aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties across RGB and infrared imagery. This approach supports robust evaluation of open-vocabulary segmentation models across diverse environmental conditions. Our work sets a robustness-driven benchmark, providing key insights and laying the foundation for future research in open-world embodied AI perception. The benchmark and project page are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Pixel2Perspective, a multi-modal, multi-view benchmark for aerial and ground open-vocabulary segmentation, alongside the MSRIQ RGB-IR uncertainty quantification framework.
AI.motivation: Embodied AI systems need open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) that generalizes across viewpoints, outdoor conditions, adverse weather, and sensors like infrared, which remains underexplored.
AI.method: The authors curate Pixel2Perspective spanning aerial/ground perspectives, sim-to-real scenarios, and RGB/IR modalities, and propose Multi-Source RGB-IR Uncertainty Quantification (MSRIQ) to jointly model aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties.
AI.result: The work benchmarks foundational models like CLIP and advanced OVSS models across diverse environmental conditions, viewpoints, and sensor modalities.
AI.conclusion: Pixel2Perspective and MSRIQ establish a robustness-driven evaluation foundation for open-world embodied AI perception.

title: SCOUT: Risk-Guided Foundation-Model Escalation for Robust Tissue Detection in Whole-Slide Images
summary: Reliable tissue detection is essential for whole-slide image analysis, yet high average segmentation accuracy can conceal failures involving pale tissue, small fragments, and heterogeneous staining. Pathology foundation models offer transferable representations, but exhaustive inference is computationally demanding and may introduce false-positive tissue predictions. We propose SCOUT (Selective Correction of Uncertain Tissue), a risk-guided cascade that selectively refines an initial thumbnail-based tissue mask. A lightweight audit network estimates the spatial distribution of segmentation errors and prioritizes candidate regions for processing by a frozen pathology foundation model. An asymmetric consensus rule integrates the resulting predictions with the initial mask to recover missed tissue while limiting false positives. A calibrated slide-level review score additionally controls the marginal rate of unflagged case-group failures under the calibration assumptions. Evaluation on a public multi-source, multi-stain benchmark shows that SCOUT reduces the proportion of case groups requiring mask correction from 38.1% for the best released detector to 18.6%, with particularly pronounced improvements in immunohistochemistry. Source-held-out experiments demonstrate better generalization than a segmentation network trained on the same annotations, while selective inference achieves an observed failure rate no higher than processing all candidate regions. Downstream, lymph-node classification with SCOUT masks is non-inferior to that obtained with two of the three released detectors evaluated. A variant built on an openly licensed foundation model is publicly released as an installable Python package with trained weights. These results support risk-guided foundation-model inference as an effective approach to tissue detection across heterogeneous histopathology data.

AI.tldr: SCOUT is a risk-guided cascade that selectively escalates uncertain whole-slide tissue regions to a frozen pathology foundation model, cutting case groups needing correction from 38.1% to 18.6%.
AI.motivation: Thumbnail-based tissue detectors often miss pale tissue or small fragments, whereas running pathology foundation models exhaustively is computationally expensive and can add false positives.
AI.method: A lightweight audit network estimates spatial segmentation error to prioritize regions for a frozen pathology foundation model, an asymmetric consensus rule merges predictions with the initial mask, and a calibrated review score bounds unflagged failure rates.
AI.result: On a multi-source, multi-stain benchmark, SCOUT reduces case groups requiring mask correction from 38.1% to 18.6% (especially in immunohistochemistry), generalizes better on held-out sources, and matches or beats exhaustive inference failure rates with non-inferior downstream lymph-node classification.
AI.conclusion: Risk-guided selective escalation to foundation models improves histopathology tissue detection reliability at lower computational cost.

title: One Affinity, Two Axes: Bidirectional Slot Attention for Iterative Aggregation across the Structure--Detail Spectrum in Visual Retrieval
summary: Aggregating dense patch tokens into compact and discriminative global descriptors is central to visual retrieval. Although foundation models provide rich local features, existing aggregation heads still rely on single-pass mappings and lack an explicit mechanism to coordinate structural and fine-grained cues. Therefore, we propose Bidirectional Slot Attention (BiSA), which reformulates aggregation as an iterative coupled system. Cross-Axis Consensus (CAC) progressively refines learnable slots by interpreting a single shared token--slot affinity along two complementary axes. Along the competition axis, slots vie for each token under a temperature shared across all of them, determining token ownership and inducing a non-redundant scene decomposition. Along the selection axis, a slot-specific temperature governs the breadth of each slot's response, spanning a spectrum from broad layouts to sparse fine-grained details. Their consensus couples non-redundant decomposition with multi-granular slot specialization. Furthermore, the two axes expose intrinsic token-reliability cues at no extra cost: a token's claim strength under competition and its salience under selection. Progressive Token Filtering (PTF) converts these cues into a retention probability that down-weights unreliable tokens before the next CAC iteration, without any segmentation branch or external prior, forming a self-reinforcing loop of competitive decomposition, selective focusing, and feedback purification. Across all three retrieval tasks, BiSA leads on five of six place recognition benchmarks (+4.2 R@1 on Baidu Mall), tops all 16 metrics of drone--satellite geo-localization (+8.4 R@1 at 150 m), and improves instance-level retrieval on ROxford-Hard by 4.5 mAP points. Notably, the selection axis adds only 20 learnable scalars, yet improves average R@1 by 2.8 points.

AI.tldr: Bidirectional Slot Attention (BiSA) iteratively aggregates dense patch tokens using Cross-Axis Consensus and Progressive Token Filtering, leading 5 of 6 place recognition benchmarks and all 16 drone-satellite metrics.
AI.motivation: Existing single-pass feature aggregation heads lack an explicit mechanism to coordinate broad structural layouts and fine-grained local details from foundation model patch tokens.
AI.method: Cross-Axis Consensus (CAC) refines learnable slots over a shared token-slot affinity along a competition axis (shared temperature for non-redundant decomposition) and a selection axis (slot-specific temperature for multi-granular focus), while Progressive Token Filtering (PTF) down-weights unreliable tokens between iterations.
AI.result: BiSA leads 5 of 6 place recognition benchmarks (+4.2 R@1 on Baidu Mall), tops all 16 drone-satellite geo-localization metrics (+8.4 R@1 at 150 m), and gains +4.5 mAP on ROxford-Hard, with the selection axis adding only 20 learnable scalars for +2.8 average R@1.
AI.conclusion: Iterative coupled competition and selection over token-slot affinities with self-reinforcing token filtering provides a compact, high-performing global descriptor aggregator.

title: CanopyKV: Remember beyond the Crop for Fast Active Visual Reasoning
summary: Active visual reasoning enables multimodal models to answer challenging visual questions by gathering fine-grained evidence through iterative image inspection and tool use. However, accumulating crops and reasoning tokens expands the key-value (KV) cache, making compression important for reducing memory and inference costs. Existing KV compression methods typically select historical tokens based on attention, recency, or redundancy. These criteria do not explicitly distinguish locally replaced evidence from complementary information needed for future exploration: each crop refreshes a local region, while earlier views may still support subsequent decisions. Discarding such evidence can impair accuracy or require additional search, while scoring and cache reorganization can offset the computational savings from compression. We introduce CanopyKV, a training-free KV compression framework that uses parent-child crop relationships to retain complementary evidence, keeps retained history stable, and protects the state needed for ongoing reasoning. Tool metadata provides retention signals without additional attention scoring, while compact KV storage reduces subsequent attention costs. Across VisualProbe, V*, HR-Bench, and MME-Lite, CanopyKV achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and end-to-end efficiency among the evaluated KV compression methods. On MME-Lite, it retains approximately one-quarter of Dense's total KV while improving accuracy by 10.5 percentage points and accelerating complete reasoning by $1.64\times$.

AI.tldr: CanopyKV is a training-free KV cache compression framework for active visual reasoning that uses crop parent-child relationships to retain complementary evidence, accelerating MME-Lite reasoning by 1.64x with +10.5% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing KV compression methods rely on attention, recency, or redundancy, which can discard earlier views needed for future exploration or incur scoring overhead that offsets compression savings.
AI.method: CanopyKV uses tool metadata on parent-child crop relationships to identify and retain complementary evidence without extra attention scoring, keeping retained history stable and compact.
AI.result: Across VisualProbe, V*, HR-Bench, and MME-Lite, CanopyKV achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency among evaluated KV compression methods, retaining ~25% of Dense's total KV on MME-Lite while improving accuracy by 10.5 percentage points and speeding up reasoning by 1.64x.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting structural crop-hierarchy metadata from active visual tools enables faster, more accurate KV cache compression without attention-scoring overhead.

title: Where Should a Diffusion Transformer Meet Its Teacher?
summary: Representation Alignment (REPA) significantly accelerates Diffusion Transformer training by guiding intermediate student features with a pretrained visual teacher, yet existing methods typically attach supervision to a single fixed layer. As student representations evolve, however, we find that the most effective layer for alignment varies across training stages. To track this evolving layer suitability online without costly search, we measure gradient compatibility between the flow-matching and alignment objectives, and propose AdaREPA, an online routing framework that adaptively selects the supervision layer as training progresses. AdaREPA uses a softmax distribution over smoothed layer compatibility scores to sample a layer for alignment at each training step. This probabilistic routing adapts teacher supervision to the student's changing learning needs, with minimal training overhead and no additional inference cost. On ImageNet-256, AdaREPA accelerates convergence and improves generation quality across model sizes, while revealing how the most suitable layers for supervision shift over training.

AI.tldr: AdaREPA is an online routing framework that adaptively selects which Diffusion Transformer layer receives teacher representation alignment at each step, accelerating convergence and improving quality on ImageNet-256.
AI.motivation: Representation Alignment (REPA) typically supervises a single fixed student layer, even though the most effective layer for teacher alignment shifts as student representations evolve during training.
AI.method: AdaREPA measures online gradient compatibility between flow-matching and alignment objectives and samples the supervision layer at each training step from a softmax distribution over smoothed compatibility scores, adding no inference cost.
AI.result: On ImageNet-256 across model sizes, AdaREPA accelerates convergence and improves generation quality with minimal training overhead, while revealing how optimal alignment layers shift over training.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic gradient-compatibility routing matches teacher supervision to the student's evolving learning stage in Diffusion Transformers.

authors: Heitor Eduardo Ferreira Campos Morato Filpi
title: Reliable Tree Recruitment from Scarce Annotations for Forest Inventory Expansion
summary: Species-level inventories of individual tree crowns (ITCs) from UAV imagery are limited by annotation cost: in tropical forests, many species are represented by only a handful of field-validated crowns. We propose a reliable tree recruitment framework that expands a small annotated inventory by iteratively self-training a multi-task DeepLabV3 network, combining semantic segmentation with a crown-distance regression head, on RGB UAV orthomosaics. At each iteration, candidate crowns enter the training inventory only if they pass a confidence filter on class probability and distance map and a morphology filter on crown area and solidity, with at most five new crowns per species, keeping recruited samples consistent with the reference inventory. We evaluate the framework at two Brazilian sites: an Amazonian rainforest in Acre (17 species, 355 annotated crowns, 4 cm GSD) and a forest site in the Cerrado of Maranhão (4 species, 51 annotated crowns, 1.8 cm GSD). Over 20 iterations, the number of retained crowns grew from about 500 to 960 in Acre and from about 700 to over 3100 in Maranhão, while crown-level F1 exceeded single- and multi-task DeepLabV3 baselines (53.5% vs. 50.0% and 45.2%; 92.2% vs. 79.7% and 83.6%). The framework offers a low-cost route to expanding species inventories with consumer-grade UAVs and limited fieldwork.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an iterative self-training framework with confidence and morphology filters to expand UAV-based tree species inventories from scarce annotations, achieving 53.5% and 92.2% crown-level F1 at two Brazilian sites.
AI.motivation: Species-level individual tree crown (ITC) mapping from UAV imagery is bottlenecked by fieldwork annotation costs, leaving many tropical species with very few labeled crowns.
AI.method: A multi-task DeepLabV3 (semantic segmentation plus crown-distance regression) is iteratively self-trained on RGB UAV orthomosaics, recruiting up to five new crowns per species per iteration only if they pass class-probability, distance-map, area, and solidity filters.
AI.result: Over 20 iterations at Acre (17 species, 355 crowns) and Maranhão (4 species, 51 crowns), retained crowns grew from ~500 to 960 and ~700 to >3,100, and crown-level F1 reached 53.5% (vs. 50.0%/45.2% baselines) and 92.2% (vs. 79.7%/83.6%).
AI.conclusion: Confidence- and morphology-gated self-training offers a low-cost way to scale species-level forest inventories using consumer UAVs.

title: RAPID: Reconstruction Accelerated by Polarization-Informed Depth for 2D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Efficient and accurate 3D surface reconstruction from multi-view images remains a fundamental challenge in Gaussian splatting. Many existing methods rely on sparse geometric initialization and iterative densification, resulting in substantial optimization overhead and difficulties in balancing rendering quality and geometric accuracy, particularly in reflective and weakly textured regions. To address these limitations, we propose RAPID, a geometry-first framework that uses multiview polarization cues to recover dense surface priors. We integrate surface normals into depth maps using sparse geometric anchors. These depth maps are then fused across views. Curvature-adaptive sampling and oriented Gaussian initialization then support efficient optimization. Experiments on the PISR dataset demonstrate an approximately \(5\times\) speedup over PhyGaP, which is a state-of-the-art Gaussian-based reconstruction method. RAPID reduces the average optimization time from approximately 21 minutes (PhyGaP) to 4 minutes while maintaining competitive novel-view synthesis quality and mesh reconstruction accuracy. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of RAPID in accelerating Gaussian optimization from polarimetric multi-view inputs.

AI.tldr: RAPID accelerates 2D Gaussian Splatting surface reconstruction by ~5x (from 21 to 4 minutes on PISR) using multiview polarization-informed depth priors and curvature-adaptive initialization.
AI.motivation: Existing Gaussian splatting surface reconstruction methods rely on sparse initialization and iterative densification, causing high optimization overhead and poor geometry in reflective or weakly textured regions.
AI.method: RAPID integrates multiview polarization surface normals with sparse geometric anchors into fused dense depth maps, then performs curvature-adaptive sampling and oriented Gaussian initialization.
AI.result: On the PISR dataset, RAPID achieves an approximately 5x speedup over PhyGaP (cutting average optimization time from ~21 minutes to 4 minutes) while maintaining competitive novel-view synthesis and mesh reconstruction accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-first initialization from polarimetric depth priors substantially speeds up 2D Gaussian Splatting without sacrificing reconstruction quality.

title: StrideWorld: Benchmarking Scene Rigidity and Action Consistency in Interactive Video World Model
summary: Interactive video world models turn user commands into the exploration of a generated scene, which requires the scene to keep its 3D structure as the camera moves and each action to keep a stable effect. Existing benchmarks mostly evaluate these properties against references fitted to the video under test, either a scene reconstructed from its own frames or a camera trajectory aligned to the command path with a free scale. Such references can absorb gradual scene deformation and changes in pace and route length, so these errors can pass undetected. We therefore introduce StrideWorld, a benchmark whose references are fixed before the motion they judge. It evaluates scene rigidity against the ground-truth geometry of the start view, and action consistency against the stride of each action, the camera motion of one command. The stride is measured on the model's first steps and then used to test the steps that follow, so each model is judged only against its own steps. Its measurements are validated on rendered videos with known camera motion, and its scores agree with human judgments. Across \nvideos{} videos generated by \nmodels{} open models from $140$ start views, all models but one deform their scenes as the camera moves, with offsets up to $7.3$ times those of a rigid rendering along the same camera path. Most models keep a steady pace when a single action is held. Along composed routes, several models often stall, and most completed routes end away from the positions predicted by each model's own strides. Only the two models that scale commands by the estimated scene depth bring most routes close to these positions. Fine-tuning two models on a few rendered clips removes most of their mid-route stalls. Code, data, and a leaderboard are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: StrideWorld benchmarks scene rigidity and action consistency in interactive video world models using pre-fixed geometry and self-measured action strides, revealing widespread scene deformation and route stalling.
AI.motivation: Existing world-model benchmarks fit references to the generated video itself, which can mask gradual 3D scene deformation and changes in action pace or route length.
AI.method: StrideWorld fixes references before motion by comparing against ground-truth start-view geometry for rigidity and each model's own initial action stride for action consistency, validated on rendered videos and human judgments.
AI.result: Across 140 start views on open models, all but one model deform scenes (up to 7.3x rigid-rendering offsets), many stall on composed routes, only depth-scaled models stay close to stride-predicted positions, and fine-tuning two models on a few rendered clips removes most mid-route stalls.
AI.conclusion: Pre-fixed geometric and stride references expose structural and control failures in interactive video world models that self-fitted benchmarks miss.

title: Why Multi-Source Audio Fails to Compose: A Geometric Diagnosis and Its Remedy
summary: Multi-source audio-to-image generation exhibits consistent compositional failures when audio tokens occupy geometrically displaced, semantically unanchored positions in the CLIP text-token space, where the diffusion U-Net lacks the prior to reliably attend to them or ground them in distinct spatial regions. We formalize this as the geometric displacement phenomenon and expose it through a two-level clustering analysis comparing BEATs and CLAP embeddings at the raw encoder and projected CLIP token levels. Three geometric properties emerge as important: intra-class compactness, angular alignment with the CLIP text manifold, and inter-token spatial separation. We show that CLAP, whose contrastive language-audio pretraining aligns embeddings with natural language semantics, substantially outperforms BEATs on all three properties, improving the silhouette score by more than 3x and the Audio-Image Content score as well. Building on this analysis, we introduce a multi-token extension that requires no diffusion-backbone retraining and assigns each audio source to a distinct placeholder token in the CLIP tokenizer, complemented by a mixed inference-time objective that combines Attend-and-Excite with an A* spatial separation loss to resolve residual cross-token interference. For evaluation, we construct multi-audio compositional benchmarks from VGGSound (VGG2, VGG3, and VGGN) and extend six standard audio-image metrics to the multi-source setting. Across five benchmarks and four strong baselines, our method achieves strong results on the metrics most directly tied to compositional faithfulness, with AIC improvements of up to 2.25x over the strongest baseline and FID reduced by nearly 2x on two-source generation. We propose geometric displacement as a diagnostic framework for cross-modal generation systems that project learned embeddings into a pretrained contrastive space.

AI.tldr: This paper diagnoses multi-source audio-to-image compositional failures as geometric displacement in CLIP token space and resolves them using CLAP, distinct placeholder tokens, and an inference-time spatial separation loss.
AI.motivation: Multi-source audio-to-image generation frequently fails to compose sounds because projected audio tokens occupy displaced, unanchored positions in CLIP text-token space.
AI.method: After showing CLAP outperforms BEATs on compactness, angular alignment, and separation (>3x silhouette score), the authors assign each audio source a distinct CLIP placeholder token and apply a mixed inference-time objective combining Attend-and-Excite with an A* spatial separation loss without retraining the diffusion backbone.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks (including new VGG2, VGG3, and VGGN) and four baselines, the method improves Audio-Image Content (AIC) by up to 2.25x and reduces FID by nearly 2x on two-source generation.
AI.conclusion: Addressing geometric displacement in shared contrastive token spaces via aligned encoders and inference-time spatial separation enables training-free multi-source audio-to-image composition.

title: PhysResponse: Probing the Physics of Video Generation with Controlled Interventions
comment: 11 pages. This version contains the main paper and references only. Supplementary material will be added in a later revision
summary: Video generation models are increasingly viewed as world simulators, which requires not only plausible motion but dynamics that respond correctly to specified physical parameters. Existing models, datasets and benchmarks, however, largely target physical plausibility, leaving this physical parameter responsiveness insufficiently explored. We introduce PhysResponse, a benchmark that measures it at two levels: scene-conditioned simulator inversion recovers the effective gravity, friction and initial speed of generated motion, and event evaluation tests outcomes near and across critical transitions. Evaluating ten image-to-video models, we find that even the lowest parameter errors exceed those of physically correct videos by over an order of magnitude, that models rarely reproduce both outcomes of a transition pair, and that the two levels expose complementary failures that visual metrics such as PSNR miss. To supply the missing training signal, we construct 72,000 simulated videos of 20 multi-object interaction types with controlled parameters; fine-tuning on them lowers parameter errors, even on held-out interaction types, and transfers to real videos and an external physics benchmark. Continued training with a numerical encoder further lowers all three errors on held-out types. PhysResponse provides a foundation for world simulators that follow physical conditions, not just appearances.

AI.tldr: PhysResponse benchmarks physical parameter responsiveness in video generators using simulator inversion and transition events, and introduces 72,000 controlled simulation videos that reduce parameter errors via fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing video generation benchmarks evaluate visual plausibility rather than whether generated dynamics respond accurately to specified physical parameters like gravity, friction, or initial speed.
AI.method: PhysResponse evaluates models via scene-conditioned simulator inversion and critical-transition event tests, and provides 72,000 simulated videos across 20 multi-object interaction types for fine-tuning with an optional numerical encoder.
AI.result: Across ten image-to-video models, lowest parameter errors still exceed physically correct videos by over an order of magnitude and models rarely pass both outcomes of a transition pair; fine-tuning on the simulated dataset lowers errors on held-out types and transfers to real videos and an external physics benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Parameter-controlled simulation data and inversion-based evaluation provide a concrete path toward physically responsive video world simulators.

title: MLIE-CoT: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via Multi-Level Image Editing
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has proven effective in improving the reasoning abilities of large language models by breaking complex tasks into step-by-step solutions. In recent years, researchers have attempted to extend CoT reasoning to visual generative models to improve their ability to handle complex tasks. However, existing CoT methods for text-to-image generation still rely mainly on textual reasoning and therefore cannot fully use and preserve the correct semantic information already present in an image, as even the most detailed language cannot capture all visual information. With advances in image generation, models such as FLUX and BAGEL can generate images conditioned on visual inputs. Recent work has attempted to carry images forward as context in the chain of thought, but this introduces another limitation: unsuitable earlier images can strongly interfere with the model, while repeated whole-image regeneration introduces new hallucinations at each round and causes them to accumulate. To address these issues, we propose MLIE-CoT, a visual chain-of-thought framework based on multi-level image editing. MLIE-CoT learns to select the repair granularity from three levels, preserving correct semantics whenever possible during reasoning while reducing the effect of incorrect content. To improve the ability of multimodal models to route errors of different severity to appropriate repair levels, we construct an image-repair dataset covering different error cases and use it to train a repair-level router. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MLIE-CoT significantly outperforms both its base models and methods using fixed repair strategies, producing clear improvements across multiple benchmarks.

AI.tldr: MLIE-CoT is a visual chain-of-thought framework that routes errors of varying severity to three image-editing repair granularities, outperforming base models and fixed-repair strategies.
AI.motivation: Textual CoT cannot preserve fine visual details, while carrying full images forward in visual CoT causes unsuitable earlier images or repeated whole-image regeneration to accumulate hallucinations.
AI.method: MLIE-CoT learns a repair-level router trained on a constructed image-repair dataset covering diverse error cases to dynamically select among three editing granularities, preserving correct semantics while fixing errors.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks show MLIE-CoT significantly outperforms its base models and fixed-repair-strategy baselines.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive multi-level image editing prevents hallucination accumulation and improves visual chain-of-thought reasoning.

title: Explainable and CPU-Efficient Brain Tumor Classification from MRI Using Two-Phase EfficientNetB3 Fine-Tuning
summary: Brain tumors are among the most lethal neurological disorders, with over 308,000 new diagnoses annually worldwide. Accurate classification of tumor type from Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans is critical for treatment planning; however, manual radiological interpretation is time-consuming and prone to inter-observer variability. This paper proposes an automated deep learning pipeline for four-class brain MRI classification (glioma, meningioma, no tumor, and pituitary tumor) using EfficientNetB3 transfer learning with a custom classification head. A two-phase training strategy is adopted: Phase 1 trains the head with a frozen backbone (best validation accuracy: 92.77%), and Phase 2 selectively fine-tunes the top 37 layers at a 100x reduced learning rate (best validation accuracy: 94.91%). On an independent balanced test set of 1,600 MRI images, the system achieves 90.62% overall accuracy and a macro-average AUC of 0.9854. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) is integrated for class-discriminative visual explainability. The proposed system simultaneously addresses three dimensions absent in prior work: high accuracy, CPU-only computational efficiency, and clinical interpretability.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a CPU-efficient, explainable four-class brain MRI tumor classifier using two-phase EfficientNetB3 fine-tuning and Grad-CAM, reaching 90.62% test accuracy and 0.9854 macro-AUC.
AI.motivation: Manual radiological interpretation of brain MRI scans is slow and variable, while clinical deployment requires high accuracy alongside CPU efficiency and visual explainability.
AI.method: The pipeline uses EfficientNetB3 with a custom head trained in two phases: Phase 1 trains the head with a frozen backbone, and Phase 2 fine-tunes the top 37 layers at a 100x lower learning rate, paired with Grad-CAM for visual explanations.
AI.result: Validation accuracy improves from 92.77% (Phase 1) to 94.91% (Phase 2), and on an independent balanced test set of 1,600 MRI images the model achieves 90.62% accuracy and 0.9854 macro-average AUC.
AI.conclusion: Two-phase selective fine-tuning of EfficientNetB3 with Grad-CAM delivers accurate, interpretable, and CPU-friendly brain tumor classification.

title: NativeSeg: Native Vision Language Segmentation of 3D Computed Tomography via Spatial Visual Tokens and Verified Local Zoom
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Code: this https URL ; Weights: this https URL
summary: Text prompted 3D computed tomography (CT) segmentation requires both full slice context and fine boundary precision across volumes where over $80\%$ of organ prompted slices lack the queried target. Existing medical vision language models (VLMs) are largely non native segmenters: they delegate pixel delineation outside the VLM by compressing reasoning into a 1D [SEG] vector for an external Segment Anything Model (SAM) decoder, quantizing masks into lossy discrete codebooks, or issuing box prompts to stateless external SAM tools without empty slice screening or spatial state memory. We introduce NativeSeg, a native vision language segmentation framework on Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapted Qwen3.8-27B that performs dense mask decoding, volumetric triage, spatial error self diagnosis, and multiround local zoom directly over the VLM's 2D spatial visual tokens without external SAM decoders. NativeSeg decodes confidence maps from upper layer 2D spatial tokens fused with a five slice U-Net pathway, halts at zero zooms on $>91\%$ of standalone evaluations via a native presence gate (<pres>), localizes uncertain boundaries via a 20 cell multiscale error gate (<err>), and accepts zoomed updates only when predicted error decreases. Trained solely on adult CT, NativeSeg improves Round $0$ DSC by $+19.81$ and $+7.04$ points over discrete codebook and 1D [SEG] readouts on the identical backbone, reaches $86.81\%$ adult and $87.04\%$ zero shot pediatric DSC, and safely refines 2D nnU-Net ($89.52\%$ adult; $86.86\%$ pediatric), 3D SegVol ($86.81\%$), and 3D VoxTell ($89.85\%$).

AI.tldr: NativeSeg performs native 3D CT text-prompted segmentation directly on Qwen3.8-27B's 2D spatial visual tokens with presence/error gates and verified local zoom, reaching 86.81% adult and 87.04% pediatric DSC.
AI.motivation: Existing medical VLMs delegate segmentation to external SAM decoders or lossy codebooks without empty-slice screening or spatial memory, despite >80% of organ-prompted CT slices lacking the target.
AI.method: NativeSeg decodes confidence maps from upper-layer 2D spatial tokens fused with a five-slice U-Net pathway on LoRA-adapted Qwen3.8-27B, uses a presence gate (<pres>) to halt >91% of evaluations at zero zooms, localizes boundary errors via a 20-cell multiscale gate (<err>), and accepts zooms only when predicted error drops.
AI.result: Trained only on adult CT, NativeSeg improves Round 0 DSC by +19.81 and +7.04 over codebook and 1D [SEG] readouts, reaches 86.81% adult and 87.04% zero-shot pediatric DSC, and safely refines nnU-Net (89.52% adult; 86.86% pediatric), SegVol (86.81%), and VoxTell (89.85%).
AI.conclusion: Native spatial token decoding with gated error-verified zoom eliminates external SAM dependencies and improves 3D CT segmentation accuracy and robustness.

title: Retroactive Concept Bottleneck Models for Exemplar-Free Class-Incremental Learning
summary: Exemplar-free class-incremental learning (EFCIL) requires models to learn new classes sequentially without retaining training samples from previous tasks. Continual concept bottleneck models (CBMs) make their predictions interpretable by identifying visual concepts in an image and using them to score each class. However, these methods typically focus on preserving learned concepts or approximating past classes with generated features, which can leave new concepts underused in old-class predictions. We propose RetroCBM, which retains a small set of vocabulary-independent statistics relating frozen visual features to the embedding space of a pretrained vision-language model. Even after earlier training images have been discarded, we can use these statistics to supervise new concepts. To do so, we develop a retroactive regression rule that yields the same predictor for each new concept as class-balanced ridge regression on all images seen so far. We then reproject the stored statistics to recover the full-history squared classification loss and thus learn how much each new concept should contribute to old-class predictions. Since the classifier may use systematic concept errors to distinguish nearby classes, we further introduce a graph-weighted penalty on the margin shifts caused by those errors. Across six datasets, RetroCBM outperforms state-of-the-art interpretable methods in all class-incremental settings, with an 18.1\% relative gain in mean average incremental accuracy over the strongest exemplar-free baseline.

AI.tldr: RetroCBM is an exemplar-free class-incremental concept bottleneck model that stores compact feature-embedding statistics for retroactive ridge regression, achieving an 18.1% relative gain over the strongest baseline.
AI.motivation: Continual concept bottleneck models typically focus on preserving old concepts or generating synthetic features, leaving newly learned concepts underused when predicting old classes.
AI.method: RetroCBM stores small vocabulary-independent statistics linking frozen visual features to VLM embeddings, enabling exact retroactive ridge regression for new concepts across all historical data, and adds a graph-weighted penalty on margin shifts from systematic concept errors.
AI.result: Across six datasets, RetroCBM outperforms state-of-the-art interpretable methods in all class-incremental settings, yielding an 18.1% relative gain in mean average incremental accuracy over the strongest exemplar-free baseline.
AI.conclusion: Storing compact cross-modal statistics allows exemplar-free continual CBMs to retroactively integrate new concepts into old-class predictions without retaining past images.

title: EviScope: Evidence-Conditioned Sampling for Long-Range 3D Detection
summary: Query-based camera-radar detectors choose where and over which frames each object query samples from the query's position or feature. We test whether radar evidence around the query should also set these choices at the 150 m range of MAN TruckScenes, where recall differs across object-level radar-return counts within every range band. EviScope is a minimal test: the current frame's returns form a non-learned bird's-eye evidence field, which each query reads at its decoded centre to scale its radial sampling extent and to weight eight frames. It adds 5,450 parameters (0.009%) to RaCFormer, with no latency increase in our timing. Our module-free recipe exceeds the published TruckScenes mAP (25.9 over seven runs against 24.1), so we measure the module only against its own baseline at matched seeds. The evidence a query reads rises with its object's return count (Spearman 0.51) but captures zero-return objects only in part, and the learned radius tracks it ($\rho\approx-0.91$ in four runs). Over seven four-epoch pairs the module changes NDS by $+0.31\pm0.36$ and mAP by $-0.27\pm0.22$ (mean $\pm$ SE). Against a geometry-only conditioner with the same parameter count, trained at three matched seeds, it is higher by $+1.25\pm0.72$ NDS and $+0.87\pm0.21$ mAP, on mAP in every pair, and the control's mean NDS is near the baseline's. An exploratory far-range gain failed an internally pre-specified held-out test, and large inference-time substitution penalties also occur without query-local evidence: neither learned allocation nor inference-time dependence substitutes for matched end-to-end comparisons.

AI.tldr: EviScope tests conditioning RaCFormer's 3D detection sampling on local radar-return evidence at 150 m on MAN TruckScenes, finding small, statistically noisy differences (+0.31 NDS, -0.27 mAP) over a strong baseline.
AI.motivation: Query-based camera-radar detectors choose sampling locations and frames from query features alone, even though recall varies with object-level radar-return counts at long range (150 m).
AI.method: EviScope builds a non-learned bird's-eye evidence field from current-frame radar returns, which each query reads at its decoded center to scale radial sampling extent and weight eight frames, adding 5,450 parameters (0.009%) to RaCFormer.
AI.result: Against its own matched-seed baseline (25.9 mAP vs. 24.1 published), EviScope shifts NDS by +0.31 +/- 0.36 and mAP by -0.27 +/- 0.22 over seven pairs, beats a geometry-only control by +1.25 +/- 0.72 NDS and +0.87 +/- 0.21 mAP over three seeds, and fails an internal held-out test for far-range gains.
AI.conclusion: Local radar-evidence conditioning outperforms a parameter-matched geometry control but does not yield a clear net gain over the tuned RaCFormer baseline, underscoring the need for matched end-to-end comparisons.

title: ShoWorld: Shape-Faithful Multi-Hypothesis Occupancy World Model
summary: Occupancy world models struggle to forecast moving objects due to motion uncertainty and shape distortion. A single trajectory can average plausible futures into an implausible path, and repeated re-voxelization can erode or inflate object shape even under correct motion. We introduce ShoWorld to address these challenges through separate motion and shape representations. The motion forecaster predicts probabilistic trajectories conditioned on scene layout, nearby agents and the future ego trajectory. Each hypothesis is rendered into occupancy and fused according to its probability to retain alternative futures. The shape component predicts sub-voxel points with occupancy probabilities and offsets from local geometry. These points move rigidly with the object, and voxel occupancy follows the probability that at least one occupied point falls within it. This representation reduces shape distortion under motion. ShoWorld achieves state-of-the-art results on Occ3D-nuScenes. With ground-truth occupancy and ego trajectory, it improves mIoU and IoU by 6.56 and 9.16 points overall and by 6.06 and 5.53 points on dynamic classes.

AI.tldr: ShoWorld is an occupancy world model that separates motion and shape representations to forecast moving objects with less motion uncertainty and shape distortion, achieving state-of-the-art results on Occ3D-nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Existing occupancy world models suffer from motion uncertainty, where a single trajectory averages plausible futures into an implausible path, and shape distortion, where repeated re-voxelization erodes or inflates object shapes even under correct motion.
AI.method: ShoWorld separates motion and shape: a motion forecaster predicts probabilistic trajectories conditioned on scene layout, nearby agents, and future ego trajectory, rendering and fusing each hypothesis by probability, while a shape component predicts sub-voxel points with occupancy probabilities and local geometry offsets that move rigidly with the object.
AI.result: On Occ3D-nuScenes with ground-truth occupancy and ego trajectory, ShoWorld achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving mIoU and IoU by 6.56 and 9.16 points overall and by 6.06 and 5.53 points on dynamic classes.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling probabilistic motion forecasting from rigid sub-voxel shape representation effectively preserves object geometry and multi-hypothesis futures in occupancy world models.

title: Anchoring with Visual Evidence: Explicit Semantic Anchors for Joint Change Detection and Captioning
summary: Joint change detection and captioning seeks to localize changes and describe them from bi-temporal remote sensing images. A key challenge is translating dense visual evidence into the semantic conditions that guide description generation. We propose Explicit Semantic Anchors (ESA), a supervised interface that exposes entity presence, temporal appearance variation, and spatial extent. A prediction-guided readout combines visual features and predicted change probabilities, and three factor heads estimate the corresponding anchor activations. These activations guide generation through two complementary routes. The context route maps the three factor activations to three separate memory tokens, one per factor, and appends them to the dense visual memory, while the lexicon route produces an additive vocabulary bias at each decoding step. Dense visual memory remains available for spatial detail and information beyond the explicit factors. Anchor targets are derived from existing images and change annotations, requiring no additional anchor-level language annotation. At inference, all conditions are computed from the input image pair and the model's own predictions. Experiments on LEVIR-MCI and WHU-CDC show strong joint detection and captioning performance, supporting the use of supervised visual attributes as explicit conditions for change description generation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Explicit Semantic Anchors (ESA), a supervised interface that translates dense visual evidence into semantic conditions to guide joint change detection and captioning in bi-temporal remote sensing images.
AI.motivation: Joint change detection and captioning must translate dense visual evidence into semantic conditions for description generation, which existing methods struggle to do explicitly without extra anchor-level language annotations.
AI.method: ESA uses a prediction-guided readout combining visual features and predicted change probabilities with three factor heads to estimate entity presence, temporal appearance variation, and spatial extent, guiding generation via a context route (three factor memory tokens appended to dense visual memory) and a lexicon route (additive vocabulary bias at each decoding step), trained using targets derived from existing images and change annotations.
AI.result: Experiments on LEVIR-MCI and WHU-CDC demonstrate strong joint change detection and captioning performance.
AI.conclusion: Supervising explicit visual attributes as semantic anchors provides an effective, annotation-free interface for conditioning change description generation.

title: Comparing Each Generation with Independent Siblings Gives Video World Model Post-Training a Proper Objective for Outcome Frequencies
summary: Video world models are used as simulators, so when a first frame leaves several physical outcomes open, repeated generations should produce each outcome as often as it occurs in the data. Physics post-training scores every generation against the single recorded future of its history, which makes single videos more faithful, but the expected score is linear in the model distribution and is maximized by always producing the most likely outcome. The log-likelihood of the recorded outcome is maximized by the data distribution, and its gradient weights agreement with the record by the inverse of how often the model produces the generated outcome, a frequency that other generations of the same history with independent noise, its siblings, can estimate. To train with this weight from a finite group, we propose SibPO, which performs Sibling-paired Policy Optimization: siblings estimate a truncated inverse-frequency weight for agreement with the record, and a second term subtracts the same weight times the agreement with the siblings, which makes the expected objective a strictly proper divergence over outcome cells at every group size. On PisaBench, SibPO lowers the KS distance to simulated landing times by 9.1-10.2% relative to the strongest method outside its reward family on three of four video models without degrading single videos, and it lowers the error of estimated robot policy success rates by 13%.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Sibling-paired Policy Optimization (SibPO), a video world model post-training objective that uses independent sibling generations to estimate outcome frequencies and match the data distribution's outcome frequencies.
AI.motivation: Physics post-training scores each generation against a single recorded future, which yields an expected score linear in the model distribution and causes models to collapse toward always producing the most likely outcome rather than matching true outcome frequencies.
AI.method: SibPO estimates a truncated inverse-frequency weight for agreement with the recorded outcome using independent sibling generations of the same history, and subtracts the same weight times agreement with the siblings to form a strictly proper divergence over outcome cells at every group size.
AI.result: On PisaBench, SibPO lowers the KS distance to simulated landing times by 9.1-10.2% relative to the strongest method outside its reward family on three of four video models without degrading single videos, and reduces the error of estimated robot policy success rates by 13%.
AI.conclusion: Comparing each generation with independent siblings gives video world model post-training a proper objective for reproducing physical outcome frequencies.

title: RAID: Representation Autoencoder for Intrinsic Decomposition
summary: Single-image intrinsic decomposition is an inherently ill-posed problem, requiring the disentanglement of strongly coupled appearance factors from a single RGB observation. Recent methods address this ambiguity with diffusion priors, at the cost of large, iterative, and often stochastic models. We show that accurate decomposition does not require a large generative model. Our key idea is to decouple reconstruction from decomposition on top of a strong pretrained representation. First, an $X \rightarrow X$ teacher learns to reconstruct each intrinsic map from DINOv3 features using a shared decoder, without paired RGB-to-intrinsic supervision. Then, a DINOv3-based student predicts the corresponding teacher representations from RGB through lightweight, modality-specific projections, enabling training on partially annotated datasets and predicting all intrinsics in a single forward pass. \textbf{RAID}, predicts intrinsic properties in the structured latent space, enabling a compact 165M-parameter model, 100x faster than diffusion-based methods. Despite its compact size, it achieves competitive or superior decomposition quality, with improved robustness to input resolution. Additionally, our learned projections yield interpretable, modality-specific feature spaces.

AI.tldr: RAID is a compact 165M-parameter representation autoencoder for single-image intrinsic decomposition that decouples reconstruction from decomposition on top of DINOv3 features, running 100x faster than diffusion-based methods.
AI.motivation: Single-image intrinsic decomposition is ill-posed, and recent diffusion-based methods address this ambiguity at the cost of large, iterative, and stochastic models.
AI.method: RAID first trains an X-to-X teacher with a shared decoder to reconstruct each intrinsic map from DINOv3 features without paired RGB-to-intrinsic supervision, then trains a DINOv3-based student with lightweight modality-specific projections to predict teacher representations from RGB in a single forward pass.
AI.result: With 165M parameters, RAID runs 100x faster than diffusion-based methods while achieving competitive or superior decomposition quality, improved robustness to input resolution, and interpretable modality-specific feature spaces.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling reconstruction from decomposition in a strong pretrained latent space enables fast, compact, and high-quality single-image intrinsic decomposition without large generative models.

title: SCRiD: Spatial and Contextual References for Generalizable AI-Generated Video Detection
summary: Generalizable AI-generated video detection remains challenging because natural motion and content variations can resemble synthesis artifacts, making isolated video discrepancies unreliable indicators of authenticity. To address this challenge, we propose Spatial and Contextual Reference-informed Detection (SCRiD), a framework that interprets video variations through complementary spatial and contextual references. Specifically, we introduce Matched-Coordinate Residual Response (MCR) to characterize temporal residual associations under motion and coordinate references with matched subpixel sampling conditions. We further develop Real-Conditioned Score Adaptation (RCSA), which learns a content-conditioned denoising reference from authentic videos and probes its responses across multiple noise scales and quality views to guide feature adaptation. To integrate these complementary sources of evidence, we design Reversible Evidence Exchange (REE) to enable information exchange through reversible symplectic updates. We train SCRiD using synthetic videos from only 4 generators and evaluate it across 88 generator or task subsets spanning 6 benchmarks. Our method achieves average ACC and AP of 72.72% and 74.23%, respectively, outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.24 and 0.81 percentage this http URL and robustness experiments further validate the effectiveness of the proposed components and the stability of SCRiD under common post-processing operations.

AI.tldr: SCRiD is a framework for generalizable AI-generated video detection that interprets video variations using complementary spatial and contextual references, outperforming baselines across 88 subsets spanning 6 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Natural motion and content variations in videos can resemble synthesis artifacts, making isolated video discrepancies unreliable for generalizable AI-generated video detection.
AI.method: SCRiD introduces Matched-Coordinate Residual Response (MCR) to characterize temporal residual associations under motion and coordinate references with matched subpixel sampling, Real-Conditioned Score Adaptation (RCSA) to probe a content-conditioned denoising reference from authentic videos across noise scales and quality views, and Reversible Evidence Exchange (REE) for symplectic evidence integration.
AI.result: Trained on synthetic videos from only 4 generators and evaluated across 88 generator or task subsets spanning 6 benchmarks, SCRiD achieves 72.72% average ACC and 74.23% average AP, outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.24 and 0.81 percentage points, and remains stable under common post-processing operations.
AI.conclusion: Grounding video authenticity analysis in spatial and contextual references significantly improves generalization and robustness in AI-generated video detection.

title: Fuse Before Reconstruct: A Novel Reconstruction Paradigm for Multimodal Industrial Anomaly Detection
comment: Preprint before peer review. Includes supplementary material. Code: this https URL
summary: Industrial anomaly detection plays a pivotal role in precision manufacturing, where joint analysis of multimodal data emerges as a critical approach to enhance detection accuracy. Feature reconstruction, a dominant paradigm for such joint analysis, is primarily implemented through intra-modal and cross-modal methods, both of which are plagued by significant limitations. Intra-modal reconstruction neglects complementary cross-modal information, while its cross-modal counterpart is prone to projection errors and ambiguous one-to-many mappings (e.g., same textures mapping to multiple geometries), leading to detection failures. To address these limitations, we propose a novel feature reconstruction paradigm, Fuse Before Reconstruct (FBR), which first fuses multimodal features and then performs reconstruction for anomaly detection. Firstly, we propose a bidirectional cross-modal attention mechanism to achieve deep feature complementarity between image and point cloud features, mitigating projection bias through channel alignment and dynamic spatial prior integration. Besides, a learnable pixel-wise gated fusion strategy is adopted to preserve multi-modal structural consistency while optimizing local feature combination. Finally, dual-path collaborative reconstruction is implemented to recover original modal features from the fused representations, where cross-modal consistency constraints effectively eliminate mapping ambiguities. Extensive experiments show that FBR achieves 98.3% I-AUROC on MVTec 3D-AD and 92.6% I-AUROC on Eyecandies, surpassing previous state-of-the-art methods by +2.9% and +4.1%, respectively.

AI.tldr: Fuse Before Reconstruct (FBR) is a multimodal industrial anomaly detection paradigm that fuses image and point cloud features before reconstructing them, achieving state-of-the-art results on MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies.
AI.motivation: Existing feature reconstruction methods for multimodal industrial anomaly detection either neglect cross-modal information (intra-modal) or suffer from projection errors and ambiguous one-to-many mappings (cross-modal).
AI.method: FBR introduces a bidirectional cross-modal attention mechanism with channel alignment and dynamic spatial prior integration, a learnable pixel-wise gated fusion strategy to preserve structural consistency, and dual-path collaborative reconstruction with cross-modal consistency constraints to recover original modal features from the fused representation.
AI.result: FBR achieves 98.3% I-AUROC on MVTec 3D-AD and 92.6% I-AUROC on Eyecandies, surpassing previous state-of-the-art methods by +2.9% and +4.1%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Fusing multimodal features prior to collaborative reconstruction resolves cross-modal mapping ambiguities and substantially improves multimodal industrial anomaly detection.

title: SCR: Detecting Backdoor-Poisoned Samples through Clean-Reference Residuals
summary: Deep neural networks are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, in which adversaries manipulate model predictions by injecting poisoned samples into training data. Detecting these samples remains challenging because legitimate semantic variation can obscure poisoning-related signals in learned representations. Consequently, class-level statistics used by existing detectors may flag benign feature deviations while overlooking poisoned samples that blend into the class distribution. In this paper, we propose Semantic Counterfactual Residualization (SCR), which uses a small set of clean reference samples to account for benign variation through sample-specific feature reconstruction. SCR identifies poisoned samples by detecting coherent deviations from these clean baselines, without requiring prior knowledge of the attacks. We evaluate SCR through experiments covering twelve dirty-label and clean-label attacks across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet. With a small clean-reference set, SCR achieves attack-averaged true positive rates above 99.5\% and false positive rates below 2\% on each dataset, outperforming eight representative detection baselines in macro-TPR.

AI.tldr: Semantic Counterfactual Residualization (SCR) detects backdoor-poisoned training samples using a small set of clean reference samples to model benign semantic variation, achieving over 99.5% TPR and under 2% FPR across three datasets.
AI.motivation: Legitimate semantic variation can obscure backdoor poisoning signals in learned representations, causing class-level statistics used by existing detectors to flag benign samples while missing poisoned samples that blend into the class distribution.
AI.method: SCR uses a small set of clean reference samples to perform sample-specific feature reconstruction that accounts for benign variation, and identifies poisoned samples by detecting coherent deviations from these clean baselines without prior attack knowledge.
AI.result: Evaluated across twelve dirty-label and clean-label attacks on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet, SCR achieves attack-averaged true positive rates above 99.5% and false positive rates below 2% on each dataset, outperforming eight detection baselines in macro-TPR.
AI.conclusion: Sample-specific counterfactual residualization against clean references provides an attack-agnostic and highly accurate way to filter backdoor-poisoned samples.

title: Beyond Appearance: Evidence-Guided Programmatic 3D Scene Reconstruction with Agentic Lighting Reasoning
comment: Project Page: this https URL Code: this https URL
summary: Image-to-code methods for 3D scene reconstruction produce executable code that generates editable digital content and supports visual simulation. However, existing methods primarily rely on appearance similarity, which provides limited guidance for distinguishing errors in geometry, materials, and illumination. Light shapes scene appearance through its interactions with geometry and materials, influencing shading, cast shadows, and reflections. We therefore present LightHarness, a VLM-based agentic framework that incorporates explicit lighting reasoning into iterative scene reconstruction. To be specific, we leverage complementary geometric, intrinsic, and illumination cues to jointly refine scene structure and appearance, and propose Lighting Reasoning Memory to maintain light-source hypotheses, which supports evidence, and revision history throughout iterations. Together, they support reasoning about partially visible and unseen sources, with evidence-guided verification directing subsequent revisions. Our framework reconstructs explicit scenes through coherent reasoning about geometry, materials, and illumination without additional training or differentiable rendering. Extensive experiments demonstrate superior image-to-code reconstruction accuracy under challenging shadows and complex illumination, further supporting downstream scene editing, object insertion, and versatile relighting.

AI.tldr: LightHarness is a VLM-based agentic framework that incorporates explicit lighting reasoning and memory into iterative image-to-code 3D scene reconstruction without additional training or differentiable rendering.
AI.motivation: Existing image-to-code 3D scene reconstruction methods rely mainly on appearance similarity, which provides limited guidance for distinguishing errors in geometry, materials, and illumination.
AI.method: LightHarness uses complementary geometric, intrinsic, and illumination cues to jointly refine scene structure and appearance, and maintains a Lighting Reasoning Memory to track light-source hypotheses, supporting evidence, and revision history across iterations for evidence-guided verification.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show superior image-to-code reconstruction accuracy under challenging shadows and complex illumination, supporting downstream scene editing, object insertion, and relighting.
AI.conclusion: Explicit agentic reasoning over light-matter interactions enables accurate, editable programmatic 3D scene reconstruction under complex lighting without training or differentiable rendering.

title: ALIVE: Bring Foundation Features to Life with Events
summary: Visual foundation models provide powerful representations for diverse tasks, but their features become stale as visual content changes between image observations. Refreshing them requires new frames and repeated runs of a computationally expensive image encoder. We introduce ALIVE, an event-based method that incrementally updates native foundation model features between image observations. Given an anchor image, ALIVE uses subsequent events to transport and correct existing multi-layer features extracted by a frozen DINOv3 encoder. Its lightweight updater is trained end-to-end using only synthetic data, without downstream task supervision, and transfers directly to real-world event streams without any adaptation. Across three real-world datasets and five task-dataset settings spanning object detection, semantic segmentation, and depth estimation, ALIVE outperforms all evaluated event-based methods in every metric. On DSEC, when the anchor frame is 200,ms old, ALIVE improves over anchor-image predictions by 30.9,mAP in detection, 11.6,mIoU in segmentation, and 15.9% in depth AbsRel. Compared with image re-encoding, ALIVE reduces FLOPs by 82.4% and latency by a factor of 2.5.

AI.tldr: ALIVE is an event-based method that incrementally updates frozen DINOv3 foundation model features between image observations, outperforming evaluated event-based methods while cutting FLOPs by 82.4% and latency by 2.5x compared to re-encoding.
AI.motivation: Visual foundation model features become stale between image frames as scenes change, and refreshing them requires new frames and repeated runs of expensive image encoders.
AI.method: Given an anchor image, ALIVE uses subsequent event streams to transport and correct multi-layer features from a frozen DINOv3 encoder via a lightweight updater trained end-to-end solely on synthetic data without downstream task supervision.
AI.result: Across three real-world datasets and five task-dataset settings (object detection, semantic segmentation, depth estimation), ALIVE outperforms all evaluated event-based methods; on DSEC with a 200 ms old anchor frame, it improves over anchor-image predictions by 30.9 mAP, 11.6 mIoU, and 15.9% depth AbsRel, while reducing FLOPs by 82.4% and latency by 2.5x versus image re-encoding.
AI.conclusion: Event-driven feature transport and correction keeps frozen foundation model representations up to date at a fraction of the compute and latency cost of re-encoding.

title: DAL: Dynamic Angular Loss for Imbalanced Medical Image Classification
comment: Accepted at the British Machine Vision Conference (BMVC) 2026. 18 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Class imbalance remains a major obstacle in medical image classification, where rare but clinically important classes are often overshadowed by majority categories. Although current strategies for reducing bias, including angle-based softmax (ABS) losses, offer strong discriminative features, their behavior in settings with a small number of severely imbalanced classes remains insufficiently understood. Previous approaches that estimate the intrinsic parameters of ABS rely on the assumption of many classes, which does not hold in medical settings.
