We derive data-driven upper and lower bounds for the scale parameter and an upper bound for the angular margin using negative-angle statistics, and use these to drive a batch-adaptive angular margin (BAAM), which we combine with dynamically-weighted cross entropy (DWCE) to define our dynamic angular loss (DAL). Across four highly imbalanced medical image classification benchmarks spanning dermatology, ophthalmology, and gastrointestinal endoscopy, our method consistently achieves superior balanced accuracy and the lowest coefficient of variation of per-class recall. Although this entails a small performance reduction on majority classes, the gains on minority categories are substantial, yielding a reliable and equitable overall classifier. Our source code is available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: Dynamic Angular Loss (DAL) combines a batch-adaptive angular margin driven by data-derived bounds with dynamically-weighted cross entropy to improve minority-class recall in severely imbalanced medical image classification.
AI.motivation: Existing angle-based softmax losses rely on many-class assumptions to estimate intrinsic parameters, which fail in medical image classification settings with a small number of severely imbalanced classes.
AI.method: DAL derives data-driven upper and lower bounds for the scale parameter and an upper bound for the angular margin using negative-angle statistics to drive a batch-adaptive angular margin (BAAM), combined with dynamically-weighted cross entropy (DWCE).
AI.result: Across four imbalanced medical image classification benchmarks in dermatology, ophthalmology, and gastrointestinal endoscopy, DAL consistently achieves superior balanced accuracy and the lowest coefficient of variation of per-class recall, trading a small majority-class reduction for substantial minority-class gains.
AI.conclusion: Adapting angular margins via negative-angle statistics yields a more equitable and reliable classifier for severely imbalanced medical imaging datasets.

title: EgoJev: Finding Evidence in Egocentric Video by Reading VLM Decisions
summary: Questions about long egocentric video often depend on one brief moment, such as the second a hand puts an object down. A vision-language model (VLM) that sees a few evenly spaced frames usually misses it. Training-free methods rank frames with a separate image-text model or ask the VLM to write a time. In a controlled test, the VLM itself locates the moment better when it chooses among labeled frames, and we read this choice from its output distribution. With the same candidates, this choice lands on the evidence more often than image-text scores or a written time span, and it compares all candidates in one decision. Based on this finding, we propose EgoJev, a training-free frame selector for wearable assistants. EgoJev reads where the evidence is from labeled thumbnails and looks again at the windows it points to. It places its few answer frames at the quantiles of the resulting distribution. One frozen VLM selects, answers and returns the evidence time, with no second model. A wearable device can encode its coarse thumbnails while it records. With Qwen3.5-4B and 8 answer frames, EgoJev raises QAEgo4D accuracy from 51.2% with uniform sampling to 62.0%, and it outperforms recent training-free frame selectors on QAEgo4D and MyEgo. A single-level version runs on a Mac and an iPhone.

AI.tldr: EgoJev is a training-free frame selector for wearable assistants that locates brief evidence moments in long egocentric videos by reading a frozen VLM's output distribution over labeled thumbnails, raising QAEgo4D accuracy from 51.2% to 62.0%.
AI.motivation: Questions about long egocentric videos often hinge on brief moments that uniform sampling misses, and existing training-free selectors either use a separate image-text model or ask the VLM to write a timestamp.
AI.method: EgoJev presents labeled thumbnails to a frozen VLM, reads its choice from the output distribution, looks again at the indicated windows, and places answer frames at the quantiles of the resulting distribution, using one VLM to select, answer, and return evidence time.
AI.result: With Qwen3.5-4B and 8 answer frames, EgoJev raises QAEgo4D accuracy from 51.2% (uniform sampling) to 62.0% and outperforms recent training-free frame selectors on QAEgo4D and MyEgo; a single-level version runs on a Mac and an iPhone.
AI.conclusion: Reading a frozen VLM's own decision distribution over labeled frames provides an effective, single-model, on-device-capable way to localize brief evidence in long egocentric videos.

title: AggCLIP: Aggregating CLIP for Zero-Shot Multimodal Anomaly Detection
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Author version of the ACM Multimedia 2026 paper
summary: Zero-Shot Multimodal Anomaly Detection (ZSMAD) aims to identify both appearance and geometric defects in novel categories without relying on target-specific training data, making it especially valuable in real-world scenarios constrained by data scarcity, privacy concerns, or high annotation costs. While recent approaches successfully adapt vision-language models like CLIP to achieve this open-vocabulary generalization, they still face significant challenges: (i) severe geometric information loss during 3D-to-2D point cloud rendering; (ii) spatially noisy 2D feature maps produced by raw CLIP patch embeddings, compounded by shallow late-stage modality fusion; and (iii) severe cross-modal semantic misalignment due to decoupled processing streams. To address these limitations, we propose AggCLIP, a novel framework that adapts frozen CLIP representations for ZSMAD by explicitly incorporating local geometric structure and visual spatial context. Specifically, to accurately localize fine-grained defects, we design a Geometry-Aware Spatial Aggregation (GSA) module that refines back-projected 3D point features via density-adaptive neighborhood weighting, alongside a Context-Aware Spatial Aggregation (CSA) module that smooths multi-scale 2D patch embeddings using a lightweight trainable adapter. Furthermore, to prevent semantic drift between modalities, we introduce a Dual-Stream Prompt Contrastive (DSPC) loss, which aligns the abstract concepts of normality and abnormality across the point cloud and RGB streams. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed AggCLIP framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies benchmarks under both one-vs-rest and cross-dataset zero-shot settings, notably surpassing the strongest competitive methods by up to 2.9% in pixel-level AUPRO.

AI.tldr: AggCLIP adapts frozen CLIP representations for zero-shot multimodal anomaly detection by aggregating local 3D geometry and 2D spatial context with dual-stream prompt contrastive alignment, achieving state-of-the-art results on MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies.
AI.motivation: Existing CLIP-based zero-shot multimodal anomaly detection methods suffer from 3D-to-2D geometric information loss, spatially noisy 2D CLIP patch maps with shallow late fusion, and cross-modal semantic misalignment.
AI.method: AggCLIP introduces a Geometry-Aware Spatial Aggregation (GSA) module that refines back-projected 3D point features via density-adaptive neighborhood weighting, a Context-Aware Spatial Aggregation (CSA) module that smooths multi-scale 2D patch embeddings via a lightweight trainable adapter, and a Dual-Stream Prompt Contrastive (DSPC) loss to align normality and abnormality across point cloud and RGB streams.
AI.result: AggCLIP achieves state-of-the-art performance on MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies under both one-vs-rest and cross-dataset zero-shot settings, surpassing the strongest competitive methods by up to 2.9% in pixel-level AUPRO.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating local geometric structure, 2D spatial context, and cross-modal prompt alignment unlocks stronger zero-shot multimodal anomaly localization from frozen CLIP models.

title: Predicting Species Splits: A Challenging Fine-Grained Benchmark for Category Discovery
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track)
summary: Widely used category discovery benchmarks have become increasingly saturated and often fail to reflect real-world discovery settings, making long-term evaluation of new methods difficult. We introduce PS-SPLIT, a large-scale fine-grained benchmark for category discovery, motivated by taxonomic splitting: the real-world process by which what was once considered a single species is found to comprise multiple distinct ones. PS-SPLIT contains 79K globally distributed, high-quality, community-collected bird images spanning 771 species, derived from 257 recent real expert-verified taxonomic splits, with associated geographic metadata and full taxonomic hierarchy. The visual differences between categories arising from real taxonomic splits can be very subtle, often requiring significant human expertise to tell apart, making PS-SPLIT a challenging benchmark which we hope will assist in advancing fine-grained category discovery research. Based on taxonomic splitting, we introduce the task of discovery by category splitting, where the goal is to determine which known categories should be subdivided into new finer-grained subcategories. We adapt four generalized category discovery methods to this setting, evaluate existing methods, and show that there is substantial room for future progress.

AI.tldr: PS-SPLIT is a 79K-image fine-grained category discovery benchmark spanning 771 bird species derived from 257 real taxonomic splits, introducing the task of discovery by category splitting.
AI.motivation: Existing category discovery benchmarks are increasingly saturated and fail to reflect real-world discovery settings where subtle visual differences require expert-level discrimination.
AI.method: The authors construct PS-SPLIT from 79K globally distributed, community-collected bird images across 771 species based on 257 expert-verified taxonomic splits with geographic metadata and full taxonomic hierarchy, and formalize discovery by category splitting, adapting four generalized category discovery methods for evaluation.
AI.result: Evaluating existing adapted methods on PS-SPLIT reveals substantial room for future progress on fine-grained category splitting.
AI.conclusion: PS-SPLIT provides a challenging, real-world-grounded benchmark to drive future research in fine-grained category discovery.

title: DrawScore: Evaluating Generated CAD Models against Engineering Drawings
summary: Automatic CAD generation is commonly evaluated with volumetric IoU, Chamfer Distance, and surface F-score, which barely penalize local errors that occupy only a small fraction of a part's volume or surface area, such as a misplaced hole or a slot on the wrong face, even though such errors are critical to manufacturing. We formalize these metrics in a unified integral form and show that the weight of a local error decays as the $(k+q)$-th power of its size, where $k$ is the dimension of the integration domain and $q$ is determined by the penalty function. Guided by this analysis, we propose DrawScore, which projects both models into three orthographic views with visible and hidden lines, as in engineering drawings, and applies a saturating penalty along the projected curves, so that the weight of a local error decays only linearly. Controlled experiments confirm the predicted decay orders, and on outputs of existing CAD generation agents, DrawScore exposes errors in outputs that IoU rates as nearly perfect. DrawScore further improves generation as a reinforcement learning reward and, for CAD generation from engineering drawings, serves as a test-time verifier without 3D ground truth or an additional reward model. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: DrawScore evaluates generated CAD models by projecting them into three orthographic engineering views with visible and hidden lines, exposing local manufacturing-critical errors that volumetric IoU misses.
AI.motivation: Standard CAD metrics like volumetric IoU, Chamfer Distance, and surface F-score barely penalize small local errors (such as a misplaced hole or slot) that are critical to manufacturing.
AI.method: After formalizing existing metrics in an integral form to show local error weight decays as the (k+q)-th power of size, DrawScore projects both models into three orthographic views with visible and hidden lines and applies a saturating penalty along projected curves so local error weight decays only linearly.
AI.result: Controlled experiments confirm the predicted decay orders; on existing CAD generation agents, DrawScore exposes errors in outputs rated nearly perfect by IoU, and it also improves generation as an RL reward and serves as a test-time verifier without 3D ground truth.
AI.conclusion: Orthographic engineering-drawing evaluation provides a more sensitive, manufacturing-relevant metric, reward, and verifier for automatic CAD generation.

title: Improving Zero-shot 3D Semantic Mapping in Offroad with Geometric Priors
summary: Semantic 3D mapping is a powerful representation that enables platform agnostic mobile robot navigation in challenging offroad conditions. Current vision foundation models can accurately predict semantics zero-shot on structured scenes but performance is compromised in natural environments. On the other hand, 3D point clouds encode valuable information for discriminating semantics in scenarios where vision foundation models fail. In this work, we propose fitting a sphericity-elevation distribution for each semantic class to act as geometric anchor. Only the points with the most confident vision foundation model predictions are considered when fitting to produce high quality geometric prior distributions. The geometric prior is fused with the vision foundation model prediction to produce the final semantic mapping. The proposed prior improves SAM3 baseline by +6.3 in mIoU and +8.9 in accuracy on the RELLIS-3D dataset, and by +1.7 in mIoU and +2.1 in accuracy on the WildScenes dataset. The source code will be made public upon paper acceptance.

AI.tldr: This paper improves zero-shot 3D semantic mapping in offroad environments by fitting per-class sphericity-elevation geometric priors from confident vision foundation model predictions and fusing them with visual predictions.
AI.motivation: Vision foundation models struggle to predict semantics zero-shot in unstructured natural offroad environments, whereas 3D point clouds contain complementary geometric cues.
AI.method: The method fits a sphericity-elevation distribution for each semantic class using only points with the most confident vision foundation model predictions, and fuses this geometric prior with the visual predictions to produce the final 3D semantic map.
AI.result: The proposed geometric prior improves the SAM3 baseline by +6.3 mIoU and +8.9 accuracy on RELLIS-3D, and by +1.7 mIoU and +2.1 accuracy on WildScenes.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight per-class 3D geometric priors effectively compensate for vision foundation model failures in zero-shot offroad semantic mapping.

title: Can Omni-modal LLMs Understand Spoken Intentions?
summary: Omni-modal large language models (omni-modal LLMs) can respond to spoken requests directly through voice and video calls. Such requests rely on the scene shared by the user and the assistant, so the same utterance may call for different help or for no response. Most audio-visual benchmarks provide questions as separate text input, and interactive benchmarks mostly score a response as a whole. It thus remains unclear whether a model recognizes when the user is asking for help, and whether its reply meets the user's need once the request is recognized. We propose O-IN-Bench to evaluate how well omni-modal LLMs understand spoken intentions. A model watches a complete video with native speech and outputs one text response, or [SILENCE] when no response is needed. O-IN-Bench contains 1,000 Chinese and English samples in five categories and 16 subcategories. Contrastive pairs combine the same request with different scene conditions to test whether the response changes with the context. A sample-specific rubric judges language, intent, and content separately, and O-IN-Engine verifies each rubric against the video. Across 30 omni-modal model configurations, the best overall score is 59.6, achieved by Gemini3.7-Flash. Gemini3.7-Flash passes 74.4% of the intent judgments but only 42.6% of the content judgments. When the speech is a conversation between peers rather than a request to the assistant, even strong models often keep responding. When a reply must satisfy several people, the best score is only 25.9. These results indicate that recognizing a request and meeting its requirements are separate abilities, and O-IN-Bench measures each of them.

AI.tldr: O-IN-Bench is a 1,000-sample bilingual benchmark for evaluating whether omni-modal LLMs understand spoken intentions in shared-scene video calls, revealing that recognizing a request and meeting its requirements are separate abilities.
AI.motivation: Existing audio-visual benchmarks provide text questions or score responses holistically, leaving it unclear whether omni-modal LLMs know when a user is asking for help and whether their reply actually satisfies the user's need.
AI.method: O-IN-Bench pairs full videos with native speech (1,000 Chinese and English samples across 5 categories and 16 subcategories) where models output a text response or [SILENCE], using contrastive pairs with identical requests under different scenes and O-IN-Engine to verify sample-specific language, intent, and content rubrics.
AI.result: Across 30 omni-modal model configurations, Gemini3.7-Flash achieves the top overall score of 59.6, passing 74.4% of intent judgments but only 42.6% of content judgments; strong models often respond to peer conversations, and the best score on multi-person requests is 25.9.
AI.conclusion: Current omni-modal LLMs are much better at detecting spoken intent than fulfilling scene-grounded content requirements, highlighting a key gap measured by O-IN-Bench.

title: Multi-Band Galaxy Novel-View Synthesis with Radiative Gaussian Fields
summary: We propose a novel view synthesis tool for galaxies based on Gaussian Splatting (GS). Unlike RGB data, where GS has achieved success, galaxy observations consist of multi-band signals from a massive number of bodies, contain complex patterns of cross-band interactions, and capture light propagation in highly heterogeneous media. As a result, the underlying physical process poses great challenges in model representation and optimization, which have not been investigated in existing research. To this end, we propose a physically inspired Gaussian Splatting method, GalaxyGS, which is equipped with physically meaningful components that capture both the energy emission mechanism of different astronomical bodies and the light propagation between them. In the absence of directly comparable baseline methods, we adopt a wide range of possible alternative approaches. Comparisons conclusively demonstrate that GalaxyGS is better in accuracy and physical fidelity across datasets and metrics.

AI.tldr: GalaxyGS is a physically inspired Gaussian Splatting method for multi-band galaxy novel-view synthesis that models astronomical energy emission and light propagation in heterogeneous media.
AI.motivation: Unlike standard RGB scenes, galaxy observations involve multi-band signals from massive numbers of bodies, complex cross-band interactions, and light propagation through heterogeneous media, which existing Gaussian Splatting methods do not model.
AI.method: GalaxyGS equips Gaussian Splatting with physically meaningful components that capture both the energy emission mechanisms of different astronomical bodies and light propagation between them.
AI.result: Comparisons against a wide range of alternative approaches demonstrate that GalaxyGS achieves superior accuracy and physical fidelity across datasets and metrics.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating astrophysical emission and light-propagation models into Gaussian Splatting enables accurate, physically faithful multi-band novel-view synthesis of galaxies.

title: Generalization of Text Line Segmentation for HTR in Historical Documents
comment: This work is going to be published in the proceedings for the Historical Image Processing workshop 2026 (HIP 2026), connected to the International Conference of Document Analysis and Recognition (ICDAR)
summary: In this paper we investigate the generalization capability of state-of-the-art object detection models (Hi-SAM, YOLO, and RT-DETR) for the automatic segmentation of text lines in historical documents. Generalization is needed because it is not practical for museums and archives to produce large amounts of labeled samples for each new collection. We also evaluate the few-shot setting by fine-tuning the networks with only a small number of training samples per target dataset. To this end, we use nine different datasets that differ significantly in visual layout and language. Additionally, we discuss why mean average precision (mAP), a classic evaluation metric for object detection, is insufficient for assessing the quality of a text line segmentation model. Depending on the dataset, our CRNN models achieve character error rates (CER) ranging from 2.48% to 7.07% per page for the segmented text lines. This is sufficient for reading comprehension and simple text searches. Finally, we quantify the resource and time requirements of training and inference in different use case settings. This forms the basis for more informed decisions about model and hardware choices based on available resources.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the generalization and few-shot fine-tuning of Hi-SAM, YOLO, and RT-DETR for historical document text line segmentation across nine diverse datasets, showing CRNN character error rates of 2.48% to 7.07%.
AI.motivation: Museums and archives cannot practically produce large labeled training sets for every new historical document collection, requiring text line segmentation models that generalize or adapt with few-shot samples.
AI.method: The authors evaluate Hi-SAM, YOLO, and RT-DETR in zero-shot and few-shot fine-tuning settings across nine datasets differing in visual layout and language, critique mAP as insufficient for text line segmentation, and measure downstream CRNN character error rates (CER) plus training and inference resource requirements.
AI.result: Downstream CRNN models achieve per-page CERs ranging from 2.48% to 7.07% across the nine datasets, sufficient for reading comprehension and simple text searches, alongside quantified compute and time profiles.
AI.conclusion: Modern object detectors with few-shot adaptation provide practical text line segmentation for diverse historical archives, and downstream CER plus resource profiling better guide model selection than mAP alone.

title: HandWorldBench: A Unified Benchmark for Hand-Centric World Models
summary: Recent advances in world models are opening new possibilities for fine-grained embodied tasks, with hand-object interaction offering a particularly demanding setting. Modeling these interactions involves capturing how hand actions change objects and how the resulting states persist over time. Yet systematic evaluation tailored to these hand-centric capabilities remains underdeveloped. To address this gap, we introduce HandWorldBench, a unified benchmark that systematically evaluates hand-centric world models across human hands, simulated dexterous hands, and real dexterous hands along six dimensions: visual quality, hand fidelity, appearance consistency, instruction following, physical consistency, and temporal coherence. To construct the benchmark, we develop a data curation pipeline that extracts hand-object interaction clips and screens them for quality, yielding 20,500 high-quality egocentric clips from over 600 hours of footage. We then manually select 500 clips covering seven task families for evaluation. Benchmarking eleven models under a unified protocol reveals that stronger hand-pose control does not consistently translate into coherent object-state evolution and persistence or robust cross-embodiment performance, with several specialized hand-control models underperforming general-purpose text/image-to-video generators on dexterous-hand tasks.

AI.tldr: HandWorldBench is a unified benchmark of 500 curated clips across seven task families for evaluating hand-centric world models on human, simulated dexterous, and real dexterous hands.
AI.motivation: Systematic evaluation of hand-centric world models—specifically how hand actions change objects and how resulting states persist over time—remains underdeveloped.
AI.method: The authors build a data curation pipeline extracting 20,500 egocentric hand-object interaction clips from over 600 hours of footage, manually select 500 clips across seven task families, and benchmark eleven models along six dimensions: visual quality, hand fidelity, appearance consistency, instruction following, physical consistency, and temporal coherence.
AI.result: Benchmarking eleven models shows that stronger hand-pose control does not consistently yield coherent object-state evolution or cross-embodiment performance, with several specialized hand-control models underperforming general-purpose video generators on dexterous-hand tasks.
AI.conclusion: HandWorldBench exposes a gap between hand-pose control and physically consistent object-state modeling in current hand-centric world models.

title: Jeveration: System One Models Now Generate
summary: System One models such as Jev return decisions through fast, parallel prediction. In this paper, we introduce Jeveration, showing that the same decision paradigm can also generate high-quality images in a single forward pass. Jeveration builds on a frozen vision-language model, repurposing its visual-semantic knowledge for holistic image generation. The key challenge is to maintain global consistency. A single prompt admits many valid images, yet parallel predictions must converge on a coherent whole. We therefore condition all positions on a shared random state to coordinate parallel predictions, so that each draw yields a different but coherent image. Since the model tends to ignore this state under direct image supervision, we first learn a distribution over discrete image codes to guide single-pass generation. Beyond text-to-image generation, we further unify image-to-image generation and dense prediction within the same architecture, so that one checkpoint supports all three tasks, each in one forward pass. Experiments show that Jeveration generates a 512x512 image in 78 ms, up to 122x faster than existing unified models, while maintaining competitive image quality and dense prediction performance.

AI.tldr: Jeveration repurposes a frozen vision-language model for single-pass parallel image generation, image-to-image generation, and dense prediction, generating 512x512 images in 78 ms (up to 122x faster than existing unified models).
AI.motivation: Parallel System One decision models are fast, but applying them to holistic image generation requires maintaining global consistency across parallel predictions when a prompt admits many valid images.
AI.method: Jeveration conditions all positions on a shared random state to coordinate parallel predictions, first learns a distribution over discrete image codes to guide single-pass generation (preventing the model from ignoring the random state), and unifies text-to-image, image-to-image, and dense prediction in one checkpoint.
AI.result: Experiments show Jeveration generates a 512x512 image in 78 ms—up to 122x faster than existing unified models—while maintaining competitive image quality and dense prediction performance.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning parallel predictions on a shared random state guided by discrete image codes enables a single frozen VLM to perform unified, ultra-fast single-pass generation and dense prediction.

title: A$^3$Bench: Compositional Reasoning over Aggressive Interactions in Videos
summary: Recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on general video understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to reason about participant roles in aggressive interactions remains largely unexplored. Existing violence and crime datasets primarily evaluate whether aggression occurs, without testing whether models can identify who performed the action, who received it, and how participants are related within the scene. To address this gap, we introduce A$^3$Bench, a benchmark to study aggressive action and association in videos. The benchmark evaluates whether models can jointly recognize aggressive actions, distinguish aggressors from victims and bystanders, and correctly bind actions to participants under challenging distractor settings. We benchmark 17 multimodal models and find that they struggle substantially on fine-grained aggressive-scene understanding. Performance degrades consistently as reasoning complexity increases, with models frequently confusing aggressors with victims or bystanders, revealing a systematic failure in role-action association rather than coarse aggression recognition alone. We further observe that increasing model scale or generic reasoning models experience limited improvement. Finally, we explore a simple role-graph prompting strategy that encourages structured reasoning over participant interactions, leading to improvements in compositional reasoning. Our findings highlight that reliable aggressive-scene understanding remains a major challenge for current MLLMs and motivate future research on role-aware video reasoning beyond coarse violence detection. Code and dataset: this https URL.

AI.tldr: A^3Bench is a video benchmark for compositional reasoning over aggressive interactions, revealing that 17 evaluated MLLMs frequently confuse aggressors, victims, and bystanders.
AI.motivation: Existing violence and crime datasets only test whether aggression occurs, without evaluating whether models can identify who performed the action, who received it, and how participants relate in the scene.
AI.method: A^3Bench evaluates joint recognition of aggressive actions, role distinction (aggressors, victims, bystanders), and action-participant binding under distractor settings across 17 MLLMs, and explores a role-graph prompting strategy for structured interaction reasoning.
AI.result: All 17 MLLMs struggle on fine-grained aggressive-scene understanding, degrading consistently with reasoning complexity and frequently confusing aggressors with victims or bystanders; scaling models helps little, whereas role-graph prompting improves compositional reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Current MLLMs exhibit a systematic failure in role-action association during aggressive interactions, motivating role-aware video reasoning beyond coarse violence detection.

title: Read Together, Answer Apart: How Earlier Questions Help Vision-Language Models Look
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are often asked several questions about the same image in a single prompt (co-asking), yet existing evaluations report conflicting accuracy gains and hallucinations at the prompt level without tracking how individual answers change. By pairing each question's single-question and co-asked answers across 22 open-weight VLMs (1B-35B), we find that erratic net shifts reflect two opposing effects: on Densely Captioned Images (DCI), every model repairs 15.4%-29.8% of its single-question errors under co-asking, while the share of correct answers turned wrong falls from 30.8% on weaker models to 4.7% on stronger ones. Across all 14 models supporting custom attention masks, we show through attention readouts and layer-window interventions that earlier same-image questions read visual information into their question tokens in the early-to-middle layers during prefill, helping later questions concentrate image attention onto their queried targets. This visual help accumulates across the scene even across non-overlapping regions, whereas blocking earlier questions from attending to the image lowers both target localization and accuracy in all 14 models. While cross-question help is established during shared question reading, part of the co-asking damage enters later during answer decoding when the decoder attends to other question stems. We therefore introduce Read Together, Answer Apart, a training-free decoding mask that keeps shared prefill intact and isolates each answer from other stems, improving co-asking accuracy on 12 of 14 models on DCI (up to +4.71 percentage points, closing 70% of the pooled gap to asking alone) and on 10, 8, and 5 of the 14 models on WebUI, FinTabNet, and GQA (up to +11.4, +5.3, and +1.1 points).

AI.tldr: Read Together, Answer Apart is a training-free decoding mask for multi-question VLM prompts that preserves shared prefill help while isolating answer decoding from other question stems, improving co-asking accuracy on 12 of 14 models on DCI.
AI.motivation: When VLMs are asked multiple questions about an image in one prompt (co-asking), evaluations report conflicting accuracy shifts without explaining how individual answers change.
AI.method: By pairing single-question and co-asked answers across 22 open-weight VLMs (1B-35B) and running attention readouts and layer-window interventions on 14 models, the authors show earlier questions help later ones localize targets during prefill while decoding-time attention to other stems causes damage; they introduce Read Together, Answer Apart, a training-free mask keeping shared prefill intact and isolating each answer from other stems.
AI.result: Under co-asking on DCI, models repair 15.4%-29.8% of single-question errors while correct-to-wrong flips drop from 30.8% to 4.7% in stronger models; Read Together, Answer Apart improves co-asking accuracy on 12 of 14 models on DCI (up to +4.71 percentage points, closing 70% of the gap to asking alone) and on 10, 8, and 5 of 14 models on WebUI, FinTabNet, and GQA (up to +11.4, +5.3, and +1.1 points).
AI.conclusion: Separating shared visual prefill from isolated answer decoding captures cross-question visual grounding benefits while eliminating decoding-time interference.

title: Ultimate3D: Teaching Multimodal LLMs 3D Camera-Object Relations by Large-Scale Visual Instruction Data
comment: Accepted to Machine Vision and Applications 2027
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with accurately capturing camera-object relations, especially for object orientation, camera viewpoint, and camera shots. This stems from the fact that existing MLLMs are trained on images with limited diverse camera-object relations and corresponding textual descriptions. To address this, we propose a synthetic generation pipeline to create large-scale 3D visual instruction datasets. Our framework takes 3D assets as input and uses rendering and diffusion-based image generation models to create photorealistic images preserving precise camera-object relations. Additionally, large language models (LLMs) are used to generate text prompts for guiding visual instruction tuning and controlling image generation. We create Ultimate3D, a large-scale 3D-grounded 2D visual instruction dataset. Ultimate3D consists of 240K VQAs with precise camera-object annotations, and corresponding benchmark. MLLMs fine-tuned on our proposed dataset outperform commercial models by a large margin, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 29.7% on camera-object relation recognition tasks. Our code, dataset, and benchmark will contribute to broad MLLM applications.

AI.tldr: Ultimate3D is a synthetic 240K-VQA dataset and benchmark teaching MLLMs 3D camera-object relations, improving camera-object relation recognition accuracy by an average of 29.7% over commercial models.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs struggle with 3D camera-object relations such as object orientation, camera viewpoint, and camera shots due to limited diverse training data with precise 3D annotations.
AI.method: A synthetic pipeline takes 3D assets, uses rendering and diffusion-based image generation to produce photorealistic images preserving exact camera-object relations, and uses LLMs to generate text prompts for image generation and visual instruction tuning, yielding the 240K-VQA Ultimate3D dataset and benchmark.
AI.result: MLLMs fine-tuned on Ultimate3D outperform commercial models by a large margin, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 29.7% on camera-object relation recognition tasks.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale, 3D-grounded synthetic visual instruction data substantially advances MLLMs' understanding of camera-object geometry.

title: Edge-Efficient Joint RAW Image Compression and Restoration for Smart Wearable Devices
summary: Smart wearable devices, such as augmented reality glasses, increasingly rely on cameras to understand and interact with their surroundings. However, their compact sensors often capture noisy RAW images, while limited compute and power make high-quality on-device restoration difficult. This creates an emerging need to reduce both local computation and transmission cost without sacrificing image quality. Two common solutions are to offload restoration or to compress the raw data before transmission. The first makes RAW transmission costly; the second reduces the payload but can spend bitrate preserving sensor noise. We address this fundamental mismatch with an asymmetric framework for joint RAW compression and restoration that directly optimizes the transmitted representation for clean image reconstruction. A lightweight on-device encoder compresses noisy RAW measurements into a bitstream, while a higher-capacity backend decoder jointly denoises and demosaics the encoded representation. We use knowledge distillation to train a smaller encoder for tighter compute budgets. Experiments on real and synthetic data show improved rate-restoration performance over strong cascaded compression-restoration pipelines and learned compression baselines. On SIDD, our method improves PSNR by more than 1.5 dB over cascaded baselines at approximately 0.25 bits per pixel. We further validate the method on real 12 MP RAW images captured with commercial smart glasses and measure sender-side latency on both smartphone and smart-glasses hardware. The distilled encoder achieves a 27.6$\times$ NPU inference speedup over on-device NAFNet for 256$\times$256 output patches. The code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper presents an asymmetric framework for joint RAW image compression and restoration on smart wearables, improving PSNR by over 1.5 dB on SIDD at ~0.25 bpp and achieving a 27.6x NPU speedup over on-device NAFNet.
AI.motivation: Smart wearables capture noisy RAW images under tight compute and power budgets, where offloading RAW data is bandwidth-heavy and compressing noisy RAW data wastes bitrate on sensor noise.
AI.method: An asymmetric architecture pairs a lightweight on-device encoder that compresses noisy RAW measurements into a bitstream with a higher-capacity backend decoder that jointly denoises and demosaics the representation, using knowledge distillation to train a smaller encoder.
AI.result: On SIDD at ~0.25 bpp, the method improves PSNR by over 1.5 dB over cascaded compression-restoration baselines; validated on real 12 MP smart-glasses RAW images, the distilled encoder achieves a 27.6x NPU inference speedup over on-device NAFNet for 256x256 output patches.
AI.conclusion: Asymmetric joint RAW compression and restoration enables high-quality imaging on power-constrained wearables by shifting heavy denoising and demosaicing to the backend.

title: ReCoCo: From Patches to Compositions for Visual Representation Learning
summary: Self-supervised learning has produced powerful visual representations, yet learning strong dense features remains challenging. While consistency between augmented views provides strong image-level supervision, extending this principle to local visual content is less straightforward. Existing approaches often match individual patches across views or identify coherent regions, introducing uncertainties in correspondence estimation and assumptions about how visual content should be grouped. We introduce ReCoCo (Regional Composition Consistency), a principled approach that extends cross-view consistency to the regional level without requiring such correspondences or semantic grouping. ReCoCo represents the content shared between augmented views through compositions of their patch-level predictions over learned visual prototypes. By aligning these compositions, the model learns from regions containing multiple visual concepts without requiring them to be separated beforehand. ReCoCo integrates naturally with teacher-student self-distillation and introduces no additional learned parameters. Extensive experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in frozen-feature segmentation, clustering, and regional retrieval while maintaining competitive image-level recognition, alleviating the trade-off between dense and global representation quality.

AI.tldr: ReCoCo (Regional Composition Consistency) extends self-supervised cross-view consistency to the regional level using compositions of patch-level predictions over learned visual prototypes, improving dense representation quality without extra parameters.
AI.motivation: Extending self-supervised cross-view consistency to dense features is difficult because matching individual patches or grouping coherent regions introduces correspondence uncertainty and grouping assumptions.
AI.method: ReCoCo represents shared content between augmented views through compositions of patch-level predictions over learned visual prototypes, aligning these compositions without requiring explicit correspondences or prior semantic separation, and integrates into teacher-student self-distillation with zero additional learned parameters.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show substantial improvements in frozen-feature segmentation, clustering, and regional retrieval while maintaining competitive image-level recognition.
AI.conclusion: Aligning regional prototype compositions offers a simple, parameter-free way to learn strong dense visual representations alongside global features.

title: Gaspard: Expressive unified speech and gesture synthesis with continuous autoregressive flow-matching and decoupled classifier-free guidance
summary: Human communication involves highly coordinated multimodal signals such as speech and co-speech gestures. Existing approaches for generating both modalities commonly follow a cascaded pipeline, where speech is generated first and subsequently used to drive gesture generation; speech generation is therefore independent of gestures. We introduce Gaspard, a unified speech--gesture generation model based on continuous autoregressive generation with next-step flow-matching predictions, and trained on Seamless Interaction, a large-scale multimodal dataset. The heterogeneous temporal properties of speech and gesture motivate modality-specific prediction heads and decoupled classifier-free guidance over the two generation streams. This guidance rebalances the influence of speech and gesture at inference time, improving expressivity while mitigating dynamics collapse in continuous autoregressive gesture generation. Objective and perceptual evaluations show that Gaspard is a strong gesture generation model against unimodal baselines and that it produces highly synchronous speech and gestures compared to a matched cascaded system.

AI.tldr: Gaspard is a unified speech and co-speech gesture generation model using continuous autoregressive flow-matching and decoupled classifier-free guidance, producing highly synchronous speech and gestures.
AI.motivation: Existing speech and gesture generation systems typically use cascaded pipelines where speech is generated first, leaving speech independent of gestures.
AI.method: Trained on Seamless Interaction, Gaspard uses continuous autoregressive generation with next-step flow-matching predictions, modality-specific prediction heads for heterogeneous temporal properties, and decoupled classifier-free guidance to rebalance speech and gesture influence at inference time and prevent dynamics collapse.
AI.result: Objective and perceptual evaluations show Gaspard is competitive with unimodal gesture baselines and produces highly synchronous speech and gestures compared to a matched cascaded system.
AI.conclusion: Unified continuous autoregressive flow-matching with decoupled guidance enables expressive, tightly synchronized multimodal speech and gesture synthesis.

title: NereidVLA: Learning to Understand and Navigate the Underwater World
summary: Underwater navigation requires translating visual spatial cues into motion, yet marine vision-language datasets rarely include paired robot trajectories. We present NereidVLA, a vision-language-action model that transfers marine spatial knowledge to language-conditioned 3D navigation. We first train Sea2Know on approximately two million marine examples to learn target grounding, spatial relations, and scene structure without paired robot-motion supervision. We then adapt it using expert trajectories executed under simulated underwater vehicle dynamics. Given RGB histories and a language instruction, NereidVLA predicts discrete motion tokens that decode into local 3D trajectories for closed-loop tracking. Evaluation combines an independent six-dimensional underwater navigation understanding benchmark with offline prediction and closed-loop navigation. Under matched navigation training and execution settings, marine spatial pretraining increases simulation success from 72.4% to 84.4%. Without fine-tuning on the real test environment, NereidVLA achieves 78.75% success in laboratory-pool robot trials, compared with 47.50% for InternVLA-N1. These results show that marine spatial supervision can support downstream motion learning and physical underwater navigation.

AI.tldr: NereidVLA is a vision-language-action model that transfers marine spatial pretraining (Sea2Know) to closed-loop 3D underwater navigation, boosting simulation success from 72.4% to 84.4% and reaching 78.75% success in real pool trials.
AI.motivation: Underwater navigation requires mapping visual spatial cues to motion, but marine vision-language datasets rarely contain paired robot trajectories.
AI.method: NereidVLA first trains Sea2Know on ~2M marine examples for target grounding, spatial relations, and scene structure without robot-motion supervision, then adapts it on simulated expert trajectories so that given RGB histories and language instructions, it outputs discrete motion tokens decoded into local 3D trajectories for closed-loop tracking.
AI.result: Marine spatial pretraining increases simulation navigation success from 72.4% to 84.4%; without fine-tuning on the real test environment, NereidVLA achieves 78.75% success in laboratory-pool robot trials versus 47.50% for InternVLA-N1.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale marine spatial pretraining without paired trajectories transfers effectively to physical, closed-loop 3D underwater robot navigation.

title: ShadowTransfer: A Geographic Transfer Benchmark for Overhead Shadow Detection
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets. 53 pages. Project page: this https URL . Code: this https URL . Data: this https URL (DOI https://doi.org/10.57967/hf/11483)
summary: Overhead aerial imagery feeds dense-prediction pipelines that are routinely trained in one geographic region and deployed in another, yet no benchmark measures how shadow detection models transfer across regions. Existing overhead shadow datasets either lack a geographic transfer protocol or rely on automatically generated labels. We introduce ShadowTransfer, a benchmark of 4,500 human-verified shadow masks across three U.S. cities at two native resolutions, paired with a leave-one-city-out evaluation protocol. Under vanilla training, holding out the test city costs 3.5 to 7.8 mIoU across four architectures, the gap remains significant when the training set grows from 225 to 900 images, and six of eight adaptation methods degrade more than vanilla training on average. We propose a three-probe framework that diagnoses where and how the transfer breaks: the failure operates in feature space, beyond the reach of pixel-histogram matching, shows up as a confidence collapse on shadow pixels while background confidence stays intact, and is recoverable by retraining different architectural components depending on the model: encoder for some, decoder for others. These findings replicate on INRIA building footprints, suggesting they describe geographic transfer beyond shadows. Guided by the diagnosis, we build Spectral Information Bottleneck (SIB), a plug-in module with one component per finding. Across the 9 (architecture, held-out city) cells, SIB has the smallest mean gap to the within-city upper bound of the ten methods we evaluate (6.42 mIoU), level with FDA. The benchmark, LOCO protocol, code, and trained models are released to support reproducible evaluation of geographic transfer in overhead dense prediction.

AI.tldr: ShadowTransfer is a 4,500-image geographic transfer benchmark for overhead shadow detection, alongside a diagnostic framework and Spectral Information Bottleneck (SIB) plug-in that reduces the cross-city transfer gap to 6.42 mIoU.
AI.motivation: Overhead shadow detection models are routinely trained in one city and deployed in another, yet no benchmark measures geographic transfer with human-verified labels, and most existing adaptation methods degrade performance.
AI.method: ShadowTransfer provides 4,500 human-verified shadow masks across three U.S. cities at two resolutions with a leave-one-city-out protocol; a three-probe diagnostic reveals feature-space failure and shadow-pixel confidence collapse, guiding the design of the Spectral Information Bottleneck (SIB) plug-in module.
AI.result: Vanilla training loses 3.5 to 7.8 mIoU on held-out cities and six of eight adaptation methods perform worse than vanilla training; across 9 (architecture, city) cells, SIB achieves the smallest mean gap to the within-city upper bound (6.42 mIoU), level with FDA.
AI.conclusion: Geographic transfer in overhead dense prediction fails via feature-space shadow confidence collapse, and targeted spectral bottlenecking mitigates this gap more reliably than standard domain adaptation.

title: PrismRestore: A Compact Restoration Toolbox for Agentic Image Restoration
summary: Agentic image restoration composes operations to handle mixed degradations, yet its toolbox often requires storing multiple restoration networks. We propose PrismRestore, which constructs a compact bank of callable restoration actions from a single frozen all-in-one model. Our approach builds on task-dependent yet overlapping channel responses in the shared model. An offline task-prior search uses activation and gradient statistics to group channels with similar response profiles, then searches task-specific modulation coefficients over non-representative channels while leaving representative channels unmodulated. The resulting prior bank enables explicit action selection and composition without additional restoration backbones or task-specific adapter modules. A state-conditioned policy learns to compose these actions using Group Relative Policy Optimization. Its objective separately normalizes fidelity and perceptual feedback within groups of trajectories sampled for the same input, and combines terminal evaluation with return-to-go derived from stepwise quality changes. Experiments on synthetic composite-degradation and real-world multi-task benchmarks show improvements over the evaluated all-in-one baselines and restoration quality competitive with multi-model agents. PrismRestore achieves these results with a single restoration backbone and faster inference than the evaluated agentic baselines.

AI.tldr: PrismRestore constructs a compact bank of callable restoration actions from a single frozen all-in-one model and learns a GRPO-trained policy to compose them, matching multi-model agents with faster inference.
AI.motivation: Agentic image restoration handles mixed degradations by composing operations, but typically requires storing multiple separate restoration networks.
AI.method: An offline task-prior search groups channels by activation and gradient statistics and searches task-specific modulation coefficients over non-representative channels of a single frozen all-in-one model; a state-conditioned policy then composes these actions using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with separately normalized fidelity and perceptual feedback.
AI.result: On synthetic composite-degradation and real-world multi-task benchmarks, PrismRestore outperforms evaluated all-in-one baselines and matches multi-model agentic baselines using a single backbone and faster inference.
AI.conclusion: Channel-modulated action banks paired with GRPO policy composition enable compact, fast, and effective agentic image restoration from a single backbone.

title: Unified Law for Visual Tasks (The Four Laws of Computer Vision)
comment: Preview version (main paper only); This work began in December 2024. Project page at this https URL GitHub org at this https URL Hugging Face org at this https URL This is an empirical article that attempts to unify thousands of visual tasks through a single methodology. Patent pending (inventors: SF and DM)
summary: In this paper, we propose a Unified Law for Visual Tasks, which could be further divided into Four Laws of Computer Vision, with the goal of enabling a single framework or method to uniformly train on and perform nearly all visual tasks. Our starting point is an inspiration and hypothesis: if the world information is encoded into image, which we call World Snapshots, then image processing is world processing, and image generation is World Snapshot generation. Furthermore, if all visual and visualization tasks can be reformulated as generation tasks, then a unified method, World Snapshot Models (WSMs), can perform the vast majority of visual tasks, much as large language models have largely unified natural language processing. This paper validates these laws across more than 1,000 trained and evaluated visual tasks (defined by distinct input-output mappings) and presents a unified training framework for future visual-task research and applications.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the Unified Law for Visual Tasks (Four Laws of Computer Vision) and World Snapshot Models (WSMs), reformulating visual tasks as World Snapshot generation and validating the approach across over 1,000 visual tasks.
AI.motivation: Unlike NLP, which has been largely unified by large language models, computer vision remains fragmented across task-specific architectures and training objectives.
AI.method: Treating images as World Snapshots encoding world information, the authors reformulate visual and visualization tasks as generation tasks defined by input-output mappings and train unified World Snapshot Models (WSMs) under a single framework.
AI.result: The proposed laws and unified training framework are validated across more than 1,000 trained and evaluated visual tasks.
AI.conclusion: Framing visual tasks as World Snapshot generation provides a promising path toward a single unified paradigm for computer vision.

title: UltraTex: Aligning Physical Knowledge for High-Fidelity PBR Texture Generation
comment: Accepted to ACM Transactions on Graphics (SIGGRAPH Asia 2026). Project page: this https URL
summary: Generating physically based rendering (PBR) texture maps for a 3D mesh from a single reference image is highly ambiguous, as the observed appearance entangles material identity, surface reflectance, and illumination. While current generative methods produce realistic albedo maps, they still struggle to infer accurate metallic and roughness attributes for relighting. We present UltraTex, a cascaded multi-view framework that moves beyond appearance matching by integrating physical knowledge into multi-view diffusion-based PBR generation. UltraTex first jointly predicts albedo and world-space shading normals to generate more detailed albedo maps, and then predicts metallic-roughness (MR) maps conditioned on the generated albedo, reference image, and material semantic priors. To inject material semantics, a lightweight adapter transforms hidden-layer features of a vision-language model (VLM) into intrinsic material representation tokens, providing part-level knowledge anchors for MR estimation. To model material-light interaction, photometric representation alignment guides intermediate diffusion features toward ground-truth material renderings under controlled lighting. This makes metallic and roughness variations observable through highlight intensity, specular sharpness, and local reflectance contrast, providing stronger guidance for fine-grained material prediction without explicit lighting supervision. Extensive experiments show that UltraTex generates high-quality textures and outperforms existing open-source and commercial methods in visual fidelity, material accuracy, and physical plausibility.

AI.tldr: UltraTex is a cascaded multi-view diffusion framework that integrates VLM material semantics and photometric alignment for 3D PBR texture generation, outperforming open-source and commercial methods.
AI.motivation: Generating PBR textures for a 3D mesh from a single reference image is ambiguous because appearance entangles material identity, reflectance, and illumination, causing existing methods to struggle with metallic and roughness attributes.
AI.method: UltraTex first jointly predicts albedo and world-space shading normals, then predicts metallic-roughness (MR) maps conditioned on albedo, reference image, VLM-derived material representation tokens, and photometric representation alignment toward ground-truth material renderings under controlled lighting.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show UltraTex generates high-fidelity textures and outperforms existing open-source and commercial methods in visual fidelity, material accuracy, and physical plausibility.
AI.conclusion: Injecting VLM material semantics and photometric lighting-interaction alignment resolves material-illumination ambiguity for accurate 3D PBR texture generation.

title: torchtest2: One-Call Sanity Checks for PyTorch Models,Evaluated on Real and Unseen Architectures
summary: Many bugs in deep learning code are silent: a layer that is never called, an optimizer created before the classification head was replaced, a recurrent layer that treats the batch as time, or an ignored attention mask. The code runs, the loss decreases somewhat, and the defect surfaces, if ever, after days of GPU time. We present torchtest2, an open-source library that runs 18 sanity checks on a single batch with one call, restores the PyTorch state it touches, and adapts to model families through plugins. We evaluate it by mutation analysis with 17 classes of silent bugs on 103 models from torchvision, timm and Hugging Face transformers, on 600 random architectures and on 20 hand-written realistic bugs, against the checks of the original torchtest, overfitting a single batch, a smoke test and a training monitor in the style of AUTOTRAINER and DeepDiagnosis. Every mutant is compared with its healthy counterpart, and intervals come from a bootstrap over models. After freezing the tool, we ran it on 191 models of architecture families it had never seen: counting, for every tool alike, a failing report where the healthy model's report does not fail, it detected 78% of the injected bugs (95% CI 75-80), against 40% for the original torchtest checks and 48% for the training monitor. On real models its batch-independence check found a bug in timm's GCViT that couples the images of a batch. Real models also exposed false alarms that neither the tool's own test suite nor random architectures had revealed. Two independent collections of real silent bugs mark the limits of the approach: only 3 of 28 reproduced PyTorch bugs from Stack Overflow and 3 of the 18 silent training errors released with TrainCheck are within reach of a pre-training model tester. A median check takes 1.0 s. We release the library, the benchmark and all raw results.

AI.tldr: torchtest2 is an open-source library running 18 single-batch sanity checks in ~1.0 s to catch silent PyTorch model bugs, detecting 78% of injected bugs on 191 unseen architectures.
AI.motivation: Silent bugs in deep learning code—such as unused layers, stale optimizers, or ignored attention masks—allow training to run and waste days of GPU time before surfacing.
AI.method: torchtest2 runs 18 one-call sanity checks on a single batch, restores touched PyTorch state, adapts to model families via plugins, and is evaluated via mutation analysis (17 bug classes) across 103 real models, 600 random architectures, 20 hand-written bugs, and 191 unseen-family models.
AI.result: On 191 unseen-family models, torchtest2 detects 78% of injected bugs (95% CI 75-80) versus 40% for original torchtest checks and 48% for a training monitor, with a median runtime of 1.0 s; it also uncovered a real batch-coupling bug in timm's GCViT, though it reaches only 3/28 Stack Overflow PyTorch bugs and 3/18 TrainCheck errors.
AI.conclusion: Fast, one-call single-batch sanity checks catch a large fraction of silent architectural bugs before expensive training runs, while complementarily leaving runtime training-loop errors to dynamic monitors.

title: Asymmetric Optical Image Watermarking
summary: Watermark detectors held by a provider cannot be checked by third parties, and a party that can detect a mark can usually also forge it. We study a two-layer image watermark in which the Fourier transform at the core of the pipeline is performed by a coherent optical 4F unit. Layer 1 carries an Ed25519 signature bound to the image content in Fourier magnitudes, so anyone with the public key verifies offline. Layer 2 is a key-defined carrier written by a secret phase hologram and read by a matched-filter correlator. The optics is a scalar-diffraction simulation with finite modulator bits, pixel aperture, pupil, defocus, misalignment, and sensor noise. No hardware is built. All criteria were fixed in a hashed specification before any optical result. The simulated optical signer reproduces the digital pipeline (field error 1.7e-15, bit agreement 99.997%), verifies at least 99.5% of 877 images under each of 8 post-sensor settings, one unattacked, and accepts none of 40,670 unmarked images. The optical carrier is key-selective: the matched key detects it on 99.8% of the unattacked images, and detection falls to 0% under a scale error of 1% and to 0% under a mask shift of 1 bin. Security rests on the signature and the content binding, for which we separate what is provable from what is measured.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a two-layer asymmetric optical image watermark using a simulated coherent optical 4F unit, achieving 99.5%+ public-key verification and 99.8% key-selective optical carrier detection with zero false accepts.
AI.motivation: Provider-held watermark detectors cannot be verified by third parties, and parties able to detect a mark can usually forge it.
AI.method: Using scalar-diffraction simulation of a coherent optical 4F unit (without physical hardware), Layer 1 embeds an Ed25519 signature bound to image content in Fourier magnitudes for offline public-key verification, while Layer 2 writes a key-defined carrier via a secret phase hologram read by a matched-filter correlator.
AI.result: The simulated optical signer reproduces the digital pipeline (field error 1.7e-15, bit agreement 99.997%), verifies at least 99.5% of 877 images across 8 post-sensor settings, accepts 0 of 40,670 unmarked images, and detects the optical carrier on 99.8% of unattacked images while dropping to 0% under 1% scale error or 1-bin mask shift.
AI.conclusion: Combining cryptographic Fourier-magnitude signatures with key-selective optical phase carriers enables publicly verifiable yet unforgeable optical image watermarking in simulation.

title: Streaming Generative Video Compression with Embedding Alignment and In-Context Propagation
comment: 15 pages, 18 figures, 5 tables, including supplementary material
summary: Video compression at ultra-low bitrates presents substantial challenges in preserving perceptual quality. Although pretrained video diffusion transformers (DiTs) provide powerful generative priors, existing generative video compression (GVC) methods built on them typically rely on computationally expensive VAE decoders to reconstruct video frames. Moreover, jointly refining multiple frames to exploit the inherent spatiotemporal modeling capabilities of video DiTs introduces additional buffering delay. To address these challenges, we propose SGVC, a streaming generative video compression framework that adapts a pretrained latent video DiT into a causal pixel-space refiner. Specifically, SGVC projects decoded features from a contextual pixel codec directly into the DiT input embedding space. To bridge the representation gap between codec-derived embeddings and pretrained DiT embeddings, we introduce Embedding Alignment, which aligns the projected embeddings with input embeddings extracted from the original frames during training. The refined DiT hidden states are then mapped directly to the pixel domain through a lightweight reconstruction path, bypassing the pretrained VAE decoder. To further exploit the spatiotemporal priors of the video DiT while maintaining causal decoding, we introduce In-Context Propagation, which reuses layer-wise K/V states across frames to exploit historical generative context, improving temporal consistency without requiring clip-wise buffering. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SGVC achieves competitive rate-perception performance, with average BD-rate savings of 71.97% over S$^2$VC in terms of DISTS. Project Page: this https URL

AI.tldr: SGVC is a streaming generative video compression framework that adapts a pretrained video DiT into a causal pixel-space refiner via Embedding Alignment and In-Context Propagation, achieving 71.97% average BD-rate savings over S^2VC in DISTS.
AI.motivation: Existing DiT-based generative video compression methods rely on expensive VAE decoders and multi-frame buffering, causing high compute cost and latency.
AI.method: SGVC projects contextual pixel-codec features into the DiT embedding space using Embedding Alignment against original-frame embeddings, maps refined DiT hidden states directly to pixels via a lightweight path bypassing the VAE decoder, and reuses layer-wise K/V states across frames via In-Context Propagation for causal temporal consistency.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show SGVC achieves competitive rate-perception performance with average BD-rate savings of 71.97% over S^2VC in terms of DISTS.
AI.conclusion: Bypassing VAE decoding and propagating causal K/V context turns pretrained video DiTs into low-latency, high-efficiency streaming video compression refiners.

title: Lossless Reversible Watermarking for AIGC with Applications in Authentication
summary: AIGC watermarking is commonly used for tracing, but it can also support applications such as authentication and tampering detection. We study lossless reversible watermarking, which enables exact recovery of the original watermarked image after permissible distortions. By exploiting the relatively low entropy of the information required for image generation, together with robust latent-space watermarking, we design a framework that preserves sufficient information for lossless recovery. We then apply the framework to AIGC authentication, which generally faces two key challenges. First, the authentication mechanism must resist adaptive adversaries. Second, the content relevant to authentication, such as visual designs or expressed messages, may depend on application requirements that are not known at generation time. To solve these difficulties, we incorporate cryptographic message authentication to provide unforgeability against adaptive attacks. Lossless recovery provides the original image as reference evidence, after which a suitable analyzer can be selected to make the authentication decision. Experiments on Stable Diffusion demonstrate exact recovery under a wide range of distortions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a lossless reversible watermarking framework for AIGC that enables exact recovery of watermarked images under permissible distortions and supports unforgeable authentication against adaptive adversaries.
AI.motivation: AIGC watermarking can support authentication and tampering detection, but authentication must resist adaptive adversaries and accommodate application-specific criteria unknown at generation time.
AI.method: The framework combines the low entropy of image-generation information with robust latent-space watermarking to enable lossless recovery of the original watermarked image, and incorporates cryptographic message authentication for unforgeability so an analyzer can verify the recovered reference image.
AI.result: Experiments on Stable Diffusion demonstrate exact recovery of watermarked images under a wide range of distortions.
AI.conclusion: Pairing lossless reversible latent watermarking with cryptographic message authentication provides flexible, adversary-resistant AIGC authentication.

title: LIC-Audit: How Comparable Are Reported Gains in Learned Image Compression?
summary: Learned image compression (LIC) papers often report BD-rate improvements of only a few percent. They are measured against VTM reference software whose version keeps changing: the claims we audit name 7 versions, 5 in 2025 papers alone. But how comparable are these numbers across papers, and what evidence should future papers give for such small gains? We introduce LIC-Audit, an analysis of 353 released rate-distortion curves from 36 repositories, and a controlled re-evaluation of eight public codec releases with 28,193 encode-decode records. We identify three problems. First, different VTM reference runs change BD-rates by up to 3.56 percentage points, and on CLIC Pro published numbers order 10 of 55 method pairs differently from a common computation; comparing codecs directly over a fixed quality range removes this dependence. Second, releases use different and mostly undocumented conventions for counting bits, computing PSNR, and padding images. Under consistent measurement, the GLIC method's 1.00% lead over the HPCM method on Tecnick becomes a 1.43% deficit, changing only the padding reverses the comparison of HPCM and CMIC, and most gaps narrow when MS-SSIM replaces PSNR. Third, average curves hide how much results vary from image to image, so whether a small gain is statistically significant depends on the assumed variation. An optimistic assumption calls 12.0% of comparisons between equally good codecs significant on test sets as small as Kodak, instead of 5%; a cautious one leaves 18 of 45 differences between recent codecs undecided, yet per-image results show 12 of them to be significant. Beyond auditing past results, LIC-Audit provides a versioned evaluation protocol, a public leaderboard website with a scoring tool, source-linked benchmark data, per-image measurements, and reporting guidelines, to help future LIC papers make comparable and verifiable claims of progress.

AI.tldr: LIC-Audit analyzes 353 rate-distortion curves and re-evaluates 8 public learned image compression codecs, revealing that varying VTM versions, undocumented measurement conventions, and image-level variance can reverse reported BD-rate rankings.
AI.motivation: Learned image compression papers often report small BD-rate gains against changing VTM reference versions, making it unclear how comparable or statistically significant these claims are.
AI.method: The authors audit 353 curves from 36 repositories and re-evaluate 8 public codec releases (28,193 encode-decode records) under consistent bit-counting, PSNR/MS-SSIM, and padding conventions, alongside statistical significance analysis and a versioned evaluation protocol.
AI.result: Different VTM runs shift BD-rates by up to 3.56 percentage points and reorder 10 of 55 pairs on CLIC Pro; consistent measurement turns GLIC's 1.00% lead over HPCM on Tecnick into a 1.43% deficit and reverses HPCM vs. CMIC via padding alone; per-image analysis resolves 12 of 18 undecided codec differences.
AI.conclusion: Standardized measurement conventions, fixed-quality-range comparisons, and per-image statistical reporting are essential for reliable progress claims in learned image compression.

title: Gaussian Splatoms: Direct Atomic Structure Identification in Electron Tomography
summary: Atomic electron tomography (AET) computationally reconstructs the 3D atomic structure of materials from a series of 2D projection measurements acquired at different tilt angles. Inspired by Gaussian splatting techniques from computer vision, we introduce an atom-centric parameterization for modeling AET samples. Instead of a conventional volumetric representation with a grid of voxels, we model the sample as a list of atoms, where each atom is a 3D Gaussian characterized by learned location, scale, and amplitude. The Gaussian model is a natural fit for atoms that allows us to easily incorporate prior information grounded in physics; we impose isotropy of atoms, a minimum interatomic distance, and realistic atomic radii. We show in simulation that our method is more robust than volumetric baselines to real-world imaging challenges, including a limited number of measurements and low electron dose. We further show that our method yields a more physically plausible reconstruction of an experimental 23,000 atom iron-platinum nanoparticle than a previously published volumetric reconstruction. Beyond tomography, our representation is a promising tool for any atomic resolution imaging modality (e.g. multislice electron ptychography).

AI.tldr: Gaussian Splatoms models atomic electron tomography samples as a list of isotropic 3D Gaussians representing individual atoms, yielding more robust and physically plausible reconstructions than volumetric baselines.
AI.motivation: Conventional voxel-grid volumetric reconstructions in atomic electron tomography struggle with limited tilt measurements and low electron doses.
AI.method: Inspired by Gaussian splatting, the method represents a sample as a list of 3D Gaussian atoms with learned location, scale, and amplitude, incorporating physical priors including atom isotropy, minimum interatomic distance, and realistic atomic radii.
AI.result: In simulation, the method is more robust than volumetric baselines to limited measurements and low electron dose, and on an experimental 23,000-atom iron-platinum nanoparticle it yields a more physically plausible reconstruction than prior volumetric results.
AI.conclusion: Atom-centric 3D Gaussian parameterization with physical priors offers a promising reconstruction framework for atomic-resolution imaging modalities.

title: RageVLA: Augmentation-Trained Perception and Action for State-of-the-Art Robustness on LIBERO
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models look saturated on LIBERO, yet most of them fall apart on LIBERO-PRO as soon as an object moves or the instruction asks for something new. We argue that what is missing is not scale but decoupling. In these policies, what to do is tied to where things were during training, to the scene around them and to the wording of the instruction. We cut these ties in two places. In the data, LIBERO demonstrations are re-arranged by general rules: every object and fixture is moved and rotated, tasks are carried into other environments and onto other surfaces, and every instruction is paraphrased. In the policy, a perception engine on frozen DINOv3 features, trained on this augmented data, hands the action model the scene in decoupled form: a list of objects with their positions, and a compact code of what the gripper is looking at, next to image and instruction embeddings from TinyCLIP. A flow-matching diffusion transformer, trained from scratch, acts on this view. We call this combination of Robust Augmentation and Grounded Encoding RageVLA. With 0.21 billion parameters, RageVLA sets a new state of the art on LIBERO-PRO among VLA policies, scoring 0.72 against 0.53 for the best published model, and a larger variant reaches 0.73. Two further tests on LIBERO-Object show that the policy acts on what it perceives. When the object positions it is given are shuffled while the camera images stay correct, its success falls from 0.965 to 0.215. When the target object is displaced by 28 cm, it still succeeds in 0.865 of the episodes, where $\pi_{0.5}$, run through the same harness, succeeds in 0.105.

AI.tldr: RageVLA decouples perception and action via rule-based data augmentation and a DINOv3/TinyCLIP-grounded flow-matching diffusion transformer, setting a new state of the art of 0.72 (0.73 larger variant) on LIBERO-PRO.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action (VLA) models saturate LIBERO but fail on LIBERO-PRO when objects move or instructions are paraphrased because policies couple actions to training positions, backgrounds, and exact wording.
AI.method: RageVLA augments LIBERO demonstrations by moving/rotating objects and fixtures, changing environments, and paraphrasing instructions; a perception engine on frozen DINOv3 features outputs decoupled object positions and gripper views alongside TinyCLIP embeddings, feeding a flow-matching diffusion transformer trained from scratch.
AI.result: With 0.21B parameters, RageVLA scores 0.72 on LIBERO-PRO (0.73 for a larger variant) versus 0.53 for the best published model; on LIBERO-Object, shuffling object positions drops success from 0.965 to 0.215, while displacing the target by 28 cm retains 0.865 success versus 0.105 for pi_0.5.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling grounded object-centric perception from action via systematic augmentation dramatically improves VLA generalization to object displacement and instruction variation without massive scale.

title: Facet-SLAM: Real-Time Triangle Splatting SLAM
summary: Dense SLAM systems based on 3D Gaussian splatting build maps that render photorealistically, but their surface geometry is poor, and obtaining a mesh requires extraction or fusion stages. Triangle splatting avoids this with surface primitives whose vertices can be triangulated directly into a connected mesh, yet SLAM with this representation has so far relied on photometric tracking, which is too slow for localization at sensor rate. We present Facet-SLAM, the first real-time triangle splatting SLAM system for RGB-D cameras. Fast geometric registration is the natural alternative, but it is not sufficient alone, since the mapper's optimization displaces triangles from the observed surface and makes them unreliable registration targets. We therefore separate the two roles: the tracker sets each triangle's centroid from fused depth and registers frames to these centroids by GICP, while the mapper is restricted to non-translating updates via a change of variables. Our system achieves competitive tracking accuracy at around 100 FPS on a desktop GPU and runs at sensor rate on a Jetson AGX Orin.
